topics.title: Design the before and after, not only the event
topics.theory: The pre, during and post framework

situation.text: All the effort goes into the day itself. Nothing happens before it, and nothing after.

items: Before: set expectations, wake up what people already know, and have the manager conversation.
Ask a few questions before teaching, even if people get them wrong.
After: schedule recall, a task to apply, and a check-in.
Tell learners their part: prepare, use it soon, teach someone, come back to it.

why.text: The event is the middle third. A well-run session with no preparation and no follow-up fades in a predictable way.

Trying to answer questions before learning, even wrongly, can improve what is remembered later, as long as people then meet the right answers. The gain is mostly for the points you asked about. It is a form of generation.

why.title: The pretesting effect
why.found: In five experiments, people who tried to answer questions about a text before reading it did better on a later test than people given extra reading time. This held even for questions they had got wrong at the start.
why.means: Open with a few questions on the points that matter most, then make sure the session answers them.

items.title: The middle third
items.text: The event is one part of three.

items.title: Ask first
items.text: A question before teaching primes the answer.

try.text: Map before, during and after for a real programme. Write one action for each phase, for you and for the learner.

try.title: Illustration: one programme in three parts
try.text: Before: three questions by email and a short talk with the manager. During: the session answers those three questions. After: a recall quiz in week one, one task to try on the job, and a twenty-minute check-in in week four.

items: Pre-work that is not used in the room teaches people to skip it.
Follow-up needs an owner and a date, or it does not happen.
Keep pre-work short.
Pre-questions work best for clearly stated facts. They help less with questions that need complex reasoning, and most of the evidence comes from students in laboratory studies.

quiz.q: Why ask questions before teaching?
quiz.a: Trying to answer, even wrongly, can improve later memory.

quiz.q: What should a learner do soon after the event?
quiz.a: Use what they learned.

topics.title: Design for the kind of programme it is
topics.theory: Programme types: onboarding, leadership development, compliance

situation.text: You use the same design for induction, a leadership course and fire safety.

items: Name the type of programme.
Induction: what people need in week one, then spread the rest.
Compliance: aim at what people do, and test that.
Leadership: practice on real work, over months.
Technical skills: worked examples, then practice with feedback.

why.text: Programmes differ in what success means. Induction succeeds when someone can do the job and feels they belong. Compliance succeeds when behaviour is safe and lawful. Leadership development succeeds when people lead differently.
Copying one format across all of them ignores those differences.

Research supports two of these directly. A meta-analysis of newcomers found that being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job and feeling accepted by colleagues link induction to later performance and staying. A meta-analysis of leadership training found better results with practice, feedback and sessions spread over time.

items.title: Name the type
items.text: Each has its own test of success.

try.text: Take two programmes of different types. For each, write what success would look like on the job.

try.title: Illustration: one topic, two tests of success
try.text: Fire safety. Before: a slide module and a pass mark. After: each person walks their own exit route and shows where the nearest extinguisher is. Leadership. Before: a two-day course. After: one skill practised with their own team each month.

items: Compliance training built only to prove attendance may change little.
Induction overloads week one.
Leadership courses are often events with no practice.

topics.title: Design for people early in their career
topics.theory: Early-career learners: onboarding, graduates and apprentices

situation.text: The audience is graduates and apprentices in their first job. Much of your material assumes they know how a workplace runs.

items: Check what they know. Assume little about the workplace and a lot about their ability.
Use worked examples and plenty of structure.
Teach the unwritten rules: who to ask, how to raise a problem.
Build belonging and an early win.
Involve their line manager or buddy.

why.text: Seniority and knowledge are different things. People early in a career are usually beginners in the job, so the guidance for beginners applies: more structure, more examples, support that fades.

There is no good evidence that generations learn in different ways. Research on generations at work finds small differences or none, and very few studies have tested training by generation. Age, career stage and experience explain more.

A meta-analysis of 70 samples of newcomers found three signs of settling in: being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job and feeling accepted. These linked what the organisation did, and how much newcomers sought information, to later performance, satisfaction and staying. That is the case for teaching the unwritten rules openly.

why.title: How newcomers settle in
why.found: Across 70 samples, role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance carried the effect of an organisation's induction practices and of newcomers' information seeking through to job performance, satisfaction, commitment and staying.
why.means: Design early-career programmes to build clarity, confidence and acceptance, as well as knowledge.

try.text: Take a session written for experienced staff. Mark every assumption about the workplace a newcomer would miss.

try.title: Illustration: an assumption made visible
try.text: Before: "Escalate anything unusual to the duty manager." After: who the duty manager is today, how to reach them, what counts as unusual, and a sample message. Then a practice case, with the sample message removed the second time.

items: Do not talk down. New is not the same as slow.
A beginner in a room of experts will not ask.
Their manager shapes whether any of it is used.

topics.title: Design for managers and senior leaders

situation.text: The audience is managers. They are short of time, sceptical, and have been on leadership courses before.

items: Start from a problem they have this month.
Keep input short. Spend the time on practice with real cases.
Use their experience: have them advise each other.
Set a task to try with their own team.
Follow up, with their own manager involved.

why.text: Managers bring experience, so support aimed at beginners can get in their way. They also bring habits, and habits change through practice and feedback on real work.

A meta-analysis of 335 samples found that leadership training works on average. Programmes did better when they were built on a needs analysis, gave feedback, used several methods including practice, and spread sessions over time. Face-to-face and on-site delivery were also linked with better results.

why.title: A meta-analysis of leadership training
why.found: Across 335 samples, leadership training improved reactions, learning, behaviour at work and results. It was more effective when based on a needs analysis, when it included feedback and practice, and when sessions were spaced, on site and face to face.
why.means: Build a leadership programme from a diagnosed need, with practice and feedback in every session and gaps between sessions.

items.title: Over time
items.text: One event rarely changes how people lead.

try.text: Take a leadership topic. Design ninety minutes with no more than fifteen minutes of input.

try.title: Illustration: ninety minutes on difficult conversations
try.text: Ten minutes of input on one way to open the conversation. Sixty minutes in threes, each manager rehearsing a real conversation they are due to have while the others give feedback. Twenty minutes to plan when they will hold it and who will ask how it went.

items: Experienced people can be beginners in a new skill.
Status makes it hard to practise in front of peers. Build safety.
Models with neat names sell well. Check the evidence.
The meta-analysis pools many kinds of programme. It shows what tends to go with better results, not that any one design will work in your setting.

topics.title: Design for executives
topics.theory: Executive education: short time, status in the room and learning from peers

situation.text: You have ninety minutes with an executive team. Phones are on the table and nobody wants to be taught.

items: Agree with the sponsor what one decision or change the session is for.
Send a one-page brief in advance.
Open with their data or their problem.
Have them work with each other. You facilitate.
End with who will do what, by when.
Offer a private follow-up.

why.text: Executives have little time and much at stake in front of peers. Being seen not to know can feel costly, so safety is likely to matter more as rank rises. In practice they often give more weight to the views of peers than to those of a trainer.
These are observations from practice. The research on what works for executives in particular is thin.

One piece of research does bear on the safety point. A study of 51 teams in a manufacturing company found that teams whose members felt safe to take risks with each other showed more learning behaviour, and that this went with better team performance. It studied ordinary work teams, not executives.

items.title: Status
items.text: Not knowing is costly. Protect people.

try.text: Design a ninety-minute executive session with one purpose and no more than ten minutes of input.

try.title: Illustration: one purpose
try.text: Before: "An update on customer complaints for the executive team." After: "By the end, the team agrees which two complaint types to fix first and who owns each." The one-page brief carries the data, so the ninety minutes go on the decision.

items: The most senior person can close the room down by speaking first.
Do not simplify the content. Shorten it.
A session with no decision is forgotten.

topics.title: Know the learner's working day before you design
topics.theory: The modern learner and their context

situation.text: The design assumes people will do an hour of pre-work at a quiet desk. Your learners work shifts on a shop floor.

items: Find out when, where and on what device people can learn.
Ask what interrupts them.
Fit the design to that: shorter pieces, offline access, protected time.
Ask managers to release the time.
Test with two or three real learners.

why.text: A design that does not fit the working day is unlikely to be used. Time, place, device and interruptions decide whether people can take part at all.

The popular claim of a fixed, short attention span is not supported. A review of lecture studies found no good data for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes. People are busy and interrupted, which is a different problem with a different answer.

Designing by generation is not supported either. A meta-analysis of 20 studies and about 20,000 people found that generations differed little or not at all in job satisfaction, commitment and intention to leave. A 2020 report from the US National Academies concluded that generational labels are not a sound basis for managing people. It found that age, career stage, experience and working conditions explain more, and that people within a generation differ about as much as people across generations.
Very few studies have tested training by generation at all. Ask about each group's working day, experience and role, and design for those.

why.title: Generations at work, a meta-analysis
why.found: Pooling 20 studies and 19,961 people across four generations, the differences in job satisfaction, commitment to the organisation and intention to leave were small and in many cases close to zero. The authors concluded that meaningful generational differences probably do not exist for these attitudes.
why.means: Do not build separate designs for age cohorts. Find out about people's roles, experience and working conditions.

try.text: Shadow or interview two learners about a normal day. List three changes your design needs.

try.title: Illustration: a design refitted to a shift
try.text: Before: sixty minutes of online pre-work on a desktop. After: three five-minute pieces that work on the shared tablet in the break room, with ten minutes released at the start of a shift and a printed card for the shop floor.

items: Mobile-friendly does not mean a phone is the right place to learn it.
Learning in people's own time has a cost. Say who bears it.
Do not design around generations.

parts.title: Design the course
parts.summary: Objectives, design models, sequencing and pace.

topics.title: Write objectives you could observe

situation.text: The course aims say people will "understand" and "be aware of". Nobody can tell whether it worked.

items: Start from what people must be able to do at the end.
Write each objective as something you could watch someone do.
Decide how you will assess it before you plan the teaching.
Check every activity and every assessment against an objective. Cut what matches none.

why.text: Designing backwards means choosing the capability first, then the assessment, then the teaching. Objectives, activities and assessment must point at the same target. When they do not, the course is misaligned, and people are taught one thing and assessed on another.

Bloom's taxonomy is a useful ladder for pitching the level of thinking. The 2001 revision names six levels: remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate and create. Its authors say the levels overlap, so use it as a guide, not a strict hierarchy.

items.title: Observable
items.text: If you cannot see it, you cannot assess it.

try.text: Take a set of vague aims. Rewrite them as observable objectives. Check each activity and assessment against them.

try.title: Illustration: an aim rewritten
try.text: Before: "Understand the complaints process." After: "Given a written complaint, log it, choose the right category and send the holding reply within the standard time." The assessment is three sample complaints handled at a desk.

items: Tightly specified objectives can narrow learning. Leave room for judgement.
Higher-order skills are harder to write as objectives. Describe the performance, not a checklist.
An objective nobody assesses is a wish.

quiz.q: What is wrong with "understand"?
quiz.a: You cannot observe it, so you cannot assess it.

quiz.q: What is the order in backward design?
quiz.a: Capability, then assessment, then teaching.

quiz.q: What is alignment?
quiz.a: Objectives, activities and assessment all point at the same target.

openPoints: Mager, Preparing Instructional Objectives: not searched for or opened.

The publisher page for Understanding by Design does not spell out the three stages of backward design. The order 'capability, then assessment, then teaching' fits the chapter order but was not read in the publisher's own words.
The watch item that tightly specified objectives can narrow learning has no checked source.
checkFindings: Biggs (1996) confirmed. It sets out constructive alignment: objectives stated as performances, teaching activities chosen to produce them, and assessment of the same performances. This supports the alignment paragraph.

Wiggins and McTighe confirmed on the Pearson page for the expanded second edition, which Pearson published with ASCD. The page lists backward design as the first chapter and has chapters on thinking like an assessor before planning the teaching. The ASCD page itself was not among the search results.

Anderson and Krathwohl (2001) was not opened as a book. Krathwohl (2002) is the short overview of that revision by one of its editors and is listed in its place. The Bloom sentence now gives the six revised levels and the reason it is not a strict hierarchy.
Mager is removed from the list because it could not be opened.
topics.tierReason: Backward design and constructive alignment are widely used design frameworks set out in books and conceptual papers. No experimental test of them was opened.

topics.title: Use design models as checklists, not rules
topics.theory: ADDIE, SAM, Gagné and Merrill, used critically

situation.text: Someone insists the project must follow ADDIE, or SAM, step by step.

items: Learn the main models well enough to borrow from each.
Use ADDIE as a list of phases not to forget.
Prototype early when the brief is uncertain.
Use Gagné or Merrill to check a single lesson has the parts it needs.
Pick and blend to fit the project. Say why.

why.text: ADDIE (analyse, design, develop, implement, evaluate) is a useful checklist. Its critics say it is dated and less efficient than iterative ways of working. SAM, the Successive Approximation Model, is an iterative alternative that its authors present as simpler. Gagné offers a sequence for one lesson. Merrill centres learning on real problems.
These are lenses, not laws. Kolb's learning cycle is influential and its evidence is contested.

items.title: Lenses, not laws
items.text: Choose the model that fits the project.

items.title: Prototype early
items.text: A rough version teaches you more than a plan.

items.title: Check the lesson
items.text: Does it have a real problem, activation, demonstration, application and integration?

try.text: Take one real project. Say which model or blend you would use, given its constraints.

try.title: Illustration: blending for one project
try.text: A new product launches in six weeks and the brief keeps changing. Use the ADDIE phases as a list so evaluation is not forgotten. Build a rough first session in week one and test it with three people. Check each lesson has a real problem, a demonstration and practice.

items: A model can become a ritual. Ask what each step is for.
Clients may expect the model they know. Explain your choice in their terms.
Do not teach Kolb's cycle as proven.
The case for SAM over ADDIE is made by SAM's own authors. Treat it as an argument, not a tested result.

topics.title: Start with full support, then take it away

situation.text: Newcomers are thrown at a full problem on the first morning and sink.

items: Break content into pieces small enough to hold.
Begin with a fully worked example.
Move to part-worked problems, where people finish the solution.
End with problems solved alone.
Remove each support once people no longer need it.

why.text: Structure is not neutral. A sequence that starts with full support and withdraws it lets a newcomer climb without overload. This applies the expertise reversal effect: support that helps at first holds people back later.

There is a competing finding. Letting people struggle with a problem before teaching can work better under some conditions. One reading is that the two bodies of evidence meet on prior knowledge: struggle is more likely to help people who know enough to learn from it.

why.title: The expertise reversal effect
why.found: This review brings together studies showing that the teaching methods that work best change with what the learner already knows. Guidance that helps beginners can stop helping, or get in the way, once people know more.
why.means: Check prior knowledge first, start beginners with full support and take each support away as they improve.

items.title: Fade the support
items.text: Take it away as skill grows.

items.title: Prerequisites first
items.text: Teach what the next thing depends on.

try.text: Take one topic. Design a progression from worked example to independent practice, with support that fades.

try.title: Illustration: fading on one task
try.text: Reading a customer invoice. First, a fully worked invoice with each check explained. Next, an invoice with the first three checks done and two left to finish. Last, a fresh invoice with no notes. People who pass a quick check at the start skip to the last one.

items: Support left in place too long bores experienced people.
Struggle first is not a licence to leave newcomers stuck.
Check prior knowledge before choosing the starting point.

quiz.a: A part-worked problem that the learner finishes.

quiz.q: What do you do with support as skill grows?
quiz.a: Remove it.

quiz.q: Who benefits from struggling before being taught?
quiz.a: Most likely people who already know enough to learn from the struggle.
