topics.title: Put the hard content where the energy is
topics.theory: Pacing, attention and the energy curve

situation.text: The session runs at one flat intensity from nine to five, and the room fades after lunch.

items: Break content into segments and change the activity between them.
Plan the opening, the dips and the close on purpose.
Put demanding work where energy is high.
Where energy dips, re-order, add recall or take a break.
Treat breaks as part of the learning.

why.text: There is no fixed attention span. Attention depends on interest, difficulty and design, and on how well the session is taught. A review of lecture studies found no good data for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes.
Breaking material into segments is widely recommended to help people process it. A pause between segments also gives people time to take stock.

why.title: Attention span during lectures
why.found: This review traced the claim that attention falls after ten to fifteen minutes and found it rests mostly on repeated citation, with little sound primary data. The most consistent pattern was that attention varied with the teacher more than with the format.
why.means: Do not plan around a fixed attention limit. Plan for variety that serves the content, and work on delivery.

items.title: Do not push through a dip

try.text: Map the energy of a full-day agenda. Re-order it so demanding content sits where energy is highest.

try.title: Illustration: one day re-ordered
try.text: Before: policy update at nine, the hardest case study straight after lunch. After: the hard case study at ten, a recall quiz and paired discussion after lunch, the policy update in a short slot mid-afternoon, and a break before the close.

items: Variety for its own sake distracts. Each change should serve the content.
Do not quote a "ten-minute attention span". The source is weak.
Claims about natural attention cycles are promising, not settled.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Bradbury (2016), Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more? Advances in Physiology Education.

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Is there a fixed attention span?
quiz.a: No. Attention depends on interest, difficulty and design.

quiz.q: What do you do when energy dips?
quiz.a: Re-order, add recall or take a break. Do not push harder.

quiz.q: What are breaks for, besides rest?
quiz.a: They give people time to take stock before the next segment.

topics.tierReason: The attention span myth is well examined, but the advice on energy, breaks and placing hard content has only limited support that could be checked.
openPoints: Mayer, the segmenting principle. Not opened. Rey and colleagues (2019), a meta-analysis of the segmenting effect, is the source to check. The web search allowance for this run ran out before this could be looked up. Only pages already returned by an earlier search could be opened.
Wilson and Korn (2007), Attention during lectures: beyond ten minutes, would be a second source on the myth. Not opened.
No source was opened for an energy dip after lunch, for the effect of breaks on learning, or for natural attention cycles. The page already calls the last of these unsettled.
Bradbury (2016) is classed by PubMed as an editorial. It is a review of the literature, not a new study.
checkFindings: Replaced the attention-span placeholder with Bradbury (2016). It supports the draft's warning not to quote a ten-minute attention span. It does not address a shrinking span, so that wording was replaced with what the source examined.
Added the source's main positive finding, that attention varied more with the teacher than with the format.
The draft said memory begins to settle in the gap between segments, in the why section and in a quiz answer. No source could be opened for this, so both were softened.
Mayer's segmenting principle could not be opened. The sentence now says segmenting is widely recommended.

topics.title: Use problems, cases or enquiry when judgement is the goal

situation.text: You want people to exercise judgement. The course gives them rules and a quiz.

items: Choose a realistic problem or case with no single right answer.
Check people have the knowledge the case needs.
Have small groups work it, with a clear output.
Bring out the reasoning, not only the answer.
Close with the principles the case shows.

why.text: Problems and cases suit judgement, because people practise weighing evidence and deciding. They work when people already have enough knowledge to reason with.
For newcomers, working things out with little guidance is slow and overloading. Teach the basics directly first.

Pooled studies of problem-based courses in higher education found a clear gain in skills. Students gained slightly less knowledge, but remembered more of what they did learn. Guidance is what makes the difference. Discovery with no help did worse than direct teaching. Discovery with feedback, worked examples and prompts to explain did better than other methods.

why.title: Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
why.found: Two pooled analyses covered 164 studies. Discovery with no help did worse than explicit teaching (d = -0.38). Discovery with support such as feedback, worked examples and prompts to explain did better than other methods (d = 0.30).
why.means: Keep the problem or case, and build in guidance, feedback and a debrief.

items.title: Knowledge first
items.text: People reason with what they know.

items.title: Draw out the principle
items.text: Do not stop at the answer.

try.text: Write one case for your subject, with the decision to be made and the output you want from groups.

try.title: Illustrative: from rules to a case
try.text: Before: a slide of escalation rules and a five-question quiz. After: groups of three get a messy customer complaint with two defensible responses. They have 15 minutes to choose one and write their reasons. The debrief compares the reasoning, then names the principles.

items: A case with an obvious answer is a quiz.
Groups drift without a deadline and an output.
Several cases beat one. People generalise from variety.
Most of the research comes from universities and medical schools. Workplace courses are less studied, so check your own results.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Kirschner, Sweller and Clark (2006), Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work. Educational Psychologist, 41(2).
Schmidt, Loyens, Van Gog and Paas (2007), Problem-based learning is compatible with human cognitive architecture. Educational Psychologist, 42(2). A reply to Kirschner and colleagues.
Hmelo-Silver (2004), Problem-based learning: what and how do students learn? Educational Psychology Review, 16(3).
Dochy, Segers, Van den Bossche and Gijbels (2003), Effects of problem-based learning: a meta-analysis. Learning and Instruction, 13(5).
Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich and Tenenbaum (2011), Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1).

topics.bodyStatus: 5 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What are problems and cases best for?
quiz.a: Judgement.

quiz.q: What must people have first?
quiz.a: Enough knowledge to reason with.

quiz.q: How should you close a case?
quiz.a: With the principles it shows.

topics.tierReason: Pooled studies show problem-based and guided enquiry methods help skills and application, but unguided discovery does worse than direct teaching, so the result depends on prior knowledge and on how much guidance you give.
openPoints: The watch item 'Several cases beat one. People generalise from variety.' rests on the analogical transfer literature. No source for it was opened. Left unchanged.
checkFindings: Kirschner, Sweller and Clark (2006) supports the draft: guided teaching beats minimal guidance for novices, and the advantage fades once people have enough prior knowledge. No text change needed.

Added Schmidt and colleagues (2007), the published reply, because a competent reader would expect it. It accepts the point about novices but argues problem-based learning is guided, not minimally guided. This fits the draft's 'knowledge first, then cases' position.

Hmelo-Silver (2004) supports the first step (a complex problem with no single right answer, small groups, reflection). It also says most studies are in medical and gifted education. Added a watch item on that limit.

Dochy and colleagues (2003): skills clearly better, knowledge slightly lower but better retained. The draft did not mention the knowledge cost, so a paragraph was added to why. The pooled skills figure (0.46) is in the results section, not the abstract, so it is left off the page.
Alfieri and colleagues (2011) added as the study block. Both effect sizes are in the abstract.

parts.title: Design the experience
parts.summary: Who is in the room, the journey they take, and where it drags.

topics.title: Design for the range of people, not the average
topics.theory: Personas and the myth of the average learner

situation.text: The course is designed for "the typical learner". In the room, nobody is typical.

items: List the ways your learners really differ: prior knowledge, motivation, context, constraints.
Build two or three personas from real data.
Design for the edges as well as the middle.
Offer more than one way to take in content and to show learning.

why.text: Almost nobody is average on every measure, so a design aimed at the average fits few people. One person can be strong on one dimension and weak on another.
This is about real differences such as prior knowledge and context. It is not learning styles, which the evidence does not support.

items.title: Nobody is average
items.text: A design for the average fits no one.

items.title: Not learning styles
items.text: Variability is real. Teaching to styles is not supported.

try.text: Build two contrasting personas for a real course. Name one design change each one demands.

try.title: Illustrative: two personas, two changes
try.text: A spreadsheet course. Persona one is new, has never written a formula and dreads tests. Persona two is an analyst, bored by basics and short of time. Design changes: an optional primer and practice file for one, a skip-ahead challenge for the other.

items: Invented personas are stereotypes. Ground them in data.
Too many personas paralyse the design. Two or three is enough.
Designing for the edges often helps the middle too.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Rose (first published 2016, edition linked 2017), The End of Average.
CAST (2024), Universal Design for Learning Guidelines, version 3.0.
Pruitt and Grudin (2003), Personas: practice and theory. Conference on Designing for User Experiences.
Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008), Learning styles: concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3).

topics.bodyStatus: 4 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Why not design for the average learner?
quiz.a: Almost nobody is average on every measure.

quiz.q: Name three real ways learners differ.
quiz.a: Any three of: prior knowledge, motivation, context, constraints.

quiz.q: How is this different from learning styles?
quiz.a: These differences are evidenced. Matching teaching to learning styles is not.

topics.tierReason: Personas and designing for a range of people are widely used design practice with little direct testing in training. The warning about learning styles is well supported.
openPoints: The sentence 'One person can be strong on one dimension and weak on another' is a main idea in Rose's book, but the publisher's description does not state it. Left unchanged.
'Two or three personas is enough' is practitioner advice. No source confirmed a number.
checkFindings: Build note followed: 'Stefaniak (2020), Learning Experience Design' is not in the list and could not be searched for. Pruitt and Grudin (2003) is added as a verified reference for personas built from data.

Rose: the publisher's description confirms the argument that no one is average and that systems built for a typical person fail most people. The page opened is the 2017 HarperCollins edition, with the subtitle 'Unlocking our potential by embracing what makes us different'. The 2016 first edition date came from a search listing, not from the publisher page.
CAST: the current version is Guidelines 3.0, released 30 July 2024. Its three headings are multiple means of engagement, of representation, and of action and expression. This supports step four.
Pashler and colleagues (2008) added to support the learning styles sentence. Two short strings were reworded so they say what the review says.
The Pruitt and Grudin abstract supports grounding personas in qualitative and quantitative data. It does not discuss stereotypes or the right number of personas.

topics.title: Map the journey from first email to follow-up

situation.text: You have designed the day in detail. The joining instructions and the week after were left to someone else.

items: Map the whole journey: first hearing about it, pre-work, the event, first use, follow-up.
Mark the moments that can build or break motivation and belonging.
Design the first contact and the first session with care.
Design the return to work.

why.text: Two fragile parts of a programme are the start and the return to work. If you design only the event, those are left to chance.
People judge an experience largely by its most intense moment and by how it ends. That is a reason to design a strong high point and a deliberate close.

A pooled analysis found that the peak and the end shape how people rate an experience afterwards about as strongly as the average of the whole, and that length hardly matters. This is about how the programme is remembered and rated. It does not show that people learn more.

why.title: A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule
why.found: Across 174 effect sizes, ratings given after an experience were strongly related to its peak and its end (r = 0.58). That was about as strong as the link with the average of all moments. The length of the experience had almost no effect.
why.means: Design the high point and the close on purpose, and do not treat good ratings as proof of learning.

items.title: Beyond the event
items.text: The journey starts with the first email.

items.title: Moments that matter
items.text: A few points decide how it feels.

items.title: Peak and end
items.text: People remember the high point and the finish.

try.text: Map the full journey for a real course. Mark the moments that matter and design the high point and the ending.

try.title: Illustrative: a two-day course, mapped
try.text: The map shows three weak moments: a joining email with no reason to come, a flat last hour and silence afterwards. The redesign adds a short note from the manager, a closing practice round and a check-in two weeks later.

items: Intensive formats need a designed "after" most of all.
A journey map is a guess until you test it with learners.
The administration is part of the experience.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Stickdorn, Hormess, Lawrence and Schneider (2018), This Is Service Design Doing. O'Reilly.
Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber and Redelmeier (1993), When more pain is preferred to less: adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6).
Alaybek and colleagues (2022), All's well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 170.
Hoogerheide and Paas (2012), Remembered utility of unpleasant and pleasant learning experiences: is all well that ends well? Applied Cognitive Psychology, 26(6).

topics.bodyStatus: 4 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Which two parts of a programme are easily left to chance?
quiz.a: The start and the return to work.

quiz.q: What do people judge an experience by?
quiz.a: Its most intense moment and its ending.

quiz.q: Where does the journey begin?
quiz.a: When someone first hears about the programme.

topics.tierReason: Journey mapping is a service design practice with little direct testing in training. The peak-end finding is well supported for how experiences are rated afterwards, not for how much is learned.
openPoints: No source was opened for the importance of the first contact or of the return to work (the training transfer literature). The steps are left as practitioner advice.
checkFindings: The placeholder 'The outline cites the service-design literature without naming a study' is replaced with Stickdorn and colleagues (2018). The publisher's description does not mention journey maps, but the table of contents on the same page lists them in several chapters. The authors' own method page was also read. It says maps built on assumptions can mislead and should be replaced with research-based ones, which supports the watch item on testing the map with learners.

'Kahneman, the peak-end rule' is replaced with the 1993 cold-water study. The page opened is the Association for Psychological Science page for the article. It shows the abstract and journal but not the author list or year, which are taken from the standard citation.

Alaybek and colleagues (2022) confirm the peak-end effect is large, and add that the average of the experience matters about as much. The draft's 'largely by its most intense moment and by how it ends' slightly overstates this. A paragraph was added to why to give the fuller picture and to separate ratings from learning.
Hoogerheide and Paas (2012) tested the rule in a learning task with primary school children. The page opened is the record in the authors' university repository, not the journal page.
The claim that the start and the return to work are 'the most fragile' parts had no source. Softened in the paragraph and the quiz.

topics.title: Plan a peak and a proper ending
topics.theory: The emotional arc and experience mechanics

situation.text: The content is sound and the session feels flat from start to finish.

items: Open a question people want answered before you answer it.
Set tasks where challenge matches skill.
Plan one high point and build towards it.
Close on purpose. Do not run out of time.
Use story and challenge only where they carry the content.

why.text: Emotion affects attention, motivation and memory, so the feel of a course is a design matter. Curiosity arises from a gap between what people know and what they want to know. Absorption arises when challenge and skill are balanced.
Engagement is a means. A session can be enjoyable and teach little.
A planned high point and a deliberate close change how people rate and remember the session. That is worth having, but it is a rating effect. Check learning separately.

why.title: Curiosity and memory for answers
why.found: People read trivia questions and rated their curiosity. They spent tokens or waiting time to see answers they were more curious about. One to two weeks later they recalled surprising answers better when they had been more curious.
why.means: Open with a question people want answered, let them guess, then give the answer.

items.title: Match challenge to skill
items.text: Too easy bores. Too hard frightens.

try.text: Design the emotional arc of one session. Say where you create curiosity, where you aim for absorption, and how you close.

try.title: Illustrative: an arc for one session
try.text: A data protection session opens with a realistic email and one question: what went wrong here. People guess before the answer comes. The hardest case sits two thirds of the way in. The last ten minutes are a short practice and one commitment.

items: Interesting but irrelevant material can lower learning.
Game elements can backfire. See the topic on gamification.
A big finish with no follow-up is theatre.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Kang and colleagues (2009), The wick in the candle of learning: epistemic curiosity activates reward circuitry and enhances memory. Psychological Science, 20(8).
Alaybek and colleagues (2022), All's well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 170.
Park, Flowerday and Brünken (2015), Cognitive and affective effects of seductive details in multimedia learning. Computers in Human Behavior, 44.

topics.bodyStatus: 3 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Where does curiosity come from?
quiz.a: A gap between what people know and what they want to know.

quiz.q: When does absorption arise?
quiz.a: When challenge and skill are balanced.

quiz.q: Is engagement the goal?
quiz.a: No. It is a means to learning.

topics.tierReason: Single ideas here have support, such as curiosity helping memory and endings shaping ratings, but designing an emotional arc to improve learning in training has little direct testing.
openPoints: Csikszentmihalyi (1990), Flow: no publisher page could be opened, so the book is not in the list. The sentence 'Absorption arises when challenge and skill are balanced' is therefore unchecked and left unchanged.
Loewenstein (1994), The psychology of curiosity, Psychological Bulletin: the abstract page could not be opened. The theory is described in Kang and colleagues (2009), which is listed in its place.

Sundararajan and Adesope (2020), Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect, Educational Psychology Review. Found in search at link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-020-09522-4 but the page would not load. It would be a better source than Park (2015) for the watch item. A 2025 multi-level meta-analysis in the same journal (10.1007/s10648-025-10099-z) also appeared in search and was not opened.
The opening sentence 'Emotion affects attention, motivation and memory' has no opened source.
checkFindings: 'Thaler and Sunstein, Nudge' is removed. Nothing in the topic text draws on it and it was not opened.

The curiosity sentence is supported. Kang and colleagues (2009) describe the information-gap account as curiosity arising from a gap between what a person knows and wants to know, and found that higher curiosity went with better later recall. The copy read is the one hosted on a co-author's university page.
The watch item on irrelevant material was stated as a rule. The one study opened shows a mixed result, so it now says 'can'.
Alaybek and colleagues (2022) support planning a high point and a close, for ratings. A short paragraph was added so readers do not read this as a learning effect.
No effect size is given for this topic because none of the sources tests the whole practice.

topics.title: Remove the friction that frustrates, keep the friction that teaches

situation.text: Learners complain the course is hard. Some of that difficulty teaches. Some is the login page.

items: List every point where learners struggle.
Sort each one: does it teach, or does it only frustrate?
Remove the second kind: confusing navigation, unclear instructions, admin, technical barriers.
Keep the first kind: recall, effort, working it out.

why.text: Some friction is the effort that builds lasting learning. Some is waste. Confusing the two is a common and costly mistake, because smoothing everything removes the learning along with the annoyance.
Polish does not replace effectiveness. A good-looking course can still fail to teach.

The difficulties that help include spacing, recall from memory, mixing topics and making errors you then correct. A difficulty stops being useful when people lack the background to overcome it. Learners often feel they are learning less under these conditions, which is why they ask for them to be removed.
Trying a problem before being taught is one such difficulty. Pooled studies found it beat teaching first, by a moderate margin. Younger children did better when taught first.

why.title: When problem solving followed by instruction works
why.found: A pooled analysis of 53 studies and 166 comparisons. Problem solving followed by instruction did better than instruction followed by problem solving (g = 0.36). The gain was larger when the design followed productive failure principles closely. Pupils in school years 2 to 5 did better with instruction first.
why.means: Let adults attempt a hard, solvable problem before you teach the method, then teach it properly.

items.title: Protect the effort
items.text: Do not smooth away recall and struggle.

try.text: Run a friction audit on a real course. Classify each point and decide what to remove and what to protect.

try.title: Illustrative: sorting a friction list
try.text: Learners report four struggles: a login that times out, instructions spread over three emails, recall questions at the start of each module, and a case with no model answer until they have tried it. Remove the first two. Keep the last two, and say why.

items: Learners will ask you to remove the useful difficulty too. Explain why it stays.
Walk through as a newcomer. You cannot see friction you are used to.
Confusion that never resolves is not productive.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Bjork and Bjork (2020), Desirable difficulties in theory and practice. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 9(4).
Sinha and Kapur (2021), When problem solving followed by instruction works: evidence for productive failure. Review of Educational Research, 2021.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of friction?
quiz.a: Friction that teaches, and friction that only frustrates.

quiz.q: Name two examples of friction to remove.
quiz.a: Any two of: confusing navigation, unclear instructions, admin, technical barriers.

quiz.q: What happens if you smooth everything?
quiz.a: You remove the learning with the annoyance.

openPoints: The aesthetic-usability effect (Kurosu and Kashimura 1995, Tractinsky and colleagues 2000, Norman's Emotional Design) was not searched for. If the owner wants the point back, it needs one of those sources.
The Sinha and Kapur abstract also gives a larger estimate after adjusting for publication bias. It is left out because the method could not be judged from a summary.
The claim that confusing the two kinds of friction is a common and costly mistake has no source. It is the page's own argument.
checkFindings: Bjork and Bjork (2020) confirmed on the authors' own lab page. It is a short commentary with no abstract, so the text itself was summarised. It supports the idea that some difficulty builds lasting learning and adds the condition that the learner must be able to overcome it.
Kapur's productive failure confirmed through the Sinha and Kapur (2021) meta-analysis. The effect size comes from its abstract.

The Norman reference is removed. The first pass warned that the attribution is doubtful, and it could not be checked. The sentence that people judge attractive designs as easier to use is removed with it.
The label no longer says 'see topic 1.3'.
topics.tierReason: Effortful practice such as recall, spacing and trying a problem before being taught is supported by pooled studies, but it only helps when learners can meet the challenge, and the friction audit itself is an untested practitioner tool.

topics.title: Build anticipation before the event
topics.theory: Anticipation, priming and what happens before training

situation.text: The joining email is a calendar invite and a car park map.

items: Tell people why this matters to them and what they will be able to do.
Send one question to think about, or a short task.
Have the manager talk to them before they come.
Give a first sight of the people and the place.
Keep it short.

why.text: What happens before training affects what people get from it. A pooled analysis looked at five pre-training steps: advice on what to pay attention to, strategies for checking your own understanding, advance organisers, goal orientation and preparatory information. All helped learning. The first two helped most consistently.
Whether looking forward to a course changes what people take from it has not been tested directly. Treat anticipation as a reasonable aim, not a proven effect.

why.title: Pre-training interventions and learning
why.found: A doctoral meta-analysis of 359 studies with 37,038 participants. Pre-training interventions had consistently positive effects on learning. Advice on where to direct attention and strategies for monitoring your own learning gave the most consistent gains.
why.means: Before the course, tell people what to look out for and give them a question to check their own understanding against.

items.title: One question
items.text: Give people something to think about.

try.text: Rewrite a joining email so it says why, asks one question and names what people will be able to do.

try.title: Illustrative: a joining email, before and after
try.text: Before: date, room and parking. After: two lines on why the course matters to this team, one thing people will be able to do afterwards, one question to bring an answer to, and a photo of the room and the trainer.

items: Over-selling sets up disappointment.
Pre-work that is not used is resented.
Too much contact before the event is noise.
The research tested structured steps used with the training itself. A joining email is a looser version, so check your own results.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Mesmer-Magnus (2005), The impact of pre-training interventions on cognitive, skill, and affective learning outcomes: a meta-analytic examination of four decades of research. Doctoral dissertation, Florida International University.
Cannon-Bowers, Rhodenizer, Salas and Bowers (1998), A framework for understanding pre-practice conditions and their impact on learning. Personnel Psychology, 51(2).

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: Does what happens before training matter?
quiz.a: Yes. It affects what people get from it.

quiz.q: Name two things to include in a joining message.
quiz.a: Any two of: why it matters, one question, what people will be able to do.

quiz.q: How firm is the finding on anticipation?
quiz.a: Not firm. It has not been tested directly for courses.

openPoints: Mesmer-Magnus and Viswesvaran (2010), The role of pre-training interventions in learning, Human Resource Management Review, 20(4), 261 to 282: the citation is confirmed on the Florida International University record, but the abstract was not opened. Its figures may differ from the 2005 dissertation. Replace the dissertation reference with the article once its abstract has been read.
The step 'Have the manager talk to them before they come' has no checked source.
The statement that anticipation has not been tested directly for courses rests on the build note. The absence was not re-checked.
checkFindings: Build note followed in part. The 2010 journal article by Mesmer-Magnus and Viswesvaran could not be opened. The university record gives the citation and keywords only, and the index page refused. What was opened is the abstract of Mesmer-Magnus's 2005 doctoral dissertation at the same university, a meta-analysis of the same five interventions. The reference list, the corrected paragraph and the study block cite the dissertation, not the article.
'Goal framing' is corrected to 'goal orientation', the term the source uses.
Cannon-Bowers and colleagues (1998) is added. It is the framework paper that defines these pre-practice conditions.
The Van Boven and Ashworth reference stays out, as the first pass decided.
A watch item is added because the research is about structured interventions, not joining emails.
topics.tierReason: Pooled studies support specific pre-training steps such as attention advice and advance organisers, but whether a joining message or looking forward to a course changes learning has not been tested directly.

topics.title: Tell learners what to expect, and what not to

situation.text: People arrive expecting a lecture and get role-play. Or expecting answers and get questions.

items: Say in advance what the session involves, and what it does not.
Say what effort is expected of them.
Say what they will and will not be able to do at the end.
Repeat it at the start, and check for surprises.

why.text: A realistic preview lets people prepare and choose. The research behind it comes from recruitment, not training. Pooled studies of realistic job previews found that candidates who got one started with lower expectations, and that previews went with fewer leavers and better job performance. Nobody has shown the same for a training course, so treat this as a reasonable borrowing.
Being honest about limits also protects your credibility.

why.title: Realistic job previews: a meta-analysis
why.found: A pooled analysis of 40 studies. Realistic job previews went with lower starting expectations, fewer people dropping out of recruitment, lower turnover and higher job performance. Timing, medium and setting changed the size of the effect.
why.means: Give an honest preview of the course, and remember the evidence is borrowed from hiring.

items.title: Preview
items.text: What it is, and what it is not.

items.title: Honest outcomes
items.text: Do not promise mastery in a day.

try.text: Write a five-line preview for one course: what happens, what you will ask of people, what they will leave with, what they will not.

try.title: Illustrative: a five-line preview
try.text: You will spend most of the day practising in threes. There is one short role-play, and you can observe first. Bring a real conversation you need to have. You will leave with a plan for it. You will not leave an expert after one day.

items: A preview that warns too much puts people off.
Managers set expectations too. Brief them.
If the format changes, tell people.
In the recruitment studies, when and how the preview was given changed its effect. Try yours on a few people first.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Phillips (1998), Effects of realistic job previews on multiple organizational outcomes: a meta-analysis. Academy of Management Journal, 41(6). Research on recruitment, not on training.

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What should a preview say?
quiz.a: What the session involves, what it does not, and what effort is expected.

quiz.q: Where does the research on realistic previews come from?
quiz.a: Recruitment. Job previews went with lower starting expectations and fewer leavers. The idea is borrowed for training, not tested there.

quiz.q: What does honesty about limits protect?
quiz.a: Your credibility.

openPoints: Studies of previews before training were not opened: Hicks and Klimoski (1987), Academy of Management Journal, and Tannenbaum, Mathieu, Salas and Cannon-Bowers (1991), Journal of Applied Psychology. Both are leads from memory. If confirmed, the rating could rise to C.
Premack and Wanous (1985) was not searched for. Phillips (1998) is the later meta-analysis.
The sentence that honesty about limits protects your credibility is practitioner advice with no source.
checkFindings: The placeholder is replaced with Phillips (1998), a meta-analysis of realistic job previews. The page now says plainly that this research is from recruitment.
The unsupported sentence about expectation gaps is removed from the why section and the quiz.
The abstract gives directions of effect and no effect sizes, so none is quoted.
topics.tierReason: The evidence for realistic previews comes from recruitment. No study of previews given before a training course was opened, so for training this is sensible practice, not a tested method.

topics.title: Use game elements only where they help

situation.text: Someone proposes points, badges and a leaderboard to "drive engagement".

items: Say what behaviour you want more of.
Use game elements that give clear goals, feedback and visible progress.
Be wary of competition and rewards for tasks people already value.
Tie every element to the objective.
Check whether learning improved, not only activity.

why.text: A pooled analysis of gamification studies found small positive effects on three kinds of outcome: what people learned (g = 0.49), their motivation (g = 0.36) and their behaviour (g = 0.25). The effect on what people learned held up in the more rigorous studies. The other two were less steady.
Rewards can reduce interest in tasks people already enjoy. Leaderboards can motivate those near the top and discourage the rest.
In the same analysis, a story wrapped round the tasks helped behaviour, and so did competition when it was combined with collaboration. Which design choices help learning itself is not yet settled.

why.title: The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis
why.found: Pooled effects of gamification were small and positive: g = 0.49 for cognitive outcomes (19 studies), g = 0.36 for motivation (16 studies) and g = 0.25 for behaviour (9 studies). Only the cognitive effect stayed stable in the high-rigour studies.
why.means: Expect a modest gain at best, and measure learning, not activity.

items.title: Small, variable effects
items.text: It can help. It is not a cure.

items.title: Goals, feedback, progress
items.text: The elements that earn their place.

try.text: Take one gamified element you use. Write what behaviour it drives and whether that behaviour is learning.

try.title: Illustrative: one element, checked
try.text: Before: points for every page opened, and a leaderboard. After: a progress bar that fills only when a practice task is passed, with feedback on each attempt. No ranking. The check is whether practice scores rise, not whether logins do.

items: Points for clicking reward clicking.
Novelty wears off.
Some people dislike competing. Offer another route.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Sailer and Homner (2020), The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32(1).

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: How large are the effects of gamification on learning?
quiz.a: Small on average. Steadiest for what people learn, less steady for motivation and behaviour.

quiz.q: Which game elements earn their place?
quiz.a: Clear goals, feedback and visible progress.

quiz.q: What can rewards do to tasks people already enjoy?
quiz.a: Reduce their interest.

openPoints: Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999), Psychological Bulletin: not opened. The sentence that rewards can reduce interest in tasks people already enjoy has no checked source on this page.
The leaderboard sentence has no checked source.
Later meta-analyses (Bai, Hew and Huang 2020, Huang and colleagues 2020, and others) were not searched for.
The abstract summary read did not state the comparison condition. From general knowledge the studies compared gamified with non-gamified learning.
checkFindings: Sailer and Homner (2020) confirmed on the University of Augsburg repository record. Effect sizes are from the abstract: cognitive g = 0.49, motivational g = 0.36, behavioural g = 0.25. The authors call all three small, so the draft's word 'small' stands, although 0.49 is at the upper end of that label.
Build note followed. 'Steadiest for learning outcomes' matches the abstract and is now in the page and the quiz.
'Wide variation between studies' and 'Design choices mattered' are replaced with what the abstract reports.

A paragraph is added on competition with collaboration. The page tells readers to be wary of competition, and the meta-analysis found competition helped behaviour when paired with collaboration. A practitioner would expect to see both.
Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999) is removed from the list because it was not opened in this run. The old label 'Checked on topic 1.16' is not carried forward.
topics.tierReason: One meta-analysis found small positive effects, steady for what people learn and less steady for motivation and behaviour, and what makes gamification work is still unsettled.

topics.title: Design for different minds from the start
topics.theory: Inclusion, neurodiversity and Universal Design for Learning

situation.text: A participant tells you on the day that they cannot follow fast speech, read small text or sit still for ninety minutes.

items: Ask about needs in advance, in plain words.
Offer more than one way to take in content: spoken, written, visual.
Offer more than one way to take part and to show learning.
Send materials ahead.
Build in breaks, movement and quiet.
Make adjustments normal for everyone.

why.text: Designing for a range of people from the start is fairer, and usually easier, than fixing it for one person on the day. A widely used framework suggests offering several means of engagement, of presenting content and of responding.
Many adjustments help everyone. Evidence that the framework as a whole raises learning is still developing.

items.title: More than one way
items.text: To take in, take part and respond.

try.text: Take one session. List three points where a different way of taking part would cost you nothing.

try.title: Illustrative: asking in advance
try.text: The joining form asks what would help you take part, with examples: slides in advance, captions, a seat near the door, regular breaks. Nobody is asked why. Slides go to everyone two days ahead and each hour includes a five-minute break.

items: Do not ask people to disclose a diagnosis.
This is not learning styles. It is access and choice.
In the UK, the Equality Act 2010 sets duties to make reasonable adjustments. This is general information, not legal advice.
Designing for everyone does not remove the need for individual adjustments. Some people will still need something specific, so keep asking.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: CAST (2024), Universal Design for Learning Guidelines, version 3.0.
Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008), Learning styles: concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3).

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: When should you design for different needs?
quiz.a: From the start.

quiz.q: What three things should have more than one route?
quiz.a: Taking in content, taking part and showing learning.

quiz.q: Should you ask for a diagnosis?
quiz.a: No. Ask what people need.

topics.tierReason: Universal Design for Learning is a widely used framework and the topic also covers legal duties. Direct evidence that the whole framework raises learning was not confirmed.
openPoints: Legal check not done. legislation.gov.uk, gov.uk, the Equality and Human Rights Commission and Acas could not be opened in this run, so the Equality Act 2010 is not in the reference list. The watch item says only that the Act sets duties to make reasonable adjustments, which is left as written. Before publishing, check section 20 of the Act on legislation.gov.uk and the EHRC or Acas guidance, including who holds the duty in a training setting (employer, service provider or education provider) and that the duty is owed to disabled people.

No independent review of the evidence for Universal Design for Learning was opened. Candidates to check, from memory and unverified: Capp (2017), International Journal of Inclusive Education. King-Sears and colleagues (2023), Teaching and Teacher Education. Boysen (2021), a critique comparing the evidence base with learning styles.
checkFindings: CAST: the current version is Guidelines 3.0, released 30 July 2024. The three headings are multiple means of engagement, of representation, and of action and expression. The draft's wording matches.

CAST's own page says the framework is based on scientific insights into how people learn. It gives no outcome evidence on that page. The draft's cautious sentence that evidence for the framework as a whole is still developing is kept, but it was not confirmed against an independent review.
Pashler and colleagues (2008) added to support the watch item that this is not learning styles.
'Cheaper' removed from the first why sentence, as unsupported.
Added a watch item that universal design does not replace individual adjustments. A practitioner would expect it.
The existing note 'This is general information, not legal advice' is kept unchanged.

parts.title: Assess and give feedback
parts.summary: Checking what people can do, fairly, and telling them what to do next.

topics.title: Test little and often

situation.text: The only assessment is a test at the end. By then it is too late to act on what it shows.

items: Check where people start before you teach.
Add short, low-stakes checks during the course.
Use each check to adjust what you do next.
Keep the stakes low so people will risk being wrong.

why.text: Assessment has three purposes: to find the starting point, to guide learning while it happens, and to judge it at the end. The middle one is widely seen as a strong lever on learning, though estimates of its size vary.
Every test is also a learning event, because recalling strengthens memory. A short quiz teaches as it measures.

The benefit of a test shows up later, not at once. In one well-known experiment, students who reread a passage recalled more five minutes afterwards. Students who were tested on it recalled more after two days and after a week. Rereading also made people more confident, without the lasting memory to match.

why.title: Test-enhanced learning
why.found: Students read prose passages, then either reread them or took recall tests with no feedback. After five minutes the rereaders recalled more. After two days and after one week the tested group recalled substantially more.
why.means: Swap some review time for short recall quizzes, and judge them by what people remember next week.

items.title: Checks guide teaching
items.text: Use the result to change the next step.

try.text: Take a course. Add three low-stakes checks. Say what each measures and how it changes what you do.

try.title: Illustrative: three checks in one day
try.text: Start: four questions on paper, unmarked, to see what people already know. Mid-morning: each pair explains one idea aloud while you listen. After lunch: a two-minute recall quiz. The trainer drops one planned section because the first check showed people already had it.

items: A check nobody acts on is wasted.
Graded quizzes raise the stakes and lower honesty.
Feedback timing matters. Sometimes a delay helps memory.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Black and Wiliam (1998), Assessment and classroom learning. Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy and Practice, 5(1).
Roediger and Karpicke (2006), Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3).

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What are the three purposes of assessment?
quiz.a: To find the starting point, to guide learning, and to judge it at the end.

quiz.q: Why does a quiz teach?
quiz.a: Recalling strengthens memory.

quiz.q: Why keep the stakes low?
quiz.a: So people will risk being wrong.

openPoints: The phrase 'estimates of its size vary' has no checked source. Kingston and Nash (2011) was not searched for.
The watch item 'Sometimes a delay helps memory' has no checked source.
The three purposes of assessment (diagnostic, formative, summative) are standard terms. No source for the three-part scheme was opened.
Black and Wiliam reviewed school and college classrooms. Workplace training was not their subject.
checkFindings: Black and Wiliam (1998) confirmed on a University of Glasgow copy of the article. Its summary says several studies give firm evidence that strengthening frequent feedback to learners produces substantial learning gains. This supports the paragraph on the middle purpose of assessment.
Roediger and Karpicke (2006) confirmed on PubMed. It supports 'a test teaches'. The abstract adds that rereading wins on an immediate test, so a paragraph was added.
The old label 'Checked on topic 1.3' is not carried forward.
topics.tierReason: Testing strengthens later memory in controlled studies and a large review found learning gains from frequent feedback, but the gain depends on acting on the results and the size of the formative assessment effect is debated.

topics.title: Assess the real task, not a quiz about it

situation.text: Facilitators are certified with a multiple-choice quiz. Nobody has watched them run a room.

items: Ask what the person must do in real life.
Set a task as close to that as you safely can.
Watch the performance.
Write the criteria down as a rubric and share it in advance.

why.text: A written test cannot certify a skill that is performed. Authentic assessment measures someone doing something close to the real task, in place of answering questions about it.
A rubric makes the criteria explicit, so people know what good looks like. Check that assessors agree by comparing marks on a sample.
A review of rubric research concluded that the criteria are what matter most. Criteria that count trivial things pull attention away from the substance of the work.

items.title: Match the format to the skill
Share the rubric
items.text: People should know what good looks like.

try.text: Design a performance assessment with a rubric for a real skill. Check the task mirrors the workplace.

try.title: Illustrative: certifying a facilitator
try.text: Before: a 20-question multiple-choice quiz. After: each person runs a 15-minute segment with a real group. Two observers use a shared rubric with four criteria, such as how questions are handled. The rubric is sent a week ahead.

items: Observation costs time. Budget for it.
A rubric that rewards the trivial will be gamed.
Simulations help where the real task is unsafe.
A realistic task is not valid by default. Ask the same questions of it as of any test: what the score means and what follows from using it.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Messick (1995), Validity of psychological assessment. American Psychologist, 50(9).
Brookhart (2018), Appropriate criteria: key to effective rubrics. Frontiers in Education, 3:22.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What can a written test not certify?
quiz.a: A skill that is performed.

quiz.q: What is authentic assessment?
quiz.a: Measuring someone doing something close to the real task.

quiz.q: What does a rubric do?
quiz.a: Makes the criteria explicit, so people know what good looks like.

openPoints: Wiggins (1998), Educative Assessment, Jossey-Bass: not opened.
Jonsson and Svingby (2007), The use of scoring rubrics, Educational Research Review: searched for, not found in results, not opened.
The sentence 'A written test cannot certify a skill that is performed' is the page's own argument with no checked source.
checkFindings: Wiggins, Educative Assessment, could not be reached within the search cap and is removed from the list.
Messick (1995) is listed because its summary says the same validity standards apply to performance assessments, which it discusses at length. A watch item carries that point.

The claim that rubrics make assessors more consistent is softened. Jonsson and Svingby (2007) did not appear in the search results. Brookhart (2018), a later review, was opened. It says appropriate criteria are the key to effective rubrics and found no pattern showing one kind of rubric to be more reliable.
No study block. No single study carries the topic.
topics.tierReason: Performance assessment with a rubric is established professional practice, but no study comparing it with written tests for certifying a skill was opened.

topics.title: Check the test measures what you think it does

situation.text: Scores are high and everyone is pleased. Nobody has asked what the test actually measures.

items: Ask what the assessment really measures.
Look for things that affect the score and are not the skill: reading load, cultural references, test technique.
Check two assessors would give the same result.
Check it matches the objectives and what was taught.

why.text: Validity is whether an assessment measures what it claims to. Measuring the wrong thing accurately is still useless. Reliability is whether it gives consistent results across assessors and occasions.
The two can pull against each other. Realistic tasks are often harder to mark consistently.

Validity is not a fixed property of a test. In Messick's account it is a judgement about what the scores mean and how they are used, and it includes the consequences of using them. Content, links to other measures and consequences are all evidence for the same question.

items.title: Validity
items.text: Does it measure what it claims?

try.text: Critique an assessment for threats to validity. Propose fixes.

try.title: Illustrative: what a test really measures
try.text: A customer service test uses long written scenarios. People with strong reading skills score highest, whatever their service skills. The fix: shorter scenarios, some played as audio, and a second marker on a sample to check agreement.

items: High scores on a poor measure tell you nothing.
A pass mark should be reasoned, not picked.
Assessment shapes what people study. Check what yours rewards.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Messick (1995), Validity of psychological assessment. American Psychologist, 50(9).
Biggs (1996), Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment. Higher Education, 32.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What is validity?
quiz.a: Whether an assessment measures what it claims to measure.

quiz.q: What is reliability?
quiz.a: Whether it gives consistent results across assessors and occasions.

quiz.q: Name one thing that can distort a score.
quiz.a: Reading load, cultural references or test technique.

openPoints: The statement that validity and reliability pull against each other has no checked source.
The watch item that a pass mark should be reasoned has no checked source. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014) were not opened.
The watch item that assessment shapes what people study has no checked source.
checkFindings: Messick (1995) confirmed on an index record with the abstract. It argues that validity is one thing, construct validity, covering score meaning and the consequences of score use, with six aspects. A paragraph was added because the page defined validity only as measuring what a test claims to measure.
Biggs (1996) is added for the alignment step and card. Its abstract supports aligning objectives, teaching and assessment.

The Educational Testing Service report version of Messick's paper was also read. Its body describes two faults: a test that is too narrow, and a test that picks up something other than the skill. That detail is not in the abstract, so it is not added to the page. The existing step on reading load and test technique already covers the second fault.
topics.tierReason: Validity, reliability and alignment are core professional principles of assessment set out in theory papers, not practices tested by experiment.

topics.title: Give feedback people can act on

situation.text: Feedback on the exercise reads "Great job" or "Needs work". Nobody knows what to do next.

items: Say where the person is heading.
Say how they are doing against that.
Say what to do next.
Comment on the task and the method, not the person.
Give time to act on it.

why.text: The most useful feedback answers three questions: where am I going, how am I doing, and what next. Feedback about the task and the process helps. Praise of the person is among the least effective kinds.
Fair assessment removes barriers that have nothing to do with the skill, so that it measures capability and not disadvantage.

Feedback is not always good. A pooled analysis found that it improved performance on average, yet more than a third of feedback interventions made performance worse. Feedback worked less well as it pulled attention away from the task and towards the self.

why.title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance
why.found: A meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes and 23,663 observations. Feedback improved performance on average (d = 0.41), but over one third of feedback interventions reduced it. Feedback became less effective as it moved attention from the task towards the self.
why.means: Keep feedback on the task and the next step, and leave out comments on the person.

items.title: Three questions
items.text: Where to, how am I doing, what next.

items.title: Time to act
items.text: Feedback nobody can use is wasted.

try.text: Rewrite a weak piece of feedback so it addresses the task and gives a clear next step.

try.title: Illustrative: feedback, before and after
try.text: Before: Needs work. After: The aim is a brief the group can act on without asking you questions. Yours gives the task clearly but no time limit or output. Add both, then try it on a colleague before Thursday.

items: Feedback only works where people feel safe enough to hear it.
Marking by judgement carries bias. Use rubrics and compare notes with another assessor.
Too much feedback at once is not used.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Hattie and Timperley (2007), The power of feedback. Review of Educational Research, 77(1).
Kluger and DeNisi (1996), The effects of feedback interventions on performance: a historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2).

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What three questions does good feedback answer?
quiz.a: Where am I going, how am I doing, and what next.

quiz.q: Which kind of feedback helps least?
quiz.a: Praise of the person.

quiz.q: What must follow feedback?
quiz.a: Time and a chance to act on it.

openPoints: The paragraph on fair assessment and the watch item on bias in marking have no checked source.
Wisniewski, Zierer and Hattie (2020), The power of feedback revisited, was not searched for.
The step 'Give time to act on it' and the watch item on too much feedback at once have no checked source.
checkFindings: Hattie and Timperley (2007) confirmed on a University of California, Riverside copy of the article. The abstract says feedback can help or harm. The article sets out the three questions and four levels (task, process, self-regulation, self) and judges feedback about the self the least effective. This supports the first why paragraph and two quiz answers. The article's wording for the second question is 'How am I going'. The page's 'how am I doing' is a fair paraphrase and is left.

Build note (gap 4, inclusion and neurodiversity need their own treatment here): not acted on. It asks for new content, which is the owner's decision, and no inclusion source was opened for this topic.
topics.tierReason: Feedback improves performance on average across many studies, but more than a third of feedback interventions made performance worse, so the result depends on what the feedback points at.

stages.name: Make the materials
stages.question: How do we build slides, media and e-learning that teach?
stages.wordingStatus: Draft: part names and topic titles for this stage were written for the build pack and have not been seen by Mica

parts.title: Slides, visuals and story
parts.summary: What the research on words and pictures says about slides and charts.

topics.title: Judge every slide by what it asks of the learner

situation.text: The slide looks professional and the room is still lost. Looking good and teaching well are different things.

items: For each slide, ask what the learner has to do with it.
Help them pick out what matters.
Help them organise it.
Help them connect it to what they know.
Remove whatever does none of these.

why.text: The leading theory of learning from words and pictures rests on three ideas. People take in pictures and words through separate channels. Each channel holds little. Learning needs active work by the learner.
Design either supports that work or gets in its way. The principles shift with expertise, as with cognitive load.

items.title: Two channels
items.text: Words and pictures are handled separately.

items.title: Select, organise, connect
items.text: The work a slide should support.

try.text: Take a dense slide. Say what helps the learner select, organise and connect, and what obstructs.

try.title: One slide, before and after
try.text: Before: a slide with a process diagram, a paragraph and a stock photo. After: the diagram alone, with the one step being discussed highlighted. The learner now knows where to look and what to link it to.

items: A house template can fight these principles. Change what you can.
What helps a newcomer may be redundant for an expert.
Impressive is not the same as effective.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Mayer (2020), Multimedia Learning, 3rd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler and Sweller (2003), The expertise reversal effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1).

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What are the two channels?
quiz.a: One for pictures and one for words.

quiz.q: What three things should a slide help the learner do?
quiz.a: Select what matters, organise it, and connect it to what they know.

quiz.q: Is a professional-looking slide an effective one?
quiz.a: Not necessarily.

openPoints: The publisher's page for Mayer (2020) does not spell out the three assumptions (two channels, limited capacity, active processing). They are the standard account of his theory but were not seen on the page read.
Paivio on dual coding (candidate: Clark and Paivio 1991) and Baddeley and Hitch (1974) were not opened. No searches left.
The Cambridge address that opened carries an older ISBN in its path but shows the 3rd edition (2020). Worth a click to confirm it still resolves.
checkFindings: Mayer (2020) confirmed as the 3rd edition from Cambridge University Press. The publisher describes 15 design principles drawn from more than 200 experiments and a cognitive theory of learning from words and graphics. No text needed changing.
'The principles shift with expertise' is now sourced to Kalyuga and colleagues (2003), whose abstract says techniques that help novices can lose their value or do harm with more experienced learners.
Paivio and Baddeley and Hitch were removed from the list because neither could be opened. The 'see topic 1.1' label is gone with them.
topics.tierReason: The multimedia design principles rest on a large body of experiments, but their benefit depends on the learner's prior knowledge and most studies use short lessons.

topics.title: Cut what does not serve the point

situation.text: Every slide carries a paragraph, a photo and a logo, and you read the paragraph aloud.

items: Cut anything that does not serve the point.
Mark what is essential.
Do not read out text that is on the screen.
Put words next to the picture they describe, and show them at the same time.
Cut the interesting aside that is off the point.

why.text: The main principles are coherence, signalling, redundancy and contiguity. The instinct to add more text, more decoration, more "engaging" extras often gets in the way of learning.

Interesting but irrelevant material tends to lower what people learn. A 2020 meta-analysis of 58 studies found this on average, with more harm on paper than on screen. That is the evidence behind cutting the fun but pointless bits. For material that passes quickly, narration with graphics can beat on-screen text with graphics.

why.title: Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect
why.found: Across 58 studies with more than 7,500 students, people who learned with interesting but irrelevant extras scored lower than people who learned without them. The harm was greater on paper than on screen, and greater when the extra stayed in view beside a useful diagram.
why.means: Cut the joke, photo or music that does not serve the point, above all on handouts and beside diagrams.

items.title: Cut
items.text: What does not serve the point goes.

items.title: Together
items.text: Words and pictures side by side, at the same time.

try.text: Redesign a crowded slide using coherence, signalling and redundancy. Name the principle behind each change.

try.title: A crowded slide, cut
try.text: Before: a slide with a paragraph, a photo of a handshake and a logo, read aloud word for word. After: one labelled diagram on screen. You explain it in speech and the paragraph moves to the handout.

items: Stakeholders will ask for content to be added back. Offer a handout.
Captions and transcripts are not the redundancy problem. They are an access need.
These are tendencies with conditions, not fixed laws.
Most studies of irrelevant extras used lessons of 6 to 12 minutes. Less is known about a full day in a training room.

quiz.q: What does the coherence principle say?
quiz.a: Cut what does not serve the point.

quiz.q: What should you not do with on-screen text?
quiz.a: Read it aloud.

quiz.q: What do interesting but irrelevant details do?
quiz.a: They tend to lower what people learn.

openPoints: Harp and Mayer (1998), How seductive details do their damage: not opened.
No overall effect size is given for seductive details because none was seen in the summary read.
Meta-analyses for modality (Ginns 2005), signalling (Schneider and colleagues 2018) and redundancy (Adesope and Nesbit 2012) were not opened. Those points rest on Mayer's book chapters only.
checkFindings: Mayer (2020): the contents list confirms chapters on coherence, signalling, redundancy, spatial contiguity, temporal contiguity and modality. This supports the four named principles and the narration point.
The seductive details claim was unconditional. It now cites the 2020 meta-analysis and its limits (short lessons, larger effect on paper).

Important: the journal abstract for Sundararajan and Adesope could not be opened (the repository record held citation details only and the other index refused). The findings were read in Washington State University's own news summary of the paper, written with the authors. The link and label say so. Replace with the journal abstract when it can be opened.

topics.tierReason: Cutting irrelevant material, cueing and avoiding read-aloud text are backed by many experiments and a meta-analysis, but the effects vary with format, subject and learner, and most studies use lessons of a few minutes.

topics.title: Make charts honest and quick to read

situation.text: A chart in your deck has a cut-off axis, six colours and a 3D effect.

items: Use size, contrast and position to show what to read first.
Choose the chart that fits the comparison.
Start axes where they should start, and label them.
Remove decoration that competes with the data.
Do not rely on colour alone.

why.text: A visual should make the point faster and more truthfully than words. If it does not, it is decoration.
The same data can mislead or clarify. A trainer has a duty to clarify.

items.title: Hierarchy
items.text: Show people where to look first.

items.title: Honest axes
items.text: Start bars at zero. Label any other scale clearly.

try.text: Take a misleading chart. Redraw it to show the same data honestly and clearly.

try.title: A chart, redrawn
try.text: Before: a 3D bar chart in six colours with the axis starting at 80. After: flat bars from zero, in grey, with the one bar that matters in a dark shade and labelled directly.

items: A simple chart can still mislead through what it leaves out.
Check contrast, and add labels where colour carries meaning.
Design for the back row and for a phone.

quiz.a: Make the point faster and more truthfully.

quiz.q: Name one way a chart misleads.
quiz.a: A truncated axis, a misleading scale or decoration that distorts.

quiz.q: Why not rely on colour alone?
quiz.a: Some people cannot tell the colours apart.

topics.title: Put the claim in the headline and the evidence below

situation.text: Each slide has a topic label and five bullets. The audience has to work out the point.

items: Write the headline as a full sentence that states the claim.
Put the evidence for it underneath, as a picture where you can.
Give the sequence a shape: situation, complication, resolution.
Keep the story in service of the content.

why.text: A topic label over bullets asks the audience to assemble the meaning. A sentence headline does that work for them and leaves room for evidence.
People tend to follow and remember a narrative more easily than a list of points. Experts often structure explanations badly because they have forgotten what it was like not to know.

The best-known test compared two versions of one technical talk with 110 engineering students. The claim-and-evidence slides led to better understanding, fewer misconceptions and better recall later. The comparison slides broke several design principles at once, so the study supports the whole approach. It does not show how much the headline alone adds.

why.title: How slide design affects audience comprehension
why.found: 110 engineering students saw the same technical talk with one of two slide sets. Those who saw claim-and-evidence slides understood more, held fewer misconceptions, reported less mental effort and recalled more at a later test than those who saw default topic-and-bullet slides.
why.means: Rewrite topic labels as short claim sentences and replace bullets with the evidence, shown as a picture where you can.

try.text: Convert a run of topic-and-bullet slides into claim-and-evidence slides with one thread through them.

try.title: A headline that states the claim
try.text: Before: a slide headed "Customer complaints" with five bullets. After: the headline reads "Most complaints come from late deliveries" and a single bar chart below shows it.

items: Reference material does not want a story. Make it easy to scan.
A vivid story can outweigh the evidence. Check it is true to the point.
Sentence headlines need editing to stay short.

quiz.q: What should a slide headline be?
quiz.a: A full sentence that states the claim.

quiz.q: What goes underneath?
quiz.a: The evidence, as a picture where possible.

quiz.q: When is story the wrong tool?
quiz.a: For reference material people need to scan.

'People follow and remember narrative' has no checked source (candidate: Mar and colleagues 2021 meta-analysis).
The claim about experts has no checked source on this page (candidates: Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber 1989. Hinds 1999).

Added a paragraph saying what that study does and does not show. It tested a package of six design principles against default slides, with students, and one author developed the approach.
Softened the two unsourced sentences on narrative and on experts.
Heath and Heath removed from the list because the publisher page was not opened.

parts.title: Choose the medium
parts.summary: Picking and combining media from the objective, not from fashion.

topics.title: Pick the medium after the objective

situation.text: The brief arrives as "we want a video" or "can you build an app".

items: Start from the objective and the constraints.
Ask what the objective needs: practice and feedback, discussion, or reference at the moment of use.
Weigh live against self-paced.
Check cost, audience size, how fast the content changes, and who can access it.
Then choose the medium.

why.text: Each medium has real strengths. The objective should decide between them. Choosing the medium first is a common and costly habit.
A new medium often shows inflated results that fade once the novelty wears off. That misleads buying decisions.

try.text: Take three objectives. Choose a medium for each and say why you rejected the alternatives.

try.title: "We want a video"
try.text: The objective is handling an angry caller. That needs practice and feedback, so you propose paired role-play with a short checklist, and a brief video only to model one good call.

items: Bandwidth, devices and accessibility are real limits.
The cheapest medium to make can be the dearest to maintain.
Do not let the supplier choose.

topics.bodyStatus: 1 source checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What decides the medium?
quiz.a: The objective and the constraints.

quiz.q: What is the basic trade-off between live and self-paced?
quiz.a: Richness of interaction against flexibility.

quiz.q: Why distrust early results for a new medium?
quiz.a: Novelty inflates them and then fades.

topics.tierReason: Choosing the medium from the objective is standard design practice backed by argument and by media comparison research, not a method tested directly.
openPoints: Clark and Mayer, e-Learning and the Science of Instruction (Wiley): publisher page not opened. The draft gives no year or edition. A fifth edition is believed to exist. Confirm before citing.

'A new medium often shows inflated results that fade once the novelty wears off' is unsourced. Candidate: Clark (1983), Reconsidering research on learning from media, Review of Educational Research, whose summary is believed to name novelty as a rival explanation. Not opened.
The web search allowance ran out before this topic was reached.
checkFindings: Softened an unsupported superlative.

Added Howard and colleagues (2021). Its summary reports that the fit between task and technology mattered for virtual reality training, while the display and input hardware did not. That supports letting the objective choose the medium. It is about virtual reality training only.

topics.title: Blend on purpose, and keep microlearning for what it suits

situation.text: Live time is spent presenting content people could have read. Meanwhile someone proposes turning the whole course into five-minute clips.

items: Move content delivery to pre-work.
Spend live time on practice, discussion and feedback.
Use short units for reminders and for help at the point of use.
Keep complex, joined-up skills in longer formats.

why.text: Blending means each mode does what it does best. Flipping moves content before the session so the scarce live time is used for interaction.

Short units suit reinforcement and performance support. They are a doubtful fit for complex skills, because the parts of a complex skill have to be practised together. That limit is a design judgement more than a research finding.

Expect a modest gain from flipping. A 2019 meta-analysis found flipped classes beat lecture-based teaching by a small margin, and by less in the larger studies. Checking the pre-work, for example with a short quiz, may add a little.

For microlearning, a 2025 review of 40 studies reports mostly positive results for knowledge, engagement and satisfaction. Its summary does not say how strong those studies were, so treat the support as early.

why.title: Does the flipped classroom improve learning and satisfaction?
why.found: Pooling 272 comparisons of flipped and lecture-based teaching, learning was a little better in flipped classes (Hedges' g = 0.35). In the 90 adequately powered studies the gain was smaller (g = 0.24). Satisfaction rose only slightly, and the authors suspect publication bias.
why.means: Flip to free live time for practice, check the pre-work was done, and promise a modest gain.

items.title: Blend on purpose
items.text: Say what each mode is for.

items.title: Micro has limits
items.text: Good for reminders. Poor for complex skills.

try.text: Take a single-mode course. Redesign it as a blend. State what each mode does and why.

try.title: A blend with a job for each part
try.text: A one-day product course becomes a short reading and quiz beforehand, a half-day of practice on customer cases, and three brief reminders over the following month. Each part has one stated job.

items: The flip fails if people skip the pre-work. Use it in the room.
Fragments without connection confuse.
More modes mean more handoffs to design.
