quiz.q: What does flipping move out of the live session?
quiz.a: Content delivery.

quiz.q: What is microlearning good for?
quiz.a: Reminders, spaced reinforcement and help at the point of use.

quiz.q: What is it poor for?
quiz.a: Complex, joined-up skills.

openPoints: Taylor and Hung (2022), The effects of microlearning: a scoping review: abstract page would not open.
De Gagne and colleagues (2019) scoping review: PubMed refused the page.
van Alten and colleagues (2019) and Means and colleagues (2013) were not opened.
The Låg and Sæle link is a university repository address with a session tag on the end. It opened today. A cleaner address for the same record would be better if one can be confirmed.
The flipped classroom studies compare taught classes. How well the finding carries to workplace training was not stated in the abstract.
checkFindings: The placeholder for 'the microlearning literature' is replaced by a real systematic review (Monib and colleagues, 40 studies, PRISMA method). It reports generally positive outcomes. Its abstract gives no quality appraisal, and the page now says so.

Flipping had no source. Added Låg and Sæle (2019) and a paragraph giving the size of the effect. The intended source (van Alten and colleagues 2019) did not come up with an openable page, so this meta-analysis of the same question was used.
'A complex skill cannot be learned as unrelated fragments' was reworded as a design judgement. No source read tests it.

topics.tierReason: Flipping shows a small average gain that shrinks in the better-powered studies, and the microlearning research is recent and of uncertain quality.

topics.title: Buy a medium for the method it makes possible

situation.text: A supplier promises that virtual reality, or an app, or video, will improve learning.

items: Do not expect a medium to teach by itself.
Ask which methods the objective needs.
Ask what this medium makes possible that others do not.
Buy it for those methods, then design them well.

why.text: One side of a long debate holds that media are vehicles: they deliver instruction and do not cause learning. The method teaches. The other side replies that a medium's capabilities can make methods possible that would otherwise be impractical.
Many studies comparing media find no difference. That usually means the method mattered, not the medium.

items.title: Affordances
items.text: What does this medium make possible?

try.text: Take a proposal to use a particular medium. Ask whether what it makes possible serves the method the objective needs.

try.title: Asking what the medium adds
try.text: A supplier offers an app for fire-safety training. You ask what it lets people do that a workshop cannot. The answer is spaced quiz reminders on a phone. You buy it for that, and keep the extinguisher practice live.

items: The same test applies to AI and virtual reality.
A good method in a poor medium still suffers.
Sunk cost keeps bad media in use.

quiz.q: In Clark's view, what causes learning?
quiz.a: The method, not the medium.

quiz.q: What is Kozma's reply?
quiz.a: A medium's capabilities can make some methods possible.

quiz.q: What does "no significant difference" usually mean?
quiz.a: The method mattered more than the medium.

topics.tierReason: This is a reasoned position taken from a long-running academic debate. It guides buying decisions but has not been tested as a practice.

Kozma (1994), Will media influence learning? Reframing the debate, Educational Technology Research and Development: not opened.

'Many studies comparing media find no difference' is unsourced. It needs a review or meta-analysis of media comparison studies. Clark's reply, Clark (1994), Media will never influence learning, would also round out the debate.
The Makransky link is a University of Copenhagen research-portal address on a test server. Replace it with the journal page when it can be opened.
The web search allowance ran out before this topic was reached.
checkFindings: The two named papers could not be opened, so the account of the debate is unverified.

Added two checked sources that support the watch item on virtual reality. Makransky and colleagues (2019) found a more immersive version of the same lesson produced more presence and less learning. Howard and colleagues (2021) found that fit between task and technology mattered and hardware did not.

topics.title: Offer print or self-pacing for dense reading
topics.theory: Screen versus paper, reading versus listening, handwriting versus typing

situation.text: A client wants everything on screen, or bans laptops because "handwriting is better for memory".

items: For dense reading, offer print or let people set their own pace.
Give transcripts with audio and video.
Do not ban screens outright.
Do not teach the handwriting claim as fact.

why.text: Reading comprehension can be slightly worse on screen than on paper. One meta-analysis of 54 studies found a small advantage for paper (g = -0.21 for screens against paper). The gap was larger when reading time was limited than when people set their own pace. It showed for informational text, and not for stories alone. It also grew over the years studied, so do not assume that familiarity with screens removes it.

The well-known claim that handwriting beats typing for memory has not held up. Two direct repeats of the original study found no consistent difference in test scores between people who wrote by hand and people who typed. The original explanation, that typing leads to word-for-word copying which harms learning, was not reliable in the repeat either. The fair summary is that neither tool has been shown to be better.

Adding audio to text helps less than you might expect. A review of 30 studies found only a very small overall benefit from listening while reading (g = 0.18 against reading alone), and no reliable benefit when people read at their own pace. Offer the transcript as a choice, not as something to follow alongside the audio.

why.title: Paper against screens: a meta-analysis of 54 studies
why.found: Across 54 studies, people understood text slightly better on paper than on screen (g = -0.21 for screens against paper). The gap was larger under time limits than with self-paced reading, and it showed for informational text but not for stories alone.
why.means: For dense reading, offer print or let people read in their own time, and do not treat the difference as large.

items.title: Small and conditional
items.text: The screen effect is real but slight.

items.title: Pen or keyboard
items.text: Neither is shown to be better. Let people choose.

try.text: Take three "medium X is better" claims, including the handwriting one. State the size of each effect and when it holds.

try.title: Dense reading, without a ban
try.text: A client wants a forty-page policy read on screen in a timed session. You offer a printed copy or a PDF to read beforehand at each person's own pace, and use the session to apply it.

items: People often feel they learn better one way and perform better another.
Print has an access cost for some learners.
Quote the conditions with the finding.

Morehead, Dunlosky and Rawson (2019), How much mightier is the pen than the keyboard for note-taking? A replication and extension of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014). Educational Psychology Review, 31.
Urry and colleagues (2021), Don't ditch the laptop just yet: a direct replication of Mueller and Oppenheimer's (2014) Study 1. Psychological Science, 32(3).

topics.bodyStatus: 4 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: How big is the screen reading effect?
quiz.a: Small, and mainly for explanatory text under time pressure.

quiz.q: What happened to the handwriting claim?
quiz.a: It did not hold up when the study was repeated.

quiz.q: What should you do about pen against keyboard?
quiz.a: Let people choose. Neither has been shown to be better.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis of 54 studies found a small advantage for paper that depends on time pressure and the kind of text, and the handwriting claim has not held up in direct repeats.
openPoints: Clinton (2019), Reading from paper compared to screens, Journal of Research in Reading: the publisher's abstract page could not be opened (the Wiley address was not reachable). A third-party copy of the abstract and a blog post by the author agree on the direction: a small negative effect of screens across 33 studies, limited to expository text, no difference in reading time, and better calibration on paper. Neither showed the effect size. The figure in the build note is therefore still unchecked, and the reference is left out of the list. The page states no Clinton figure.

Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014), The pen is mightier than the keyboard, Psychological Science: the PubMed page (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24760141/) returned no content and a PDF copy was blocked. Left out of the list. The two replications describe its claim.

The meta-analysis of reading against listening (Clinton-Lisell 2022, Listening ears or reading eyes, Review of Educational Research) could not be opened. The appended paragraph uses her 2023 review of reading while listening instead, which is a different question.
Watch item 'People often feel they learn better one way and perform better another' matches the calibration finding in Clinton (2019), which is not confirmed at source.
Whether summarising in your own words helps learning is a separate question with its own literature (generative learning). It was not checked and is no longer claimed on this page.
checkFindings: Build note followed. Delgado and colleagues (2018) report g = -0.21, confirmed on the abstract page hosted by the University of Haifa research portal (one author's institution, DOI 10.1016/j.edurev.2018.09.003). The draft page gave no figure, so the correct one was added.
The draft said the screen effect 'largely disappears' with self-paced reading. The summary says only that the paper advantage was larger under time limits. Corrected.
Added the finding that the paper advantage grew over the years studied, which a practitioner would expect to see.

Build note followed on handwriting. Morehead and colleagues (2019), read on the Springer publisher copy, found no consistent differences between longhand, laptop and eWriter groups and say a verdict either way is premature. A second direct replication, Urry and colleagues (2021), was added.

The draft kept 'putting ideas in your own words helps' as the lesson. Neither replication supports it. Urry and colleagues found the link between verbatim notes and worse scores was not robust. The paragraph, card and quiz item were changed.
The topic's theory line covers reading against listening, but the body had nothing on it. Added one paragraph from Clinton-Lisell (2023), read on the author's university repository and on ERIC.

topics.title: Design the handoffs between media

situation.text: The programme has a video, a workshop and a quiz. Each is fine. Nobody designed how one leads to the next.

items: Choose a pattern: content then live, live wrapped by self-paced, or short units spread over time.
Write the handoff between each pair: what to do next, and why now.
Keep terms, story and difficulty consistent across media.
Check nothing is left with no link to the rest.

why.text: A blend is only as good as its transitions. Learners should experience one programme, not a pile of separate assets.
In practice the handoff is a common place for a blend to break: instructions are missing, or the next piece does not use the last.

Research on blended design is thin on this point. A 2017 review of 20 studies names four design challenges: building in flexibility, getting people to interact, supporting how they learn, and creating a good climate for learning. It does not test handoffs as such, so treat this page as practitioner advice.

items.title: Design the joins
items.text: The transitions matter as much as the pieces.

try.text: Take a blended programme. Write the handoff between each pair of media.

try.title: A handoff, written down
try.text: The video ends with: "In the workshop you will use these four steps on your own case, so bring one." The workshop opens by asking for those cases. The quiz a week later uses the same four step names.

items: A great video followed by an unconnected quiz teaches little.
Different authors drift in terms. Keep a glossary.
Measuring across media is harder. Plan it early.

quiz.a: Its transitions.

quiz.q: What should each handoff say?
quiz.a: What to do next, and why now.

quiz.q: What keeps a blend feeling like one programme?

topics.title: Use immersive technology for what it does best

situation.text: A client has bought headsets and wants "something in VR".

items: Ask what must be practised that is dangerous, rare, costly or impossible to stage.
Use immersive tools for that.
Keep sessions short and brief people before and after.
Offer an alternative for people who cannot use a headset.
Compare the cost with a simpler method.

why.text: Immersive technology earns its place where real practice is unsafe or impractical: emergencies, heights, costly equipment, difficult conversations. It lets people rehearse in a setting close to the real one.

The measured gains are modest. A meta-analysis of 48 studies in schools and universities found a small overall advantage for immersive virtual reality over computer-based or traditional resources (g = 0.38). The size of the gain depended on what it was compared with. A meta-analysis of workplace training found that virtual reality did better than the alternatives it was tested against, and that the fit between the task and the technology mattered while the type of headset or controller did not.

why.title: More presence, less learning
why.found: Fifty-two students learned from the same science simulation on a desktop or in a headset. Those in the headset reported much more presence but learned less (d = 0.80 in favour of the desktop), and brain-activity measures suggested higher cognitive load.
why.means: Do not assume that a more immersive version teaches better, and test learning as well as enjoyment.

try.text: List three skills in your field that cannot be practised safely for real. Say whether immersion would add anything a role-play could not.

try.title: A case for a headset
try.text: A warehouse team must learn what to do when a racking unit starts to fail. It cannot be staged safely. A ten-minute headset scenario lets each person rehearse the response, followed by a debrief. A seated tablet version is offered too.

items: Some people feel sick in headsets.
Novelty inflates early results.
Content dates and is costly to update.
More immersion can mean less learning. In one experiment, students felt more present in a headset and learned less than on a desktop.

parts.title: Build video, audio and e-learning
parts.summary: Storyboards, production, interactivity and tracking.

topics.title: Storyboard before you produce anything

situation.text: You jump into recording and find the structure does not work once it is filmed.

items: Plan pictures, narration, on-screen text and interaction on paper first.
Write narration to be spoken, in plain conversational language.
Match words to pictures frame by frame.
Build a rough version and test it.

why.text: Changes are cheap on paper and expensive in the edit. The storyboard is where the decisions about load and layout are made.
An expert's raw material is not a script. It has to be reorganised for someone who does not know the subject.

try.text: Storyboard a two-minute teaching segment: picture, narration and on-screen text for each frame.

try.title: A storyboard catches the problem
try.text: A three-column page: sketch of the picture, the words to be spoken, and any on-screen text. Reading it aloud to a colleague shows that frame four explains a term before frame two has introduced it. You swap them on paper.

items: A storyboard nobody reviews saves nothing.
Plan decision points as well as the straight path.
Read the script aloud before recording.

topics.title: Get the sound right and keep videos short

situation.text: The video is forty minutes long, filmed beautifully, with echoing sound.

items: Get the audio clean first.
Keep each video short and on one point.
Let people pause, replay and skip.
Show a presenter only where a person adds something.
Cut what does not serve the objective.

why.text: Poor sound makes a video hard to follow, however good the pictures. Long, single-piece video goes against what is known about load and segmenting.
A face on screen can add social presence. It can also pull attention from the content.

The usual figure on length comes from a 2014 study of 6.9 million viewing sessions in four online university courses. People watched nearly all of a video under six minutes and far less of longer ones. That study measured how long people watched, not what they learned, so use it as a guide to attention.

why.title: How video production affects student engagement
why.found: Using 6.9 million viewing sessions from four online courses, the authors found that shorter videos held viewers much better and that informal talking-head videos held them better than polished studio ones. Engagement meant time watched and whether people tried the questions afterwards. Learning was not measured.
why.means: Keep each video to a few minutes and one point, and do not spend on studio polish.

try.text: Record and edit a short teaching video. Review it against segmenting and coherence.

try.title: One long video, remade
try.text: Before: one forty-minute recording of a whole session, made with a laptop microphone in an echoing room. After: six short videos, each on one question, recorded with a clip-on microphone, with captions and a transcript.

items: Add captions and a transcript.
Generated voices and video raise questions of quality and disclosure.
Polish is not the goal.
Sound first is production experience. The research reviews read for this page do not test audio quality.

quiz.q: What control should learners have?
quiz.a: To pause, replay and skip.

topics.title: Build interactions that make people think

situation.text: The e-learning is forty screens of "click next", with a drag-and-drop to break it up.

items: Make each interaction ask the learner to recall, decide or apply.
Give feedback that explains.
Use scenarios with choices to build judgement.
Remove interactions that only move the page on.

why.text: Interaction for its own sake adds load without learning. The useful kind makes people think: retrieve something, make a decision, see the result.
Choosing an authoring tool comes after deciding what interaction the objective needs.

try.text: Design one interaction that forces recall or a decision. Say why it is more than a click-through.

try.title: From click to decision
try.text: Before: click to reveal five facts about data handling. After: a customer email asks for a colleague's phone number. The learner chooses a reply, sees what happens next, and reads why the safer choice was right.

items: "Engaging" interactions can crowd out learning.
Branching multiplies the work. Keep the tree small.
Check it works with a keyboard and a screen reader.

topics.title: Choose tracking that fits what you need to measure
topics.theory: Standards and platforms: SCORM, xAPI, cmi5

situation.text: IT asks whether your course is "SCORM compliant". You are not sure what you need to track.

items: Decide what you need to know about the learning.
Pick the standard that can record it.
Record a few things that will change a decision.
Keep content portable between platforms.

why.text: SCORM is the long-standing reference model for packaging e-learning and reporting progress to a learning management system. Its most recent release, SCORM 2004 4th Edition, dates from 2009. xAPI records learning activity in many more settings, such as mobile learning, simulations and offline work, and keeps it in a learning record store. Version 2.0 became an IEEE standard in 2023. cmi5 is a set of rules for using xAPI with a learning management system. It covers how content is launched and how results are reported.

Suppliers tend to describe a learning management system as built around administration and a learning experience platform as built around the learner. These are market labels, not standards, so check what each product records. The wrong choice quietly limits what you can measure later.
SCORM is still widely used. The body that created it says newer specifications are overtaking it, and US defence guidance now recommends xAPI and cmi5 for new e-learning.

items.title: Measure first
items.text: Decide what you need to know.

items.title: SCORM, xAPI, cmi5
items.text: Inside the platform, anywhere, or both.

try.text: For a given delivery scenario, choose the standard and list the few things you would track.

try.title: Tracking that fits the need
try.text: A client only needs to know who finished the fire-safety module and whether they passed. A basic completion and score record is enough. Detailed tracking of every click would add work and change no decision.

items: Tracking everything teaches you nothing.
Avoid lock-in to one supplier.
Standards change. Check the current specifications.
Ask which SCORM version is meant. SCORM 1.2 and SCORM 2004 are separate versions, and you need to know which one the platform accepts.

parts.title: Accessibility, experts and upkeep
parts.summary: Building to a professional standard that lasts.

topics.title: Build to WCAG 2.2 AA from the start

situation.text: Accessibility is on the list for "after launch". It is rarely reached.

items: Make content perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
Aim for level AA of WCAG 2.2.
Fix the common failures first: text alternatives, contrast, keyboard use, colour as the only signal.
Caption video and provide transcripts.
Build it in from the start.

why.text: WCAG 2.2 is the version of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines that UK government guidance now points to. Its success criteria are graded by level. Government services are asked to meet all the A and AA criteria, so AA is the usual target. Building access in from the start is usually cheaper and easier than adding it later.
Access is wider than sight and hearing. It includes attention, memory and processing.

In the UK, what the law asks depends on who you work for. The accessibility regulations for public sector bodies require their websites, intranets and public-facing apps to meet WCAG 2.2 AA and to publish an accessibility statement. Some bodies and some content are exempt, for example live audio and video. The GOV.UK guidance lists the exemptions.

Those regulations do not cover private companies. Employers still have a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled workers, under the Equality Act 2010 in Great Britain and the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 in Northern Ireland. GOV.UK lists training opportunities among its examples. This is not legal advice. Ask the client which duties apply to them.

try.text: Audit a real asset against a WCAG 2.2 AA checklist. Fix the top failures.

try.title: Three common failures, fixed
try.text: Before: a module with a silent video, pale grey text and a drag-and-drop that needs a mouse. After: captions and a transcript, darker text, and the same question answerable with the keyboard alone.

items: Automated checkers catch only part of the problem.
Legal duties vary. Check which apply to you.
Test with a keyboard and a screen reader.

quiz.a: Any two of: missing text alternatives, poor contrast, no keyboard access, colour as the only signal.

topics.title: Write so it can be translated later

situation.text: The course is to be translated. The text is baked into the images and every example is about cricket.

items: Keep text out of images.
Leave room for text to grow.
Avoid idioms and examples that only work in one culture.
Plan a glossary and a review by a native speaker.

why.text: Design content so it can be adapted before you try to translate it. Localising is more than translating: examples, images and references have to work in the new setting.
Content not prepared for this is costly and error-prone to adapt later.

Text usually gets longer when translated from English, and short labels grow the most. W3C guidance quotes IBM figures of two to three times the length for strings of up to ten characters, and about 1.3 times for passages over 70 characters. Some scripts also need taller lines.

try.text: Take a piece of content. Find everything that would obstruct translation and redesign it.

try.title: Ready to translate
try.text: Before: a diagram with English labels drawn into the picture, and a cricket example. After: labels as editable text beside numbered points on the image, with spare room, and an example about queuing at a shop.

items: Machine translation needs human review.
Humour rarely survives.
Norms about directness and hierarchy change what works.

quiz.a: Design the content so it can be adapted.

quiz.q: Where should text not be?
quiz.a: Baked into images.

topics.title: Draw out the steps experts no longer notice
topics.theory: Working with subject experts and the expert blind spot

situation.text: The expert hands you two hundred slides and says "it is all in there".

items: Ask the expert to do the task while talking through it.
Ask what they would check, and what could go wrong.
Write down the steps they did not mention.
Reorganise the material for someone new.
Agree scope: what a beginner needs first.

why.text: Experts have automated much of what they know and lose sight of what newcomers do not know. Their explanations skip steps. This is often called the expert blind spot, or the curse of knowledge.
Your job is not to transcribe the expert. It is to surface what they no longer notice and put it in learnable order.

In one study, trainee teachers with more advanced maths were more likely to assume pupils must master equations before word problems. Pupils' real results point the other way. Knowing a subject well can mislead you about how a beginner learns it.

why.title: Cognitive task analysis-based training: a meta-analysis
why.found: Training built on a structured analysis of how experts think and decide beat training built on other ways of gathering content, with a large average effect (Hedges' g = 0.871). The number of studies was small and results varied a good deal by method and setting.
why.means: Do not build from the expert's slides alone. Watch them work and question them about the decisions they make.

items.title: Reorganise
items.text: Expert order is not learning order.

try.text: Interview someone on a skill they know well. Find at least three steps they left out at first.

try.title: The steps nobody mentioned
try.text: A senior engineer explains a safety check in four steps. When you watch her do it, she also glances at a gauge and wipes a seal first. Neither was mentioned. Both go into the learner's version.

items: Experts disagree. Reconcile them before you build.
Protect learners from the information dump.
Respect the expert's time and credit them.
There are more than a hundred named methods for drawing out expert knowledge, and little evidence on which works best. Keep yours simple: watch, ask, write down, check back.

topics.title: Keep one current version of everything
topics.theory: Asset management, versioning and the toolchain

situation.text: There are four versions of the deck in three folders, and nobody knows which is current.

items: Keep one approved version in one place.
Name and date versions the same way every time.
Build templates that already meet your design and access standards.
Decide who owns, reviews and retires each asset.
Tag assets so they can be found.

why.text: Content that cannot be found, updated or trusted decays and misleads. Production is a system to maintain, not a run of one-off files.
Templates make work faster and more consistent, and carry good practice with them.

try.text: Design a simple versioning scheme for a real content library. Say how a stale asset is found and retired.

try.title: One current deck
try.text: Before: "Induction deck FINAL v3 (new).pptx" in three folders. After: one file in one shared folder, named by course, version and date, with an owner and a review date on the first slide. Older copies go to an archive folder.

items: Rules nobody follows are worse than none. Keep them light.
Old versions linger in inboxes. Link, do not attach.
Review dates need someone to act on them.

An archived copy of the old content maintenance page was read: it describes setting a review date and getting a reminder. It is not linked because the live page has moved.
Halvorson and Rach (2012), Content Strategy for the Web: not opened.
'Templates make work faster and more consistent' has no source.

That is the only support found. It backs 'one current version' and review in principle. It does not cover naming schemes, templates, tagging or owners. No research evidence was found, and the rating says so.
No text changed.

stages.name: Run the room
stages.question: How do we facilitate, in person and online?
stages.wordingStatus: Draft: part names and topic titles for this stage were written for the build pack and have not been seen by Mica

parts.title: Hold the room
parts.summary: Presence, questions, group dynamics and story.

topics.title: Slow down and use the pause

situation.text: You talk fast when nervous, fill every silence, and have been told communication is "93 per cent non-verbal".

items: Slow down.
Pause after a key point and after a question.
Vary pace and volume on purpose.
Read nerves as readiness.
Prepare and rehearse. Presence is built.

why.text: Presence is the composure and attention that let you hold a room. It comes from preparation and practice more than personality. A pause gives people time to think and signals confidence.

The "93 per cent" figure adds 38 per cent for tone of voice to 55 per cent for the face, leaving 7 per cent for words. Those weights come from 1960s experiments on how people judge liking and disliking. Their author says they apply only when someone is talking about their own feelings or attitudes. When you teach, your words carry the content.

Nerves and excitement feel alike in the body. In one set of experiments, people who told themselves they were excited before singing, speaking in public or doing maths performed better than people who tried to calm down.

items.title: Content matters
items.text: The 93 per cent claim is a myth.

try.text: Deliver a short segment on camera. Get structured feedback on pace, pause and presence.

try.title: The same opening, twice
try.text: First run: a trainer reads the three aims in one breath and moves straight on. Second run: she says the first aim, stops for two slow breaths, looks round the room, then gives the next. Same words. The second version gives people time to take each aim in.

items: Claims about reading body language are overconfident.
Presence changes on camera. Practise both.
Do not perform a personality that is not yours.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Mehrabian (1981), Silent Messages: Implicit Communication of Emotions and Attitudes.
Brooks (2014), Get excited: Reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement.

No account of how the Mehrabian figures are misapplied was opened other than the author's own page.
Whether the Brooks (2014) result has been replicated was not checked.

The draft said the 93 per cent figure comes from a narrow study. The author's page points to two original sources and describes experiments on like and dislike. Text and quiz answer changed to say experiments on liking and disliking.

The draft sentence that what you say still matters most is not something the source says. It was replaced with a narrower sentence.

The PubMed record for Mehrabian and Ferris (1967), Journal of Consulting Psychology, was opened and confirms the paper and date but shows no abstract, so it is not in the links.

topics.title: Ask, then wait

situation.text: You ask "any questions?", wait one second, and move on.

items: Decide whether this moment needs telling or drawing out.
Ask open questions.
After asking, wait several seconds.
Receive a wrong answer in a way that keeps the person contributing.
Use pairs first so everyone thinks.
Wait again after an answer before you respond.

why.text: Presenting sends content to an audience. Facilitating draws learning out of a group. A skilled trainer knows which the moment needs.

In studies of school lessons, teachers usually waited about one second after a question. When they waited three to five seconds, answers got longer, more pupils answered and pupils asked more questions. Most people wait far too little.

This research comes from school classrooms, not workplace training. Treat three seconds as a starting point, not a rule. A long silence after an unclear question only adds confusion, so make the question clear first.

why.title: Wait-time and rewards as instructional variables
why.found: From five years of recorded primary science lessons, teachers waited about one second for an answer and replied within about a second of getting one. When both waits were stretched to three to five seconds, pupils gave longer answers, offered more answers unprompted, asked more questions and sounded more confident.
why.means: Count to three in your head after you ask and again after someone answers, and expect to adapt this for adults.

try.text: Facilitate a short discussion with open questions and deliberate waiting. Note what the silence produced.

try.title: Any questions?
try.text: Before: "Any questions? No? Good." One second, then the next slide. After: "What would make this hard to use on Monday? Take a moment." The trainer counts slowly to five in her head. Someone speaks on four. She waits again before replying.

items: Silence feels longer to you than to the room.
Know when to hold your own expertise back.
Do not let the confident few answer everything.

quiz.a: Several seconds.

quiz.q: What does waiting produce?

Rowe studied two waits: after the question and after the answer. The draft covered only the first. A step was added for the second.
The evidence read is all from schools. A caveat was added so the page does not imply it was tested with adults at work.
Stahl (1994) notes that three seconds is a convention, not a strict cut-off, and that silence after an unclear question adds confusion. Both points were added.

Tobin (1987) is a review across subjects and school grades and concludes that wait time appears to help higher-level learning by giving more time to think. It was added because the task asked for it to be checked.

topics.title: Manage the group, not only the content

situation.text: One person dominates, two have gone quiet, and a disagreement is brewing.

items: Watch the group as well as the content.
Give dominant voices a job and quieter ones a turn.
Build individual accountability into group tasks.
Deal with conflict early and in private where you can.
Protect safety while you do it.

why.text: Group dynamics do not sort themselves out. The well-known model of forming, storming, norming and performing is a useful lens. It was built from a review of about 50 earlier studies, many of them of therapy groups, and not from new data on work teams. Real groups do not move through the stages so neatly.
People tend to contribute less in a group than alone. Giving each person a visible part counters that.

try.text: Plan how you would handle three difficult-group situations while protecting safety. Role-play one.

try.title: A job for the loudest voice
try.text: One person answers every question. At the next task the trainer asks him to keep time and write up the group's points. She gives everyone two minutes to note an answer alone, then asks two quieter people to read theirs out first.

items: Norms about speaking up and silence differ between cultures.
Publicly correcting someone costs the whole room.
Large groups need structure, not volume.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Tuckman (1984), This Week's Citation Classic: Developmental sequence in small groups. The author's own account of the 1965 paper.

quiz.a: No. They need managing.

quiz.q: How should you use the forming-storming model?
quiz.a: As a lens, not a script.

quiz.q: What counters people coasting in groups?
quiz.a: Individual accountability.

topics.tierReason: The stage model is a synthesis of older studies used as a lens, and the steps for handling a group are professional practice. The social loafing research behind individual accountability could not be opened in this run.

topics.title: Use a story to make the point concrete
topics.theory: Storytelling and the curse of knowledge

situation.text: You explain an abstract idea three times and it does not land.

items: Find a short, true story that shows the idea.
Make it concrete: a person, a place, what happened.
Say the point it makes.
Use an analogy from something the group already knows.
Check the story serves the point.

why.text: A well-chosen story makes an abstract point concrete and easier to remember. A meta-analysis found that people understood and recalled stories better than essays. People who know a subject well find it hard to set that knowledge aside and judge what a newcomer will follow. This is called the curse of knowledge. Naming it helps you guard against it.
Practitioner writing on communication suggests that ideas which last tend to be concrete, unexpected and to carry some feeling. Treat that as a rule of thumb.

why.title: Stories against essays: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across more than 75 samples and over 33,000 participants, stories were understood and recalled better than essays. Results varied a great deal between studies and there were signs of publication bias.
why.means: Use a short story to carry an abstract point, and do not expect every story to help.

items.title: Concrete
items.text: A person and an event beat an abstraction.

try.text: Tell a short story that makes one abstract idea concrete. Check it against the risk of distraction.

try.title: From rule to story
try.text: Abstract: "Handover errors come from assumed knowledge." Story: "On a night shift a nurse wrote 'usual dose' on a chart. The agency nurse who took over had never met the patient." Then say the point: write what a stranger would need.

items: A vivid story can outweigh the evidence.
Keep a bank of stories and retire the stale ones.
Other people's stories need permission.
The authors of the story meta-analysis warn against forcing all content into story form. Use a story where it fits the point.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Mar and colleagues (2021), Memory and comprehension of narrative versus expository texts: a meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin and Review.

quiz.q: What does a story do for an abstract idea?
quiz.a: Makes it concrete and memorable.

quiz.q: Why do experts explain badly?
quiz.a: They find it hard to set aside what they know and see the subject as a newcomer does.

quiz.q: What must a story do?
quiz.a: Serve the point.

Hinds (1999), The curse of expertise, would be a closer source for experts misjudging novices. Not opened.
The seductive details research (Sundararajan and Adesope 2020) on the risk of distraction was not opened.
The watch item that a vivid story can outweigh the evidence has no source.

The paper's experiments were on economic judgements, so its use here is an extension.

topics.tierReason: One meta-analysis found stories are understood and recalled better than essays, but the studies varied widely, showed signs of publication bias, and tested texts, not a trainer's spoken stories.

topics.title: Set up the room before you plan the session
topics.theory: The learning environment: physical, virtual and hybrid

situation.text: You arrive to find a boardroom table, no wall space and a projector at the far end.

items: Ask about the room before you design: layout, light, sound, wall space, access.
Arrange seating for the activity: small tables for group work, a horseshoe for discussion.
Check everyone can see, hear and get in.
Arrive early and move the furniture.
Online, the platform is the room. Set it up the same way.

why.text: The same content lands differently in a well or badly arranged space. Layout signals what kind of session this is: rows say "listen", small tables say "work together".
Research on learning spaces is mostly from schools and universities. For workplace training, treat this as informed practice.

One university study compared the same course, with the same lecturer, in a room with round tables and a room with rows. In the round-table room the lecturer talked less and led more discussion, although he meant to teach both groups the same way. It was one course with about forty students, so take it as an illustration.

items.title: Layout signals
items.text: Rows or tables send a message.

try.text: Draw the room for your next session. Mark where groups work, where you stand and what people can see.

try.title: The boardroom table
try.text: The room has one long table and the plan has four group tasks. The trainer arrives forty minutes early, pushes the table to the wall and sets four clusters of chairs round flipchart sheets taped to the windows. She checks the screen from the back seat.

items: A fixed room may need a changed activity.
Check step-free access, hearing loops and quiet space.
Temperature and noise can distract. Check both.

quiz.a: Before you design.

quiz.q: What does layout signal?

quiz.q: What is the room when you teach online?
quiz.a: The platform.

topics.title: Train the team together when the work is done together

situation.text: Five people from five teams attend a teamwork course. They return to teams who were not there.

items: Where the work is done as a team, train the team together.
Practise the team's real tasks.
Practise communication, handovers and speaking up.
Debrief as a team after practice and after real work.
Give each person a turn at another role.

why.text: Team skills are different from individual skills. A team has to coordinate, share a picture of the task and back each other up. Those are learned by practising together.

A meta-analysis of 93 results from 2,650 teams found that team training had a moderate, positive effect on how teams think, feel, work together and perform. A later meta-analysis of 129 healthcare studies found the same direction. A third found that teams and individuals who debriefed did about 20 to 25 per cent better than those who did not.

These studies compare team training with none. They show that what is trained, how stable the team is and how big it is all change the result. They do not test whether training the whole team beats training a few members, so treat that step as sound reasoning.

why.title: Does team training improve team performance?
why.found: Pooling 93 results from 2,650 teams, team training had a moderate, positive effect on team thinking, attitudes, teamwork and performance. Training content, team stability and team size changed the size of the effect.
why.means: Train teams on their real work, and expect better results from stable teams with focused content.

items.title: Debrief
items.text: After practice and after the real thing.

try.text: For one team you train, list the three moments where coordination fails. Design practice for one.

try.title: Same course, two ways
try.text: Before: five people from five teams spend a day on generic teamwork. After: one ward team spends a morning practising its own shift handover, swaps roles for the second run, and ends with fifteen minutes on what to keep and what to change.

items: Team-building days are not team training.
Rank silences people. Make it safe to speak up.
Releasing a whole team is costly. Plan cover.

quiz.a: When the work is done as a team.

quiz.q: What do teams need to practise?

quiz.q: What helps teams learn from practice?
quiz.a: A structured debrief.

A separate meta-analysis on team building exists (Klein and colleagues 2009, seen in search results only) and reports that team building has effects of its own, so do not read the item as saying team building does nothing.

topics.title: Adjust for the cultures in the room

situation.text: A discussion method that works at home falls silent with a group from several countries.

items: Find out who will be in the room.
Vary how people contribute: writing first, pairs, then the group.
Be explicit about what you are asking for.
Speak plainly and avoid idiom.
Ask a local colleague what to watch for.

why.text: Groups differ in how directly people speak, how they treat rank, and what silence means. A method that assumes everyone will challenge the trainer does not travel.

Models that score countries on cultural dimensions are widely used and criticised for treating a country as one culture. A meta-analysis of 558 studies that used the best-known model found that about 80 per cent of the variation in cultural values lies within countries, not between them.

why.title: Does country equate with culture?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 558 studies using Hofstede's framework found that about 80 per cent of the variation in cultural values sits within countries. The authors conclude that country is often a weak stand-in for culture.
why.means: Find out about the people in the room. Do not predict a person from a passport.

try.text: Take one discussion activity. Add a written step and a pair step before the group step.

try.title: Three ways in
try.text: Before: "Who disagrees with this?" Silence. After: everyone writes one concern on a card. Pairs compare cards. Each pair reads out one concern, not their own. The trainer says plainly that she wants to hear the problems.

items: Guessing someone's culture from their name is a mistake.
Working in a second language is tiring. Slow down.
Humour and examples may not travel.
Books that place countries on scales are practitioner guides. Use them for questions to ask, not for predictions about a person.

quiz.q: How can you give everyone a way in?

quiz.q: What is the risk of country models?

parts.title: Teach online
parts.summary: Remote and hybrid sessions on their own terms.

topics.title: Design against video-call fatigue

situation.text: Your in-person day has been moved online unchanged. By mid-afternoon people are drained.

items: Use a wider view, and do not hold constant close-up eye contact.
Suggest people hide their own image.
Build in movement and audio-only stretches.
Reduce what people must watch at once: faces, chat and slides.
Give people a choice about cameras.

why.text: One researcher proposes four likely causes of video-call fatigue: too much close-up eye contact, seeing yourself constantly, sitting still, and the extra effort of sending and reading non-verbal cues. He says the four have not yet been tested directly, so treat them as likely, not proven. Each has a design answer.
Fatigue is a feature of the setting, not a failing of the learner.

why.title: A scale for video-call fatigue
why.found: The authors built a 15-item questionnaire covering general, social, emotional, visual and motivational fatigue, and tested it with 2,724 people. People with more frequent, longer and more closely packed video meetings reported more fatigue. This is survey data, so it shows a link, not a cause.
why.means: Shorten live blocks and put gaps between them.

try.text: Take a tiring online session. Redesign it against the four causes.

try.title: The afternoon block
try.text: Before: three hours of slides with all cameras on in gallery view. After: forty-minute blocks. One block is a phone call in pairs while walking. Cameras are optional during input, and the trainer shows people how to hide their own image.

items: Cameras on may help connection and may cost energy. Let people choose.
Splitting attention between chat and slides is a load problem.
In survey data, more frequent, longer and closely packed video meetings go with more fatigue. Keep live blocks short and leave gaps.

quiz.q: Name the four proposed causes of video-call fatigue.
quiz.a: Close-up eye contact, seeing yourself, sitting still, and the effort of sending and reading cues.

quiz.q: Whose failing is the fatigue?
quiz.a: Nobody's. It comes from the setting.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off with cameras on?
quiz.a: Connection against energy.

openPoints: Fauville and colleagues' second paper, on non-verbal mechanisms and why fatigue is higher for women, is the survey test of the four causes. It appeared in search results but was not opened.
Shockley and colleagues (2021) on camera use and fatigue: not opened.
No source for cameras helping connection.
checkFindings: Bailenson (2021): the paper's four headings are eye gaze at a close distance, cognitive load, an all-day mirror and reduced mobility. The draft described the cognitive load argument as reading cues only. It covers sending them too. The why text and quiz answer were corrected.
The summary says the arguments rest on theory and earlier research and have not been tested directly in video calls. The first-pass softening was right and is now stated in the author's terms.
Bailenson's own remedies (hide self-view, smaller faces, audio-only calls, a set-up that lets you move) match the page's steps.
The watch item that shorter is better was replaced with the survey finding from Fauville and colleagues (2021). The camera item was softened.
topics.tierReason: The four causes are a theoretical argument that its author says has not been tested directly, and the supporting evidence read is survey data.

topics.title: Build connection, thinking and direction online

situation.text: The online course is a set of videos and a forum nobody posts in.

items: Help people feel present as real people.
Set tasks that make people think and discuss, and bring discussion to a conclusion.
Be visibly there: design, guide and steer.
Find the weakest of the three and add one move to strengthen it.

why.text: A widely used framework says good online learning needs three kinds of presence working together: social, cognitive and teaching. It was built to describe written, discussion-based courses in universities.
A common weak pattern is content with a thin teaching presence and little of the other two.

why.title: Learning in communities of inquiry: a review
why.found: The authors reviewed the studies that used the framework up to 2008. Few measured learning, and those that did mostly used a single survey question on how much students felt they had learned. They concluded the evidence did not show deep learning arising from the model.
why.means: Use the three presences as a design checklist, and measure learning yourself.

try.text: Audit an online course for the three presences. Add one move to strengthen the weakest.

try.title: The silent forum
try.text: Before: "Post your thoughts on week two." Nobody does. After: "Post one case from your own work where this failed. Reply to one other person with a question." On Friday the tutor posts a short summary of what the group concluded.

items: The framework is widely used and has its critics. A 2009 review found that few studies had measured learning at all, and most relied on students rating their own learning.
A forum needs a reason to post.
Presence takes facilitator time. Budget for it.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Garrison, Anderson and Archer, Critical thinking and computer conferencing: a model and tool to assess cognitive presence. A paper by the framework's authors that sets out the three presences.
Rourke and Kanuka (2009), Learning in communities of inquiry: a review of the literature. Journal of Distance Education.

quiz.a: Social, cognitive and teaching.

quiz.q: What does weak online learning often lack?
quiz.a: Social and cognitive presence.

quiz.q: What is teaching presence?
quiz.a: The design, guidance and steering that hold the rest together.

topics.title: Keep live time for interaction

situation.text: A two-hour webinar has ninety minutes of slides and ten minutes for questions.

items: Move anything one-way to pre-work.
Use polls, chat, breakout rooms and shared documents to get people thinking.
Give each breakout a clear task, a named reporter and a time.
Use pairs before whole-group discussion.
Have a second person run the technology.

why.text: Live time is scarce. Spend it on what needs real-time interaction. If a live session has no interaction, it should not be live.
The tools are instruments for taking part and recalling, not novelties.

The research is on formats, not on this advice. One meta-analysis found live online learning did slightly better than self-paced online learning on what people learned, and no clear difference from the classroom. Another found blended courses beat classroom teaching, but those courses also gave people more time and more interaction, so the mix alone may not be the cause.

try.text: Redesign an online session so every live minute is interactive. Move the rest to pre-work.

try.title: Ninety minutes of slides
try.text: Before: ninety minutes of slides, ten for questions. After: the slides go out as a twenty-minute recording. The live hour opens with a poll on the recording, then breakouts with one case each, a named reporter and eight minutes on the clock.

items: An empty breakout room is a design failure.
Fewer cues online. Ask people what they are thinking.
Have a plan for when the platform fails.

quiz.q: What should live time be used for?
quiz.a: What needs real-time interaction.

quiz.q: What does a breakout need?
quiz.a: A clear task, a named reporter and a time.

quiz.q: Why have a producer?
quiz.a: So the facilitator can attend to the learners.

topics.title: In hybrid, design for the remote person first

situation.text: Half the group is in the room and half is on a screen at the end of the table.

items: Design the remote experience first.
Give remote people a voice early and often.
Pair remote and in-room people.
Check sound and sightlines from the remote end.
For self-paced parts, build in recall, spacing and a steady rhythm.

why.text: Hybrid is hard to do well, because remote people easily become spectators. A review of 47 studies found that remote students often feel left out, take part less and struggle to signal that they want to speak. Designing for them first is a practical answer. It has not been tested head to head.
Self-paced study can lose people. Spacing, recall and a facilitator's regular presence are sensible ways to keep them going. No source on completion has been checked for this page.

why.title: Synchronous hybrid learning: a review
why.found: Reviewing 47 studies, the authors found that hybrid sessions widen access but are hard to teach. Remote students often feel excluded and are more passive, and sound quality is decisive. Most studies were case studies and only one was an experiment.
why.means: Plan the remote experience and the sound first, and check both from the remote end.

items.title: Equal experience
items.text: Design it. It will not happen by default.

try.text: Plan a hybrid session that gives remote and in-room people an equivalent experience. List the moves.

try.title: Who speaks first
try.text: Before: the room talks for ten minutes, then someone asks if the people online have anything to add. After: each question goes to a remote person first. Every in-room pair has a remote partner on a laptop. A colleague at the remote end checks the sound.

items: If you cannot make it fair, run it all online.
Room microphones decide whether remote people can take part.
Side conversations in the room exclude the screen.
The research on hybrid sessions is young. Most of it is case studies from universities, with very few comparisons.

quiz.a: The remote person's.

quiz.q: What happens otherwise?
quiz.a: They become spectators.

quiz.q: What helps people finish self-paced study?
quiz.a: Spacing, recall and a facilitator's regular presence.

parts.title: Judgement and recovery
parts.summary: What experienced trainers do when the plan stops working.

topics.title: Know why a tip works before you use it

situation.text: A colleague swears by a trick: always start with an icebreaker, always end on a quiz.

items: For each tip, ask what principle makes it work.
Keep the tips that rest on one.
Drop the ones that are habit.
Write the principle next to the tip.
Adapt the tip when conditions change.

why.text: A tip you understand you can adapt. A tip you copy breaks when conditions change.
Some craft lore is sound and some is superstition. The test is the same one you apply to any learning claim.

try.text: Take five tips from practice. For each, find the principle behind it or mark it as folklore.

try.title: Always start with an icebreaker
try.text: Tip: always start with an icebreaker. Principle: people speak up more once they have spoken once. Adapted for a team that already knows each other: skip the game and open with a paired question about the topic.

items: Experienced people defend habits. Ask what it is for.
Breaking a rule is earned by knowing its purpose.
Your own favourites need the same test.

deeper.text: A link means the paper's published summary was read and supports what this page says. "Not checked yet" means the reference has not been opened.

items.label: The outline draws on earlier modules and gives no separate source.

topics.bodyStatus: Draft, written from the curriculum outline. Sources not checked yet.

quiz.q: Why attach a principle to a tip?
quiz.a: So you can adapt it when conditions change.

quiz.q: How do you tell sound lore from folklore?
quiz.a: Ask what principle makes it work.

quiz.q: When may you break a rule?
quiz.a: When you know what it is for.

openPoints: Possible sources, not opened: Dunlosky and colleagues (2013) and Kirschner and van Merriënboer (2013).
The example principle, that people speak up more once they have spoken once, has no source.
When checked, a D rating is the likely result, since this is professional reasoning with nothing to test directly.
checkFindings: No search was spent on this topic, so it stays unchecked. The page cites no source and makes no research claim apart from its illustrative example.

topics.title: Rehearse what could go wrong

situation.text: The projector fails, a participant turns hostile, and the main activity falls flat.

items: Before the session, imagine it has gone badly and ask why.
List the three most likely failures.
Rehearse a response to each.
Carry a version that needs no technology.
When it happens, protect people's dignity first.

why.text: These are predictable situations, not rare accidents. A plan for recovery matters as much as the plan for the session.
Good improvising rests on preparation.

The pre-mortem comes from Gary Klein, who describes it as a team exercise at the start of a project. Everyone assumes the project has failed and writes down why. He cites earlier research suggesting that imagining an event has already happened helps people find reasons for it. Using it alone before a session is an adaptation.

try.text: Run a pre-mortem on a real session. List three likely failures and rehearse a recovery for each.

try.title: Ten minutes the night before
try.text: The trainer imagines the session went badly and writes why: the projector failed, the case study ran long, one person argued with everything. She prints the key slide as a handout, marks which exercise to cut, and plans a line for taking the argument to the break.

items: Over-planning for disaster can make you rigid.
Timing goes wrong more often than technology.
Know what you would cut.

quiz.a: Imagining the session has failed and asking why, before it happens.

quiz.q: What matters as much as the session plan?
quiz.a: A plan for recovery.

quiz.q: What comes first when things go wrong?
quiz.a: People's dignity.

topics.title: Change the plan when the room tells you to

situation.text: You are twenty minutes into the plan and the room has gone quiet in the wrong way.

items: Watch for energy, confusion and withdrawal.
Ask the room what is happening.
Change the plan: slow down, switch activity, take a break.
Online, ask more often.

why.text: The plan is a guess to be revised against what the room tells you. Delivering the plan while the room switches off is a failure.
Be modest about reading people. Cues are easy to misread and may differ between people and cultures. Asking is a safer check than guessing.

The idea that experienced people read a situation quickly comes from studies of firefighters, paramedics, pilots and chess players. Research on teachers noticing what a class is doing comes mostly from schools and has not been checked for this page. Treat reading the room as a skill to practise, not a proven method.

try.text: Practise responding to a room that shifts from engaged to disengaged. Debrief what you noticed and did.

try.title: Quiet in the wrong way
try.text: Twenty minutes in, nobody is writing. The trainer stops. "I may have lost you. Hold up one to five fingers for how clear this is." Mostly twos. She drops the next two slides and works one example on the flipchart.

items: Silence can mean thinking.
Online there are fewer cues.
Do not abandon the plan at the first yawn.

quiz.a: A guess to be revised against the room.

quiz.q: What is more reliable than reading faces?
quiz.a: Asking.

quiz.q: What do you do when the room switches off?
quiz.a: Change something.

topics.title: Review your own sessions

situation.text: You have run the same workshop for five years and it has not improved.

items: After each session, write what worked, what did not, and why.
Pick one weakness to work on next time.
Ask a peer to watch and comment.
Swap cases with other trainers.
Sit in someone else's session as a learner.

why.text: Experience alone does not reliably turn into expertise. Reflection helps. There are two kinds: adjusting while it happens, and learning afterwards. The second kind has been tested. A meta-analysis found that people and teams who held a structured debrief did about 20 to 25 per cent better than those who did not.
Experts decide fast by drawing on experience. Reviewing cases is a deliberate way to add to that store.

The idea of reflecting while you work comes from Donald Schön, who studied five professions, none of them teaching or training. It is a way of describing practice, not a tested method. The debrief studies cover teams and individuals in many fields. A trainer's own written review is a reasonable extension.

why.title: Do debriefs improve performance?
why.found: Pooling 46 samples and 2,136 people, debriefs improved performance by about 20 to 25 per cent compared with no debrief (d = 0.67). The effect held for teams and individuals, and in real and simulated settings.
why.means: Review each session in a set format with a clear focus, and act on one point.

items.title: Other eyes
items.text: A peer sees what you cannot.

try.text: Design a routine for reviewing your own sessions. Say how you will target one weakness.

try.title: Three lines after each session
try.text: Worked: the paired case study. Did not: the closing summary ran out of time, again. Why: the plan has no slack after lunch. Next time: cut one afternoon exercise and ask a colleague to watch the last half hour.

items: As you improve, you forget what newcomers find hard.
Reflection without change is a diary.
Feedback forms are a weak source.

topics.title: Look after yourself, and know your professional limits

situation.text: You deliver four days a week, travel on the fifth, and a participant asks you for advice well outside your field.

items: Plan recovery after delivery days.
Limit consecutive delivery days.
Know what you are qualified to advise on, and say when something is outside it.
Keep what participants tell you in confidence, within stated limits.
Declare any interest you have in what you recommend.
Have a peer you can talk cases through with.

why.text: Facilitating is tiring work. A tired trainer is likely to notice less and have less patience.

Professional bodies publish codes of conduct. The CIPD Code of Conduct and Ethics, in force since 1 January 2023, asks members to refer on work outside their expertise, protect confidential information, act honestly and disclose conflicts of interest. It applies to CIPD members. This page gives general principles.

items.title: Your limits
items.text: Say when it is outside your field.

try.text: Write three lines: what you advise on, what you refer on, and who you refer to.

try.title: Outside your field
try.text: At the break a participant describes a dispute with her manager and asks if she has a legal case. The trainer says: "That is outside what I can advise on. Acas or your union rep would be the place to start." She does not offer a view.

items: A participant in distress needs referral, not coaching.
Selling a follow-on product from the front of the room is a conflict of interest.
Safeguarding duties may apply. Check them.

stages.name: Make it stick
stages.question: How does it survive the return to work?
stages.wordingStatus: Draft: part names and topic titles for this stage were written for the build pack and have not been seen by Mica

parts.title: Get it used at work
parts.summary: Transfer, follow-up and coaching.

topics.title: Treat transfer as a design problem

situation.text: People leave the course keen, and a month later they work exactly as before.

items: Treat use at work as the goal of the design.
Check the three influences: the learner, the design, the workplace.
Find where it broke down.
Design for new situations as well as familiar ones.

why.text: Transfer is the point of training and it often fails. You will hear that only 10 per cent of training transfers to the job. That figure traces to a 1982 magazine article, which opened with a training director's guess and gave no data. A 2011 review found no behavioural evidence behind it. No single percentage fits all training, so do not quote one. The problem behind it is real.
Applying a skill to a similar situation is easier than applying it to a new one. The second has to be designed for.

A meta-analysis of 89 studies found transfer was linked to the learner's ability, conscientiousness and motivation, and to a supportive workplace. These links were stronger for open skills such as leadership than for closed skills such as using software. Results looked better than they were when the same person rated both the training and its use.

why.title: Transfer of training: a meta-analytic review
why.found: Across 89 studies, transfer was positively related to cognitive ability, conscientiousness, motivation and a supportive work environment. Most links were stronger for open skills such as leadership than for closed skills such as software. Links were inflated when one source supplied both measures in the same setting.
why.means: Check the learner, the design and the workplace, and get evidence of use from someone other than the learner.

items.title: Transfer is the point
items.text: A good event is not enough.

items.title: A guess
items.text: The 10 per cent figure has no data behind it.

try.text: Take a programme that did not transfer. Check it against the three influences and find where it failed.

try.title: Finding where it broke
try.text: Illustration. A team learns a new handover routine and says they like it. A month on, nobody uses it. The trainer checks the three influences. People can do it and the practice was realistic. The shift pattern leaves no time for it. The fix is in the workplace.

items: The workplace is easy to neglect. A supportive one is linked to more transfer.
Blaming the learner is the easy answer.
Do not quote the 10 per cent figure. Say what you saw change at work instead.

quiz.q: What are the three influences on transfer?
quiz.a: The learner, the training design and the workplace.

quiz.q: How should you treat the "10 per cent of training transfers" figure?
quiz.a: As a guess with no data behind it. Do not quote it.

quiz.q: Which kind of transfer is harder?
quiz.a: Applying a skill to a new situation.

topics.title: Plan the first use at work before people leave

situation.text: The course ends with "any final questions?" and a feedback form.

items: Practise on tasks that look like the job.
Vary the examples and settings.
Before people leave, have each write when and where they will first use it.
Use the form "when X happens, I will do Y".
Tell their manager what they planned.

why.text: Practice across varied examples helps people apply a skill in new settings more than repeating one example. Transfer should be built into every part of a course, not added on the last afternoon.

A specific if-then plan makes follow-through more likely than a general intention. A meta-analysis of 94 tests found a medium to large benefit for people who added such a plan to a goal, compared with holding the goal alone.

why.title: Implementation intentions and goal achievement
why.found: Across 94 independent tests, people who formed an if-then plan reached their goals more often than people who only held the goal. The effect was medium to large (d = .65). The plans helped people get started and stay on course.
why.means: Have each person write one when-and-where plan for first use before they leave the room.

items.title: When X, I will do Y
Before they leave
items.text: Plan the first use in the room.

try.text: Take a course that ends at the event. Add varied practice, a first-use plan and an if-then statement.

try.title: Before and after
try.text: Illustration. Before: "I will give better feedback." After: "When I finish Friday's one-to-one with each person, I will name one thing they did well and one thing to change." The second names the moment and the action.

items: Action plans written in a rush are forgotten.
A plan with no follow-up is weak.
Prior knowledge changes what transfers.

topics.title: Use 70-20-10 as a reminder, not a formula

situation.text: A strategy document says learning should be "70 per cent experience, 20 per cent social, 10 per cent formal".

items: Use the model as a reminder that most learning happens outside courses.
Do not use the numbers to set budgets.
Design the on-the-job part: stretch tasks, reflection, feedback.
Design the social part: coaching, peers, communities.

why.text: The numbers come from Center for Creative Leadership research in the 1980s, in which successful executives looked back on the events that had shaped them. The ratio itself was set out later, in a 1996 planning guide by Lombardo and Eichinger. A 2018 review found the evidence for the 70 per cent claim weak and the studies behind it inconsistent. The model is a useful reminder and not a validated formula.
Experience alone does not build expertise. Without reflection and feedback it levels off.
The Center for Creative Leadership itself says well-designed courses strengthen the other two parts. The model's own home does not treat it as a case for cutting formal training.

items.title: A reminder
items.text: Most learning is outside the course.

try.text: Take a "70-20-10 strategy". Rewrite it so the intent survives and the false precision goes.

try.title: Rewriting the line
try.text: Illustration. Before: "70 per cent of learning will come from experience, so the course budget falls by 70 per cent." After: "Most development happens in the work. We will design stretch tasks, feedback and peer support, and keep courses where a skill needs teaching."

items: The model is used to justify cutting formal training. That does not follow.
"Learning on the job" with no design is hoping.
Say where the numbers came from when you use them.

topics.title: Schedule the follow-up at 30, 60 and 90 days
topics.theory: Spaced reinforcement after the event, relapse prevention and coaching cycles

situation.text: The course was a success in March. By June nobody mentions it.

items: Schedule recall and a task to apply at 30, 60 and 90 days.
Ask people what will pull them back to old habits, and plan for it.
Set up regular check-ins with a manager or coach.
Send short prompts at the point of use.

why.text: A well-run event with no follow-through fades in a predictable way. Follow-up is part of the design.
Relapse prevention means naming the obstacles in advance and planning what to do when they come. Regular check-ins keep the new behaviour in view while it becomes routine.

items.title: Check-ins
items.text: Someone asks how it is going.

try.text: Design a 30, 60 and 90-day plan for a real programme. Include a step for relapse.

try.title: A relapse step
try.text: Illustration. At 30 days each person recalls the three steps from memory and tries one on a live task. Their plan includes a line such as: "When the week is too busy for the full routine, I will do step one only."

items: Follow-up needs an owner.
Reminders that only repeat content are ignored.
Measure whether it is working.
Treat 30, 60 and 90 days as a convenient convention. Fit the dates to when people will next use the skill.

topics.title: Coach with questions, not answers
topics.theory: Coaching and mentoring as a skill

situation.text: A manager says they "support the learning". In practice they tell people the answer.

items: Decide whether the moment needs coaching, mentoring or teaching.
Agree the goal.
Ask where things stand now.
Ask what the options are.
Ask what the person will do, and when.
Listen, and wait.

why.text: Coaching draws the answer out of the person. Mentoring shares experience. Teaching passes on knowledge. A common structure for a coaching conversation, set out in Whitmore's Coaching for Performance, runs through goal, reality, options and will. Will means what the person will do. Some versions call the last step way forward.

Two meta-analyses find that workplace coaching has positive effects on skills, performance, wellbeing and how people pursue their goals. The studies are few. One of the two looked only at coaching by trained internal or external coaches and left out managers coaching their own staff, so the evidence for manager coaching is thinner. Coaching is also a common way to follow up after a course.

why.title: Does workplace coaching work?
why.found: Pooling 17 studies of coaching by internal or external coaches, the authors found positive effects on skills, on attitudes and on results. Internal coaches did better than external ones. Face-to-face and online coaching did not differ, and nor did longer and shorter programmes. Coaching by line managers was left out.
why.means: Offer coaching as follow-up with some confidence, and do not assume a manager's coaching will work as well as a trained coach's.

try.text: Run a coaching conversation on a peer's real goal. Get feedback on your questions and your waiting.

try.title: Telling and asking
try.text: Illustration. Telling: "Send the client the revised plan today." Coaching: "What do you want from this client by Friday? Where are things now? What could you do? Which will you do, and when?" Then the manager waits.

items: A structure can become a script. Listen first.
Some people need telling. Know when.
Managers need time to coach.
The research is mostly on trained coaches. A manager also judges the person's work, which can make open answers harder to give.

topics.title: Make the new behaviour easy to start and easy to repeat

situation.text: People know what to do and agree with it. They do not do it.

items: Pick one behaviour and make it specific.
Attach it to something that already happens: after the Monday meeting, I will.
Make the first step small.
Remove an obstacle: a template, a shortcut, a reminder at the point of use.
Have someone notice when it happens.

why.text: Knowing is not doing. One widely used model says behaviour depends on capability, opportunity and motivation together. A course usually addresses the first.

Habits form when an action is repeated in the same setting until the setting prompts it. In one study, 96 volunteers repeated a chosen eating, drinking or activity behaviour daily for 12 weeks. The time to become close to automatic ranged from 18 to 254 days. Among the people whose progress could be tracked well, half took longer than about two months.

In the same study, missing a single day did not noticeably set people back. The behaviours were simple health actions that people chose for themselves, so treat the timings as a rough guide for workplace skills.

A meta-analysis of 94 tests found that people who wrote an if-then plan reached their goals more often than people who only held the goal. That is the reason for attaching the behaviour to something that already happens.

why.cite: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts and Wardle (2010)
why.title: How are habits formed
why.found: 96 volunteers repeated a self-chosen eating, drinking or activity behaviour daily for 12 weeks and rated how automatic it felt. Time to near-peak automaticity ranged from 18 to 254 days. Missing one opportunity did not materially affect the process.
why.means: Plan support for months, not weeks, and tell people one missed day does not undo the habit.

try.text: Take one behaviour from a course. Write the cue, the small first step and one obstacle to remove.

try.title: Cue, small step, obstacle removed
try.text: Illustration. Behaviour: log each client call. Cue: "When I put the phone down, I will open the log." Small first step: one line only. Obstacle removed: a pinned shortcut to the log. The team lead mentions it at the weekly meeting.

items: There is no fixed number of days for a habit. Popular figures of a few weeks have no support in the study above.
If the workplace punishes the new behaviour, it stops.
Too many new behaviours at once means none.
