topics.title: Build a job aid when a course is the wrong tool
topics.theory: Learning in the flow of work

situation.text: People are in the middle of a task and stuck. They do not need a course. They need the answer.

items: Ask when people will need this: learning it, applying it, fixing a problem, or coping with a change.
For applying, fixing and changing, build a job aid.
Write it to be scanned.
Put it where the work happens.

why.text: One framework, from Gottfredson and Mosher, lists five moments of need: when something is new, when people want more, when they must apply it, when something goes wrong, and when things change. The last three happen during work. It is a practitioner model and has not been tested as a whole.
At those moments a checklist that can be found is often more use than a course that has to be remembered.
A standard book on job aids splits them into two kinds. Planners are used just before or after the task. Sidekicks are used during it. Decide which you are building before you write.

try.text: Take a task. Design a job aid for the moment of need.

try.title: A course or a card
try.text: Illustration. Staff run a month-end report once every four weeks and forget the steps each time. A half-day course would be forgotten too. A one-page checklist pinned inside the reporting tool answers the question at the moment it comes up.

items: A job aid nobody can find is useless.
Some skills must be in the head. Do not replace those.
Keep it current.

topics.title: Grow a community of practice, do not announce one

situation.text: Leadership announces a "community of practice" and sets up a channel. Three weeks later it is silent.

items: Start from a shared problem people care about.
Set a regular rhythm of contact.
Make it safe to share half-finished work.
Seed it, then step back.

why.text: A community of practice is a group who share a concern for something they do and get better at it by interacting regularly. Some organise themselves. Most need cultivating, and an announcement alone does not make one.
All three parts are needed: a shared domain, a real community and a developing practice.

try.text: Design the launch conditions for a community: its domain, its rhythm, and how safety will be built.

try.title: Announced and grown
try.text: Illustration. Announced: a new channel called "Facilitators' community" and a launch message. Grown: five facilitators who all struggle with quiet online groups meet for 30 minutes each fortnight, bring one half-finished plan each, and invite others once it is useful.

items: A community needs someone to tend it.
Newcomers learn at the edge first.
Measure usefulness, not posts.

topics.title: Keep graduates involved

situation.text: The programme ends with a certificate and you never hear from the group again.

items: Plan what happens after the last session.
Give graduates a reason to stay in touch.
Offer mentoring and peer groups.
Invite graduates to teach or support newer learners.

why.text: Graduation can be a move into a continuing relationship. A network of past learners can keep the learning in use and supply new teachers. This is practice wisdom and not a research finding.
Teaching newer learners can deepen the graduate's own learning.

why.title: Learning by teaching
why.found: A meta-analysis of 28 studies compared students who prepared to teach, or prepared and then taught, with students who studied without expecting to teach. Both groups learned more, and those who went on to teach learned most. Teaching with real interaction helped more than teaching without it.
why.means: When graduates help a newer cohort, have them explain and answer questions, not only sit in.

try.text: Design a plan that gives graduates a reason to stay connected and a way to contribute.

try.title: After the certificate
try.text: Illustration. Six weeks after the last session, graduates are invited to a one-hour meeting to bring one case each. Two volunteer to sit in on the next cohort's practice session and give feedback. The ask is one hour.

items: A mailing list is not a community.
Keep the ask small.
Get consent before using graduates as proof.

topics.title: Teach others to train

situation.text: Demand outgrows what you can deliver. Someone else has to run your sessions.

items: Let new trainers watch you first.
Have them deliver a part while you watch.
Give feedback on one thing at a time.
Pass on the reasons, not only the slides.
Observe before you sign someone off.

why.text: Trainers learn the craft by watching, guided practice and feedback. Teaching people to teach multiplies your reach.
It is also how standards spread or slip. Hand on the evidence and the caveats with the material.

The research here is thin and comes mostly from health and social care. One review found that train-the-trainer programmes usually improved knowledge or practice. Programmes that mixed interactive methods with written materials looked best, and the right mix is still unclear.

why.title: Does train-the-trainer work?
why.found: A systematic review found 18 studies in health and social care. Thirteen reported better knowledge, clinical behaviour or patient outcomes, three a possible effect and one none. The studies were too varied to pool and carried a moderate risk of bias.
why.means: Build your handover from interactive practice plus materials, and check the result by observing, since the evidence will not do that for you.

items.title: Observe
items.text: Sign off on what you have seen.

try.text: Design a short train-the-trainer plan for one skill. Say how you would observe, give feedback and judge readiness.

try.title: Handing over a session
try.text: Illustration. A new trainer watches the session once. Next time she runs the 20-minute practice activity while you observe. You give feedback on one thing: her instructions. She runs the whole session only after you have watched her do each part.

items: Quality drifts as more people deliver.
A script produces readers, not trainers.
Budget time to observe.

topics.title: Curate what exists before you create more

situation.text: You are asked for a new course on a subject where good material already exists, inside and outside the organisation.

items: Search what exists first.
Judge each source: accurate, current, right level.
Choose a few and put them in order.
Add what is missing: your context, a task, a check.
Credit sources and respect licences.
Set a review date.

why.text: Making new content is slow and costly. Selecting and arranging good existing material can meet the need faster, if someone exercises judgement over it.
A list of links is not curation. The value is in the selection, the order and the task that makes people use it.

UK copyright law has a narrow exception for copying to illustrate a point in teaching. Official guidance says the use must be non-commercial, fair and acknowledged. If your training is commercial, do not assume it covers you. Link to the material, or get permission or a licence. This is general information and not legal advice.

try.text: For one topic, pick three existing sources. Write one line on why each, and one task that uses them.

try.title: A list and a curated set
try.text: Illustration. A list: twelve links on giving feedback. Curated: three sources in order, one line on why each is there, and a task. "Read the second, then rewrite the feedback you gave last week." A review date sits at the top.

items: Links break. Check them.
Copyright applies to training materials.
Too many sources is the same as none.

topics.title: Build a culture where learning is expected
topics.theory: Learning culture and the learning organisation

situation.text: The organisation says it values learning. Nobody has time for it, and mistakes are hidden.

items: Look at what leaders do, not what the posters say.
Ask whether people have time, permission and a reason to learn.
Make one practice routine: a short review after each project.
Have leaders talk about what they are learning and what went wrong.
Notice and credit people who share what they know.

why.text: Culture is what people do repeatedly and what is rewarded. A trainer cannot install it. A trainer can help leaders change a few routines.

The "learning organisation" is an influential management idea. One well-known article breaks it into three parts: a supportive environment, concrete learning processes, and leaders who reinforce learning. The article comes with a survey for scoring each part. Treat a score as a prompt for discussion and the idea as a direction. It is a framework and not a tested method.
The review routine is the best-supported step here. Research on debriefs, also called after-action reviews, finds that teams and individuals who hold them perform better than those who do not.

why.title: Do debriefs improve performance?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 46 samples compared people and teams who held debriefs with control groups who did not. Debriefs improved performance by roughly a fifth to a quarter (d = 0.67). The effect was similar for teams and individuals and in real and simulated settings.
why.means: Start with a short, structured review after each project, with a clear focus and the right people in the room.

try.text: Ask three people in one team when they last learned something at work and what made it possible.

try.title: One routine
try.text: Illustration. After each project the team spends 20 minutes on three questions: what did we expect, what happened, what will we do differently. The director goes first and names one decision she got wrong. Notes go where the next project team will see them.

items: A learning platform is not a culture.
Reviews that hunt for blame teach people to hide.
Change takes years. Promise a start.

parts.title: Practice and consolidation
parts.summary: How to schedule practice so it lasts.

topics.title: Leave time for memory to settle

situation.text: The schedule is back-to-back from Monday to Friday, with revision the night before the test.

items: Leave gaps between practice sessions.
Protect sleep.
Come back to material by recalling it.
Avoid teaching similar things back to back.

why.text: Memories are stabilised over time, and sleep helps. How much it helps depends on what was learned and when the sleep comes. The gaps between practice give that time, which is one likely reason spreading practice works.

Recalling something makes it easier to recall later. One proposed reason is that a recalled memory is stored again. That idea, called reconsolidation, is less settled in people than it is often made to sound, so do not build a design on it. New learning can also disturb recent learning, and gaps may reduce that.
A large review of spaced practice found that the best gap grows with how long the memory has to last. For something people must keep for months, space the sessions by days or weeks and not by hours.

try.text: Take a crammed schedule. Redesign its rhythm so memory has time to settle.

try.title: A week with room in it
try.text: Illustration. Before: five full days, a new topic each hour, revision on Thursday night. After: new material in the mornings, practice in the afternoons, ten minutes of recall at the start of each day, and the two similar procedures on different days.

items: Keep claims about sleep stages modest.
Gaps without recall are just gaps.
Clients read white space as wasted time. Explain it.

quiz.a: In the gaps between practice, and during sleep.

quiz.a: Makes it easier to recall later. Why it does so is still debated.

quiz.q: What reduces interference between new and recent learning?

topics.title: Space and mix the practice, then stop drilling

situation.text: The group drills one procedure fifty times in a row and looks excellent by the end of the hour.

items: Mix related tasks.
Set recall at widening or regular intervals over days and weeks.
Stop drilling once people can do it.
Use the time saved for a later session.
Drill to automatic only the basics that free up thinking.

why.text: Blocked practice looks better during the session. Mixed practice often produces better learning later, though the benefit depends on the material. It is strongest when the things being learned are easy to confuse with each other. Practising past the point of first success helps a lot a week later, and the advantage shrinks over the following weeks.
The time is better spent on a later, spaced session than on more repetition now.

why.title: What overlearning buys
why.found: In two experiments 218 students learned geography facts or word definitions, some to a low level and some well past the first perfect run. One week later the overlearners recalled far more. Tested up to nine weeks later, most of that advantage had gone.
why.means: Stop once people have it right, and spend the saved time on a later session.

items.title: Mix
items.text: Looks worse now, often lasts longer.

try.text: Design a spaced, mixed practice plan for a real skill. Say when you stop drilling.

try.title: Fifty in a row, or fewer and mixed
try.text: Illustration. Before: one procedure drilled fifty times in an hour. After: three related procedures practised in mixed order until each person gets each right twice. Then stop. The same three come back for ten minutes two days later and again the next week.

items: Newcomers may need some blocked practice first.
Learners prefer blocked practice. Explain the choice.
Recall that always fails is dispiriting. Pitch it.
Mixing does not suit everything. In one meta-analysis it helped with pictures and maths problems and did worse than blocking for word lists.
The studies behind this are of facts, categories and maths problems. For a hands-on procedure, test the mixed version on a small group first.

quiz.q: Which lasts longer?

quiz.q: What do you do once people can do it?
quiz.a: Stop drilling and come back later.

'Drill to automatic only the basics that free up thinking', 'Newcomers may need some blocked practice first' and 'Learners prefer blocked practice' have no opened source.

topics.title: Add a follow-up layer to any format

situation.text: You run a retreat, a webinar series and a self-paced course. None has anything after the end.

items: For each format, plan what follows: recall, a task to apply, a review.
Put dates on it.
Deliver it through the channel people already use.
Check whether it is being used.

why.text: Spacing and recall have helped across many ages, materials and settings, so they are a sound bet for any format. Few studies test them after a retreat or a webinar series. Without follow-up, expect much of the content to fade.
How the follow-up is delivered depends on the format: a cadence of calls after a retreat, spaced quizzes in a self-paced course.

why.title: Spaced questions by email
why.found: In a randomised trial 115 medical students were emailed short case questions with explanations on one of two topics, repeated over several months. They learned their emailed topic better than the other group did. About nine months later the gain had lasted for one topic and not the other. The authors could not separate spacing from simply seeing more content.
why.means: Send short spaced questions through a channel people already use, and check whether the gain lasts.

items.title: A layer
items.text: Follow-up is part of the product.

try.text: Take one format. Design its follow-up in full: what, when and how spaced.

try.title: A layer after a webinar series
try.text: Illustration. After the last webinar, three short messages go out in the team's usual chat at one, three and six weeks. Each asks one recall question and sets one small task. A 30-minute review call is in the diary at week eight.

items: Spaced-repetition tools suit facts better than judgement.
Too many messages get muted.
Sell it with the event, not after.

topics.title: Teach learners how to study

situation.text: Learners revise by re-reading and highlighting, and feel well prepared.

items: Teach self-testing, spacing, explaining in your own words, and teaching someone else.
Explain why effortful study works better than it feels.
Help people build a routine they will keep.
Have them plan, check and review their own study.

why.text: Re-reading and highlighting are what learners say they rely on, and a major review rates both as low value. It rates self-testing and spaced practice highest. Explaining in your own words comes in the middle, with less evidence behind it. Learners need to be told this, because easy study feels productive.
The most lasting thing a course can leave is a learner who knows how to make anything stick.

why.title: Which study techniques work
why.found: A review of ten study techniques rated practice testing and spaced practice as high utility, because they help across ages, materials and real classrooms. Self-explanation and mixed practice were rated moderate. Re-reading, highlighting and summarising were rated low.
why.means: Teach self-testing and spacing first, and tell learners plainly that re-reading and highlighting do little.

try.text: Write a personal plan for consolidating what you have learned. Choose techniques you will keep up.

try.title: Showing why feelings mislead
try.text: Illustration. Half the group re-reads a page twice. The other half reads it once, then writes down what they recall. Each person predicts their score. A short quiz two days later lets them compare the prediction with what happened.

items: People return to highlighting under pressure.
A plan too ambitious is dropped.
Model the techniques in your own sessions.

topics.title: Decide what you will measure before you design
topics.theory: Evaluation planning, baselines and success measures

situation.text: Evaluation is discussed for the first time after the course has run.

items: Before you design, agree what will change if the programme works.
Choose two or three measures of that.
Record where things stand now.
Decide who collects what, and when.
Write it into the proposal.

why.text: You cannot show a change without a starting point. Deciding measures first also sharpens the design, because it forces agreement on what the programme is for.
This is the same discipline as designing backwards from objectives, applied to the whole programme.

try.text: For one programme, write what will change, two measures and where each stands today.

try.title: Illustrative: a measure agreed up front
try.text: Before: "We will send a feedback form afterwards." After: "Managers should give feedback in every monthly one-to-one. We will count how many do so now, and count again eight weeks after the course."

items: Sponsors may not have data. Help them find a proxy.
Measures chosen late favour what is easy.
Agree who owns the data.

topics.title: Use Kirkpatrick as vocabulary, not proof

situation.text: The evaluation is a feedback form. Scores are high, so the course is declared a success.

items: Use the four levels as shared words: reaction, learning, behaviour, results.
Do not assume one level leads to the next.
Plan to reach behaviour and results.
Consider other approaches that ask different questions.

why.text: The four-level model is the dominant framework and a useful vocabulary. The levels are often wrongly treated as a causal chain. How much people liked a course relates only weakly to what they learned.
Evaluation often stops at reaction and learning, the levels furthest from what a sponsor is paying for. People can also mistake a session that felt easy for one they learned from.

Critics go further than the causal chain. Holton argued the four levels are a list of outcomes, not a model, because they leave out what sits between a course and a result, such as motivation and the workplace. Bates added that the levels tell you whether training worked but not how to make it work better. Kirkpatrick's reply was that the levels are meant to be practical.

The evidence on reaction forms is not all one way. One meta-analysis found that ratings of usefulness were a better guide to learning and to use at work than ratings of enjoyment. A later one found no difference between the two. Neither supports reading a happy room as a trained one.

why.title: How the levels of training evaluation relate to each other
why.found: This meta-analysis split reactions into enjoyment and usefulness, and split learning into immediate, retained and demonstrated skill. Ratings of usefulness were more strongly related to learning and to performance on the job than ratings of enjoyment were.
why.means: If you use a reaction form, ask whether the content is useful for the job, and still measure learning and behaviour separately.

items.title: Vocabulary, not proof
items.text: The levels are not a chain.

items.title: Liking is not learning
items.text: Reaction scores say little about learning.

try.text: Take a real feedback-form evaluation. Redesign the plan to reach behaviour and results.

try.title: Illustrative: two evaluation summaries
try.text: Before: "People loved the day, so it worked." After: "People rated the day highly. In a short scenario test most could handle the task. In six weeks we will ask managers what they see."

items: Return on investment figures need cautious assumptions.
A method that studies the best and worst cases can tell you more than an average.
Do not drop reaction data. Know what it can tell you.

quiz.a: At reaction and learning.

openPoints: Kirkpatrick and Kirkpatrick, third edition: the publisher's page shows a 2008 date for the listing. The third edition is generally cited as 2006, which the label uses. Check against the book's copyright page.

Phillips, Return on Investment in Training and Performance Improvement Programs: the publisher's page does not state the year. 2003 is the usual citation for the second edition. Check before publishing.
How often evaluation stops at each level: Alliger and Janak counted this in published studies, but the summary does not give the result. No current survey figure was found.
Thalheimer's LTEM is a natural "other approach" for step four but is cited on the survey and analytics pages, not here. Consider a cross-link.

Kirwan (2025), Measuring the effectiveness of L&D: time to move on from Kirkpatrick and Phillips, International Journal of Training and Development, looks relevant but the journal page would not open.
checkFindings: Alliger and Janak (1989): the summary confirms the paper questions three assumptions of the four levels, that they ascend, are causally linked and are positively correlated. This supports "do not assume one level leads to the next". The summary gives no figures, so none are used.

Alliger and colleagues (1997) added. Its summary says usefulness ratings relate more strongly to learning and transfer than enjoyment ratings. It gives no correlations in the summary, so no numbers are on the page.

Sitzmann and colleagues (2008) added, with a caution. Its summary does not state the size of the reaction to learning link. It says reactions mainly reflect course features and the trainer's style, predict changes in motivation and confidence, and that enjoyment and usefulness reactions did not differ in their relation to learning. This disagrees with Alliger and colleagues on usefulness, so the page now reports both.

Uttl and colleagues (2017) added for university teaching: no significant link between student ratings and learning in multi-section studies, and earlier positive results put down to small studies and publication bias. This is about students rating lecturers, not workplace training, and is used only as supporting evidence.
Holton (1996) and Bates (2004) added and summarised in a new paragraph, since the draft named critics only through Alliger and Janak.
Softened "Most evaluation stops at reaction and learning, the levels a sponsor cares about least" and the matching quiz question. Softened "People can even rate easy, fluent sessions highest".
Kirkpatrick book: the publisher's page confirms the four levels are reaction, learning, behaviour and results.

topics.title: Ask better questions on the feedback form

situation.text: The form asks "How would you rate the trainer?" and "Was the venue comfortable?"

items: Ask what people can now do, in specific terms.
Ask what they will use, and when.
Ask what would stop them.
Use answer choices that describe a level, not a number from one to five.
Keep it short, and leave one open question.

why.text: Satisfaction scores relate weakly to learning. They tell you more about the course and the trainer's style, and about people's confidence. A form can still be useful if it asks about understanding, intention to use and support at work.

Will Thalheimer argues for surveys that ask about learning effectiveness, such as understanding, realistic practice and motivation to apply, in place of satisfaction ratings. He proposes answer choices that describe a level in words. This is a practitioner's method. Even a well-written form is a hint, to be backed by a measure of what people can do.

why.title: What trainee reactions do and do not reflect
why.found: This meta-analysis found that reactions mainly reflect features of the course. The strongest predictors of reactions were the trainer's instructional style (rho = .66) and human interaction (rho = .56). Reactions predicted changes in motivation and confidence from before to after training.
why.means: Read reaction scores as feedback on delivery and on confidence, not as a measure of learning.

items.title: Barriers
items.text: What will get in the way?

try.text: Rewrite a feedback form to five questions. None may ask whether people enjoyed it.

try.title: Illustrative: one question rewritten
try.text: Before: "How would you rate the trainer? 1 to 5." After: "How able are you to give feedback using the model? I could not do it yet. I could do it with my notes. I could do it unaided. I could show a colleague how."

items: People answer politely. Make it anonymous.
A form cannot show behaviour change.
Read the open answers.
Confidence is not competence. A form reports what people believe they can do.

quiz.a: What people can do, what they will use and what would stop them.

quiz.q: What can a form not show?
quiz.a: Behaviour change.

topics.title: Measure what people do differently

situation.text: The sponsor asks, "Did it make a difference?" You have attendance figures.

items: Decide which behaviour should change and how you would see it.
Use observation, manager reports and performance data.
Link the behaviour to the outcome named in the needs analysis.
Claim contribution, not sole cause.
Look for early signs before the result shows.

why.text: Training rarely acts alone. Other things change at the same time. An honest, modest claim is believed. A large one is not.
A comparison group strengthens the case where one is possible.

items.title: Behaviour, then results
items.text: Did people do it, and did it matter?

try.text: Design a behaviour-and-results plan for a real programme. Write an honest statement of what the training contributed.

try.title: Illustrative: an honest contribution statement
try.text: Before: "The course improved customer service." After: "On observed calls, more advisers now confirm the problem before offering a fix. Complaints fell over the same months. A new script launched too, so training is one contributor."

items: Self-report flatters. Where you can, use a source other than the learner.
Agree the measures before the course.
Overclaiming costs you the next project.

quiz.q: What should you claim for training?
quiz.a: Contribution, not sole cause.

quiz.q: Name two sources of evidence on behaviour.
quiz.a: Any two of: observation, manager reports, performance data.

quiz.q: Why look for early signs?
quiz.a: Business results take time to show.

topics.title: Go back later to see what stuck

situation.text: You measured on the last afternoon. Everyone could do it.

items: Set a date to check again, some weeks later. Four to twelve weeks is a common rule of thumb, not a research finding.
Ask people to do the task, or recall it, without warning them to revise.
Ask managers what they have seen.
Compare with the end-of-course result.
Use the gap to improve the follow-up.

why.text: Performance at the end of a session is a poor guide to what lasts. A delayed check shows what people kept and what they use.
A drop is normal and useful. It tells you where follow-up is needed.

The gap can run either way. Some methods that make the last afternoon look good produce little lasting learning, and some that make it look worse produce more. Only a later check tells you which you had.

why.title: Learning versus performance
why.found: This review of motor and verbal learning research concludes that performance during training is often an unreliable guide to lasting learning. Learning can happen with no visible gain at the time, and gains at the time can fade. People tend to mistake how well practice went for how much they learned.
why.means: Do not treat an end-of-course result as the measure of the course. Check again after a delay.

try.text: For one course, design a ten-minute check to run six weeks later.

try.title: Illustrative: a six-week check
try.text: On the day, everyone completes the incident form correctly with the guide open. Six weeks later, each person completes one from a short scenario with no guide. The steps most often missed become the subject of a reminder and a job aid.

items: Response rates fall with time. Keep it short.
A check that feels like a test raises anxiety. Explain why.
Agree it with the sponsor in advance.

quiz.q: Why check again later?
quiz.a: End-of-session performance is a poor guide to what lasts.

quiz.q: When?
quiz.a: Some weeks later, not on the day.

quiz.q: What does a drop tell you?
quiz.a: Where follow-up is needed.

topics.tierReason: A large body of research shows performance during or just after training is an unreliable sign of lasting learning, but the timing of a follow-up check at work is a rule of thumb.

topics.title: Separate the effect of training from everything else

situation.text: Sales rose after the sales course. They also rose in the region that did not attend.

items: Where you can, compare a group that attended with one that has not yet.
Stagger the roll-out to create that comparison.
Measure before and after in both.
List what else changed at the same time.
Ask participants and managers to estimate the share due to training, and discount it.
State your confidence plainly.

why.text: Without a comparison, any change after training may have happened anyway. A staggered roll-out is often the most practical way to get a comparison group.
Estimates from participants are weak evidence. Use them as a last resort and say what they are.

items.title: Compared with what?
items.text: The question for your own work too.

items.title: Stagger
items.text: A waiting group is a comparison.

try.text: For one programme, describe the comparison you could set up at no extra cost.

try.title: Illustrative: a comparison at no extra cost
try.text: Four depots need the same course. Two attend in March and two in May. Error rates are recorded at all four in February and April. In April the May depots are the comparison.

items: Groups differ before training. Check the starting point.
Small groups give noisy results.
Do not withhold training people need for safety.
People who volunteer first often differ from those who wait. Let the timetable decide who goes first, not enthusiasm.

topics.title: Ignore the vanity metrics

situation.text: The dashboard shows logins, completions and time spent. It says nothing about whether anyone learned.

items: Sort your figures: which show activity, and which show learning or behaviour.
Use data to find where people struggle or drop out.
Report only figures that would change a decision.
Tell learners what you collect and why.

why.text: Completion and engagement figures are easy to get. They measure activity. They do not show learning or use.
Over-monitoring costs trust.

items.title: Find the weak spots
items.text: Use data to improve the design.

try.text: Take a set of analytics. Mark which inform improvement and which are vanity.

try.title: Illustrative: sorting a dashboard
try.text: Logins and completions go in a column headed activity. Scenario scores and manager observations go in a column headed learning and behaviour. The drop-off point in module three goes to the designer as a prompt to look at that module.

items: Treat any prediction of who will drop out with caution.
A dashboard nobody acts on is decoration.
Check your data protection duties.

topics.title: Show the value in the client's own terms
topics.theory: Return on investment, return on expectations, and their honest limits

situation.text: The finance director asks what the organisation got for its money.

items: Ask the sponsor what result would make it worth it, in their words.
Measure that.
Put a money value on it only where the link is defensible.
Set it against the full cost, including people's time.
Use cautious assumptions and show them.
Report benefits you cannot price as well.

why.text: Return on investment compares the money value of results with the cost. It persuades where the link from training to result is clear, and misleads where it is not.
An alternative is to agree in advance what the sponsor expects and report against that.
A return figure is only as good as the step before it. The Phillips method expects you to separate the effect of training from other causes before you put a price on anything.

items.title: Their terms
items.text: What would make it worth it?

try.text: For one programme, write the sponsor's test of value in one sentence, and the full cost.

try.title: Illustrative: the sponsor's test of value
try.text: Sponsor's test: "New managers handle a first absence conversation without calling HR." Full cost: design and delivery fees, venue, and two days away from work for each of twelve managers. Reported alongside: benefits that were not priced, such as confidence.

items: A large return figure invites disbelief.
Not everything worth doing can be priced.
Agree the method before the course.

topics.title: Feed the results back and make the case
topics.theory: Closing the loop and the business case

situation.text: The evaluation report is filed. Nothing in the next version of the course changes.

items: Feed what you found into the next design.
State the outcome in the sponsor's language.
State what the training contributed, with its limits.
Say what happens next.
Use a case of what worked, for whom and why.

why.text: Evaluation that changes nothing is wasted. It is the input to the next version and to the next conversation with the sponsor.
Credibility comes from honesty about limits.

A common criticism of evaluation by levels is that it says whether training worked but not how to improve it. Asking what helped and what got in the way, for the people it worked for and the people it did not, gives you something to change.

try.text: Draft a one-page business case for a real programme: the outcome, the contribution and the limits.

try.title: Illustrative: closing the loop
try.text: Finding: people who practised with their manager in the first fortnight used the skill. Those who did not, had not. Change for the next run: a manager briefing before the course and a booked practice slot after it.

items: Conservative assumptions survive scrutiny.
A success story is not an average.
Report failures too.

stages.name: Training in the AI era
stages.question: What does AI change about training, and what does it leave alone?
stages.wordingStatus: Draft: part names and topic titles for this stage were written for the build pack and have not been seen by Mica

parts.title: AI in training
parts.summary: Using AI to build learning, judging the claims, and training people to work with it.

topics.title: Let AI draft, and keep a person accountable
topics.theory: Using AI to design and build learning

situation.text: You could have AI write the whole course by lunchtime.

items: Use AI for first drafts, question items, summaries and storyboards.
Brief it with the objective, the audience and the constraints.
Check every output for accuracy, bias and fit with the objective.
Keep a named, qualified person accountable.
Do the diagnosis and design decisions yourself.

why.text: AI speeds work you already know how to do well. It does not replace diagnosis, alignment and judgement about evidence.
It drafts. A professional decides.

A 2026 OECD review of the research points the same way for classrooms. Tools built or used with a clear teaching purpose tend to help. Getting a task done with a general chatbot does not by itself lead to learning.

try.text: Use an AI tool to draft an asset. Correct it against the design principles. Note what needed your judgement.

try.title: Illustration: a drafted quiz
try.text: You ask an AI tool for ten quiz questions on a fire safety course. Two test trivia, one has a wrong answer and none match the objective about choosing the right extinguisher. You keep four, rewrite three, bin three, and sign the quiz off under your own name.

items: Plausible text can be wrong.
Tell learners where AI was used.
Do not paste confidential material into a tool without permission.
If the material includes personal data, data protection law applies. Check your organisation's rules before you use a tool.

quiz.a: First drafts, question items, summaries and storyboards.

quiz.a: Accuracy, bias and fit with the objective.

quiz.q: Who is accountable?
quiz.a: A named, qualified person.

No controlled study of AI-assisted course design by trainers was found or opened. The claim that AI speeds work you already do well is left as professional judgement.
The advice to tell learners where AI was used has no checked source on this page.

topics.title: Expect moderate gains from adaptive tools
topics.theory: Adaptive tutoring and the honest evidence

situation.text: A vendor claims its adaptive platform "doubles learning".

items: Ask for the size of the effect and what it was compared with.
Expect moderate gains from well-designed systems.
Treat very large figures as outliers.
Ask what in the design produces the gain.

why.text: Reviews of intelligent tutoring systems find real, moderate gains. One review of 50 controlled evaluations found a median gain of 0.66 standard deviations over conventional teaching, and the size depended heavily on the test used. Another found a gain of 0.42 over teacher-led classes and no significant difference from one-to-one human tutoring. The famous "two sigma" figure for human tutoring has not held up. A 2011 review put human tutoring at about 0.79 against no tutoring, with step-based tutoring systems close behind at 0.76.
The gain comes from the design, not from the label.

Generative AI tutors are newer and the evidence is thinner. In one field experiment with nearly a thousand secondary school maths pupils, a plain chatbot raised practice grades, but those pupils then scored lower on a test without it than pupils who never had it. A version with teaching guardrails largely avoided the harm. In one university physics course, a carefully designed AI tutor beat an active-learning class on a short test. A 2026 OECD review draws the same line between general chatbots and tools built for teaching.

why.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning
why.found: In a field experiment with nearly a thousand secondary school maths pupils, a standard chatbot improved practice grades by 48% and a tutor version with guardrails by 127%. Once access was removed, pupils who had used the standard chatbot scored 17% lower than pupils who never had access. The guardrails largely prevented that drop.
why.means: Judge an AI learning tool by what people can do without it, and ask what in its design stops it handing over answers.

try.text: Take three vendor claims for AI or virtual reality learning. Restate each with its real effect and conditions.

try.title: Illustration: restating a claim
try.text: Vendor line: "Our adaptive platform doubles learning." Restated after questions: "In one study, people using the platform scored moderately higher on the vendor's own test than a group who read a manual. No comparison with a good trainer. No follow-up test."

items: Marketing quotes the best study.
Gains in schools may not carry to your workplace.
Adaptive pacing helps some content more than others.
Better scores while people use a tool are not proof of learning. Test them without the tool.

quiz.a: Moderate.

quiz.q: What question do you ask of any effectiveness claim?
quiz.a: Compared with what?

quiz.q: Where does the gain come from?
quiz.a: The design.

checkFindings: Build note followed: 2024 to 2026 evidence on generative AI tutors and over-reliance is added (Bastani and colleagues 2025, Kestin and colleagues 2025) and the OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 is confirmed as real (published 19 January 2026) and added.

VanLehn (2011) confirmed on ERIC. The abstract says human tutoring came out at d = 0.79, not the 2.0 widely believed, and intelligent tutoring systems at 0.76, both against no tutoring. The page now says this.

Kulik and Fletcher confirmed on the record held by the authors' institute (IDA), which describes the same meta-analysis: 50 controlled evaluations, median effect 0.66, results strongly dependent on whether tests were locally developed or standardised. The SAGE journal page returned an error, so the journal abstract itself was not opened. The IDA record is dated 2017 and does not itself name the journal.

Ma and colleagues (2014) added, confirmed on the Washington State University repository record: 107 effect sizes, 14,321 participants, g = .42 against teacher-led large-group teaching, .57 against other computer-based teaching, .35 against textbooks, and no significant difference from small-group teaching or individual human tutoring.

Bastani and colleagues: the numbers (48%, 127%, 17% lower) were read in the authors' abstract on SSRN. Publication in PNAS on 25 June 2025 was confirmed on the University of Pennsylvania record. The PNAS page itself could not be opened.

Kestin and colleagues (2025) confirmed on PubMed Central: randomised crossover trial in one Harvard introductory physics course, 194 students analysed, AI tutor built on teaching principles against an in-class active-learning lesson. The abstract says students learned more in less time. No effect size is quoted on the page because the figures came from the full text, not the abstract. The authors built the tutor and note the result covers one course and short tests.
Bloom (1984) removed from the reference list because no publisher or ERIC page could be opened. The two sigma belief is described through VanLehn's abstract instead.
The sentence saying the same holds for virtual reality was removed because nothing on virtual reality was checked.

topics.title: Set the guardrails before you scale

situation.text: The team is already using AI tools. Nobody has written down what is allowed.

items: List the risks: wrong facts, bias, privacy, loss of trust.
Require human review of anything that reaches a learner.
Disclose where AI is used.
Set rules for learner data.
Say what AI may not decide.
Name who is accountable.

why.text: The failures harm learners and your credibility directly. Rules written in advance make responsible use repeatable.
Bias in the data a tool learned from shows up in what it produces.

In the UK, data protection law applies whenever an AI tool handles personal data about learners. The ICO's guidance on AI covers accountability, transparency, lawfulness, accuracy, fairness and bias, security and data minimisation. It is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, so read the current version. Significant decisions about a person made with no meaningful human involvement have their own rules and safeguards.

If you work with clients in the EU, the EU AI Act has an article on AI literacy for organisations that provide or deploy AI systems. Changes to that article were proposed in late 2025. Check the current text before you rely on it. This page is general information, not legal advice.

try.text: Draft a short policy for a learning team: review, disclosure and data handling.

try.title: Illustration: three lines of policy
try.text: "A named designer reviews every AI-drafted item before learners see it. We tell learners where AI was used. No learner names, scores or free-text answers go into a tool the organisation has not approved. AI never decides who passes."

items: A policy nobody reads protects nobody.
The law is changing. Check current rules.
Monitoring learners has a trust cost.

quiz.q: Name three risks of AI in learning.
quiz.a: Any three of: wrong facts, bias, privacy, loss of trust.

quiz.q: What must happen before AI output reaches a learner?
quiz.a: A person reviews it.

quiz.q: What should a policy say AI may not do?
quiz.a: Make certain decisions. Name them.

topics.tierReason: This is governance and regulatory practice, which the brief rates as a practitioner framework.
openPoints: The state of the EU AI Act's AI literacy article in November 2026 is not confirmed. A law firm summary (not an official source) reported that the European Parliament's committees voted in March 2026 to keep the obligation. Whether a final amended text has been adopted was not confirmed.

The Council document linked is a working document marked LIMITE on the Council's public register. Replace it with the European Commission's AI literacy questions and answers page or the EUR-Lex text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 once either can be opened.
Application and enforcement dates for the AI literacy article (2 February 2025 and August 2026) were seen only in a law firm blog, so they are left out.
No research source on AI ethics in education (for example UNESCO guidance) could be opened.
The claim that bias in training data shows up in outputs is supported in general terms by the ICO guidance's fairness chapter, which was seen only as a chapter heading and summary.
checkFindings: The placeholder reference is replaced with official sources. ICO guidance on AI and data protection confirmed: last substantive update 15 March 2023, with a banner saying it is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act.

ICO page on the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 confirmed, updated 19 June 2026: all data protection provisions are in force, and the Act widens the lawful bases available for significant automated decisions, subject to safeguards and not for special category data.

ICO automated decision-making guidance confirmed as draft guidance under consultation (page dated 2 September 2026). It covers decisions based solely on automated processing with a legal or similarly significant effect, and safeguards including information, representations, human intervention and contesting a decision. The page says only that such decisions have their own rules, because the safeguard detail sits on sub-pages not opened.

EU AI Act: the Commission's own page on AI literacy and the EUR-Lex text were refused by the fetch tool. The only official document opened was a Council working document of 9 January 2026 carrying the Commission's answers on the Digital Omnibus on AI. It confirms that Article 4 currently places an AI literacy obligation on providers and deployers and that the Commission proposed removing it as a binding duty. The page text therefore says only that the article exists and that changes were proposed. No application date is stated.
A not-legal-advice line was added to the end of why because the topic now refers to law.

topics.title: Train people to check the AI's work
topics.theory: Training people for an AI world

situation.text: Staff paste AI answers into reports without reading them.

items: Teach what AI can and cannot do.
Practise spotting answers that sound right and are wrong.
Keep the person accountable for the result.
Build the skills that gain value: judgement, evaluation, working with others.

why.text: As AI takes over some tasks, employers still ask for human skills such as communication, collaboration and leadership alongside AI skills. Judgement and critical evaluation matter more when a tool can produce plausible work on demand.
Checking AI output uses the same test as any claim: what is the evidence, and compared with what?

Demand for AI skills shows up in job adverts. PwC's 2025 analysis of close to a billion adverts found that jobs asking for AI skills paid 56% more on average than similar jobs that did not, up from 25% a year earlier. It also reports the skills employers ask for changing 66% faster in the occupations most exposed to AI. An industry consortium found AI skills in 78% of the 50 technology roles it studied across the G7. In a survey commissioned by the UK government and published in January 2026, 97% of respondents named at least one AI skills gap.

Treat these as signals, not forecasts. They come from job adverts and employer surveys, they show links and not causes, and two of the three come from firms that sell AI services or training. In one school experiment, pupils who leaned on a plain chatbot did worse once it was taken away, which is the habit this training is meant to prevent.

try.text: For a real role, list which skills AI may automate and which gain value. Sketch training for the second list.

try.title: Illustration: spot the wrong answer
try.text: Give pairs of people three AI-written summaries of a policy they know well. One contains a confident error. Each pair marks what they would check before sending it on, and how. Then reveal the error and compare the checks people chose.

items: Predictions about jobs are uncertain. Say so.
Tools change faster than courses.
Fear gets in the way. Make it safe to ask basic questions.

topics.title: Plan reskilling around skills, not job titles
topics.theory: Reskilling at scale and skills-based organisations

situation.text: A client says half its roles will change in three years and asks for a reskilling plan.

items: List the skills the work will need, not the job titles.
Find out what skills people have now.
Find the adjacent moves: who is closest to what is needed.
Build routes with practice on real work.
Give time, and a job at the end.
Review yearly.

why.text: Planning around skills lets an organisation move people between roles as work changes. It depends on knowing what skills people have, which most organisations do not.
Forecasts of which jobs will change are uncertain. Plan for adaptability over a single prediction.

There are signs that skills needs are moving quickly. PwC's 2025 analysis of job adverts reports the skills employers ask for changing 66% faster in the occupations most exposed to AI. A 2026 UK survey for the government found that 88% of organisations rely on on-the-job training for AI skills in place of structured programmes.

items.title: Adjacent moves
items.text: Start from what people can nearly do.

try.text: For one role likely to change, list its skills and two roles those skills are close to.

try.title: Illustration: an adjacent move
try.text: A claims handler already interviews customers, reads policy wording and records decisions. The growing role is complaint investigator, which needs the same three skills plus report writing. The route is six weeks of supervised real cases and a report-writing clinic, with a named vacancy at the end.

items: Skills lists go out of date fast.
Self-rated skills are unreliable.
Reskilling without a vacancy is a course.

stages.name: Retreats and immersive learning
stages.question: When is it worth taking people away, and how do we do it safely?
stages.wordingStatus: Draft: part names and topic titles for this stage were written for the build pack and have not been seen by Mica

parts.title: Retreats and intensive experiences
parts.summary: What an intensive residential can and cannot do, and the duty of care that comes with it.

topics.title: Promise the conditions, never the transformation
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.1

situation.text: The brochure for the retreat promises "a transformation".

items: Separate ordinary learning from deep change in your aims.
Design the conditions in which deep change may happen.
Promise the conditions and the work.
Take guarantees out of your marketing.

why.text: One account, Jack Mezirow's, describes transformative learning as a deep shift in how someone makes sense of their experience, worked through by reflection.
People do report change of this kind, but it is hard to measure and no method produces it on demand. Promising it is a promise you cannot keep.

The research behind the idea is mostly qualitative. A 2007 review of 40 published studies found that interviews and case studies still dominated, with work on reflection, relationships and context. That is useful description. It is not proof that a programme can cause the change.

why.title: A review of research on transformative learning
why.found: The review covered 40 peer-reviewed studies published after the previous review in 1998. Research had moved towards how to encourage transformative learning, and qualitative designs still dominated.
why.means: Describe transformation as something some people report, and do not present it as a measured result of your programme.

items.title: Not on demand
items.text: Do not expect it from everyone.

try.text: For a real programme, mark which outcomes are ordinary learning and which would need deep change. Adjust your claims.

try.title: Illustration: rewriting the brochure
try.text: Before: "Three days that will transform your leadership." After: "Three days away from the office with time to think, honest feedback from peers and a coach, and a plan you test in your first week back."

items: Clients like big promises. Offer honest ones.
Discomfort is not proof of depth.
Most valuable learning is incremental.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What is transformative learning, in Mezirow's account?
quiz.a: A deep shift in how someone makes sense of their experience, worked through by reflection.

quiz.q: Can it be produced on demand?
quiz.a: No.

quiz.q: What can you honestly promise?
quiz.a: The conditions, not the outcome.

openPoints: The 'disorienting dilemma' and 'critical reflection' wording of Mezirow's account: not confirmed in a page that could be opened.
Mezirow and associates (2000), Learning as Transformation, and a published critique such as Newman (2012): not searched for, the search cap was reached.
The statement that deep change is hard to measure and cannot be produced on demand has no direct source. Taylor's abstract supports only that the research is mostly qualitative.
checkFindings: The placeholder reference 'Mezirow, Transformative Learning' is replaced by Mezirow's 1991 book, confirmed on Wiley's own site (author, title, year, chapters on meaning perspectives, reflection and perspective transformation).

The detail that transformative learning is set off by a disorienting experience was not in either summary read. It was removed from the paragraph and the quiz. It is the usual account of Mezirow and can go back once a source stating it is opened.
Taylor (2007) added as the evidence review. Its abstract says 40 peer-reviewed studies, mostly qualitative. A short paragraph and a study block say so.
Rated D, strictly: the page's practice is an honest-marketing stance, and the underlying idea is a theory without experimental support in the sources read.
topics.tierReason: Transformative learning is a theory studied mostly through qualitative research, and no checked source tests a method that produces it, so promising only the conditions is sound professional practice, not a tested technique.

topics.title: Design for absorption, not intensity
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.2

situation.text: The programme is built around a dramatic high point: a fire walk, a summit, a night hike.

items: Set clear goals for each activity.
Give immediate feedback.
Match the challenge to people's skill.
Keep the high point tied to the objective.

why.text: Flow is the name given to an absorbed state that people report when challenge and skill are balanced. You can set up conditions that make it more likely. You cannot guarantee it.
Intense moments are remembered. That is not the same as lasting learning, so larger claims about "peak states" need caution.

A meta-analysis of 28 studies found a moderate link between the balance of challenge and skill and reported flow. Clear goals and a sense of control were linked to it as well. The link was weaker in work and education settings. Treat the balance as a helpful condition, not a switch.

why.title: Challenge-skill balance and flow: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 28 studies, the balance of challenge and skill had a moderate relationship with flow. The relationship was weaker in work and education settings, and clear goals and a sense of control were also linked to flow.
why.means: Match the challenge to each person's skill and set clear goals, and do not promise that flow will follow.

items.title: Intensity is not learning
items.text: Memorable is not the same as useful.

try.text: Design a segment of a retreat for absorption. State the goal, the feedback and the balance of challenge and skill.

try.title: Illustration: the night hike, redesigned
try.text: Before: everyone does the same steep night hike. After: three routes of rising difficulty, a clear task at each checkpoint, a guide giving feedback as teams navigate, and a debrief that ties the task back to how the team makes decisions at work.

items: Chasing intensity can harm people.
A challenge too great for some excludes them. Offer levels.
Debrief, or the moment stays a story.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

items.label: Fong, Zaleski and Leach (2015), The challenge-skill balance and antecedents of flow: a meta-analytic investigation. The Journal of Positive Psychology.
Csikszentmihalyi (1990, Harper Perennial edition 2008), Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience.

topics.bodyStatus: 2 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: When does flow arise?
quiz.a: When challenge and skill are balanced.

quiz.q: What two things are proposed to support it?
quiz.a: Clear goals and immediate feedback.

quiz.q: Is an intense experience lasting learning?
quiz.a: Not by itself.

openPoints: Immediate feedback as a condition of flow: not confirmed in a source read.
Harris and colleagues (2021) on flow and performance: not searched for, cap reached.
The claim that intense moments are remembered but are not the same as lasting learning still has no checked source.
Print year of Fong and colleagues (2014 on the record opened, 2015 in the journal volume) should be confirmed on the journal page.
checkFindings: The placeholder 'Csikszentmihalyi, Flow' is confirmed as a book (author and title) on a bookseller page that carries the publisher's description. The HarperCollins page was not returned by search. The description presents flow as deep involvement that can be cultivated. It does not list challenge, skill, goals or feedback.

Fong and colleagues added. The abstract read gives no numeric correlation, only 'moderate', so no effect size is on the page. The record opened dates the paper 2014 (online publication). The label uses 2015 as given in the task. Confirm the print year.
Feedback as a condition for flow is not in either summary. The card and one quiz question were hedged to 'proposed'. The step 'Give immediate feedback' is kept as general good practice.
The evidence is about reported flow, not about learning. Rated C.
topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis links the balance of challenge and skill to flow, but the link is moderate, correlational and weaker in work and education settings, and nothing read shows that flow in a retreat leads to lasting learning.

topics.title: Build trust before you ask for openness
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.3

situation.text: On the first evening you ask people to share something personal. Some do. Several shut down.

items: Agree ground rules and confidentiality at the start.
Go first, at a modest level.
Let people choose how much to share, and to pass.
Stay calm and steady yourself.
Notice who needs support.

why.text: People take personal risks in a group more readily when they believe it is safe to do so. Researchers call that shared belief psychological safety, and studies of work teams link it to learning behaviour. Most of that research is on teams at work, not on retreats.
Calm breathing and a steady facilitator are sensible practices. Present them as practical ways to keep the room settled. Do not attach a scientific explanation you cannot source.

why.title: Psychological safety in 51 work teams
why.found: In a field study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company, teams that shared a belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks showed more learning behaviour. Learning behaviour in turn was linked to team performance.
why.means: Build safety first with ground rules, modest disclosure from you and a free choice to pass, and remember the evidence comes from work teams.

items.title: Keep the practice, drop the claim
items.text: Do not claim science you cannot source.

try.text: Design the opening that builds trust for an intensive session. Rewrite any scientific-sounding justification you cannot source in plain terms.

try.title: Illustration: a first evening
try.text: Before: "Share your biggest failure with the group." After: agree confidentiality and its limits, then the facilitator shares one small work mistake. People choose a question from three levels of depth, talk in pairs, and anyone may pass without giving a reason.

items: Pressure to share is a breach of care.
Confidentiality has limits. Say what they are.
You are not a therapist.

topics.title: Take people out of their routine, and plan the return
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.4

situation.text: The retreat is a success on the mountain. On Monday the inbox wins.

items: Mark the start with a clear threshold.
Take people out of their usual setting and roles.
Mark the end.
Design the return: what people take back, who they tell, what they do in the first week.

why.text: Anthropologists use the idea of a threshold, or liminal, stage for the in-between period in a rite of passage, when people have left one role and not yet taken up the next. Retreat designers borrow the idea when they take people out of their normal setting. Treat it as a design idea, not a proven mechanism of change.
The return is the part most often neglected. Without it, what happened stays there.

Time outdoors has some support, from small studies. In one, 36 city adults had lower stress hormone levels after spending time in nature, with 20 to 30 minutes the most efficient dose. In another, hikers tested about four days into a wilderness trip scored around half as much again on a creative reasoning test as hikers tested before setting off. Neither study could separate nature from rest, time off screens or who chose to take part.

try.text: Sketch a retreat's beginning, middle and end. Design the return step.

try.title: Illustration: the first week back
try.text: Before leaving, each person writes one thing to try, who they will tell and when they will do it. Managers get a short note on Friday saying what to ask about on Monday. The group meets for twenty minutes a fortnight later to compare what happened.

items: Ritual can feel forced. Keep it simple and offer a way out.
The setting supports the work. It is not the work.
Tell managers what to expect on Monday.
Do not sell the setting as science. The nature studies are small and say nothing about what people do back at work.

items.label: Turner (1969), The Ritual Process: Structure and Anti-Structure.
Hunter, Gillespie and Chen (2019), Urban nature experiences reduce stress in the context of daily life based on salivary biomarkers. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 722.
Atchley, Strayer and Atchley (2012), Creativity in the wild: improving creative reasoning through immersion in natural settings. PLOS ONE, 7(12).

quiz.q: Why do retreats take people away?
quiz.a: To step out of usual settings and roles. It is a design idea, not a proven mechanism.

quiz.q: Which part is most often neglected?
quiz.a: The return to ordinary life.

quiz.q: What should the return include?
quiz.a: What people take back, who they tell and what they do in the first week.

openPoints: Antonelli and colleagues (2019): not searched for, cap reached.
van Gennep, The Rites of Passage: not opened. Turner's description names him as the origin of the liminal phase.
The definition of the liminal stage as leaving one role before taking up the next is the standard reading but is not spelled out in the publisher's description.
The claim that the return is the part most often neglected has no checked source. Research on transfer of training is the place to look.
checkFindings: Turner (1969) confirmed on the Routledge page. The description says Turner extends van Gennep's liminal phase of rites of passage and develops the idea of communitas. That supports the page's cautious sentence about anthropologists and thresholds.

Build note followed. The SPIRIT framework is not used. Of the three studies the note names, Hunter (2019) and Atchley (2012) were read on PubMed Central and are added with their limits. Antonelli (2019) was not reached.

Hunter and colleagues: 36 participants with usable data, mostly women, self-selected, no control group, chose their own time and place. The page gives the 20 to 30 minute finding without the per-hour percentages.

Atchley and colleagues: 56 hikers, 24 tested before the trip and 32 on the trip, different people in each group. The authors report about a 50% higher score and say they cannot tell nature from time away from technology. The paper says four days in the abstract and three in one later section, so the page says 'about four days'.
No study block: no single study carries this topic.
topics.tierReason: Liminality is an anthropological idea borrowed as a design principle, and the two nature studies read are small, uncontrolled and do not test retreats or the return to work.

topics.title: Write the duty-of-care plan first
topics.source: Skills building: Transformational Experiences, topic TX.5

situation.text: The plan is full of powerful exercises. Nobody has written down what happens if someone is distressed.

items: Write the duty-of-care plan before the programme.
Tell participants in advance what is involved, and get consent.
Let people opt out without penalty.
Know your limits and have a route to professional help.
Screen for people the programme does not suit.

Do a risk assessment: identify the hazards, assess the risks, control them, record what you found and review it. Plan for incidents and emergencies, and count participants in when you assess first aid needs.

why.text: Intense experiences can bring distress to the surface. The facilitator's first duty is participant wellbeing. A trainer is not a therapist.
The intensity that makes change possible carries real risk.

In Great Britain, the Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974 puts duties on employers towards their employees and towards members of the public. It also covers self-employed people whose work could put others at risk. HSE's guidance for events says the organiser has prime responsibility for the health and safety of workers, contractors and the people attending, and that planning should be in proportion to the scale and risk of the event. HSE guidance covers Great Britain. This page is general information, not legal advice.

items.title: Informed consent
items.text: People know what they are joining.

try.text: Draft the duty-of-care protocol for an intensive programme: consent, limits and a referral route.

try.title: Illustration: one page before the programme
try.text: The plan names who is in charge of safety, lists each exercise with its risks and its opt-out, gives the nearest hospital and the venue's emergency contact, says who sits with a distressed participant, and lists the helplines and services the team will point people to.

items: Do not create drama for effect.
Check your insurance and legal duties.
Look after the facilitators too.

HSE's page on the Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974 says the Act sets duties for employers towards employees and members of the public, and for certain self-employed people towards themselves and others. HSE's self-employed guidance says the law applies if you employ anyone or your work poses a potential risk to the health and safety of others. A paragraph was added to why.

HSE risk assessment guidance (updated 24 March 2025) gives five steps: identify hazards, assess the risks, control the risks, record your findings, review the controls. Employers with five or more staff must write down significant findings. A step was added to do.

HSE event safety guidance says organisers have prime responsibility for the health and safety of workers, the public attending and contractors, that planning should be proportionate to scale and risk (page updated 11 October 2024), that organisers must have plans to respond to incidents and emergencies, and that HSE strongly recommends including the visiting public in the first aid assessment (page updated 20 January 2026).

HSE's mental health page (updated 22 April 2025) says work-related mental health risks should be assessed like other hazards. It concerns employees, which matters when participants are the client's staff and for the facilitators themselves.
A not-legal-advice note was added because the draft had none.

topics.title: Bring play into a retreat without losing the point

situation.text: The retreat has a games evening that people either love or dread.

items: Give each playful activity a purpose tied to the retreat's aim.
Place lighter play early to build trust, and deeper work later.
Offer levels of involvement.
Debrief while it is fresh.
Leave free time. Not everything needs a facilitator.

why.text: A residential setting gives time and distance from work, which makes play easier. Shared play may help people get to know each other faster.
It can also exclude. Physical challenges, alcohol and late nights leave some people out, and work against sleep.

items.title: Levels
items.text: Let people choose how far to join.

try.text: Review one retreat evening. Say what each activity is for and who it might leave out.

try.title: Illustration: a games evening with levels
try.text: The evening has a quiz table, a building challenge and a quiet corner with board games. People move between them or watch. It ends at nine, there are good soft drinks, and next morning each team names one thing it noticed about how it worked together.

items: Do not build social time around alcohol.
Check physical activities with a risk assessment.
Forced disclosure dressed as a game is a breach of care.

parts.title: Win and scope the work
parts.summary: Who buys training, the brief, the price, the proposal and what success means.

topics.title: Know who buys training, and what they are buying
topics.theory: The learning and development industry: roles, budgets and buyers

situation.text: You have a good course and no idea who in a company would pay for it.

items: Find out who holds the budget: the learning team, a business unit, or HR.
Find out who uses the result: the learners' managers.
Ask what they are buying: a skill, a compliance record, an event, or a change in results.
Learn their planning year and how they buy.
Speak to the person with the problem as well as the person who signs.

why.text: In most organisations the buyer, the sponsor and the learner are different people with different aims. A learning team often buys on behalf of a business unit that has the real problem.
What is being bought shapes what counts as success. A team buying a record of attendance wants something different from a director buying a change in performance.

The CIPD's Learning at work 2023 survey gives a UK view of the people who buy. It reported that learning budgets and headcount had recovered, and that 53% of learning staff said their team's workload had grown. Survey figures describe the people who answered. They do not measure the whole market.

try.text: For one prospective client, name the buyer, the sponsor and the learner, and what each wants.

try.title: Three people, three aims
try.text: Illustration. A learning manager wants a course that fits the budget and the calendar. The sales director wants fewer lost deals. The sales staff want to get through the day without role play. You write down all three before you propose anything.

items: Industry reports are written by bodies with something to sell. Read them critically.
Budgets are set months ahead.
Procurement rules can exclude small suppliers. Ask early.

topics.title: Sell and run a public course
topics.theory: Open courses where the learner is the buyer: motivation, pricing, drop-out and proof of value

situation.text: You plan an open course that individuals pay for themselves. No employer is sending them.

items: Describe who it is for and what they will be able to do, in their words.
Price it against what they would otherwise spend, and test the price.
Make joining easy and the first session rewarding.
Build in contact and deadlines to keep people.
Say plainly what you do not promise.
Collect evidence of results, with consent.

why.text: When the learner is the buyer, they chose to come and they bear the cost. Motivation is usually higher at the start. Nobody at work is making them finish, so drop-out is the main risk.

There is no manager to reinforce the learning, so follow-up and peer contact have to be part of the product. Research on public, self-funded courses is thinner than on workplace training, and this page rests on practice.

items.title: Follow-up is yours
items.text: There is no manager to do it.

try.text: Write the course page for one open course: who it is for, what they will be able to do, what you do not promise.

try.title: A course page that says what it will not do
try.text: Illustration. Before: "Become a confident public speaker in a weekend." After: "For people who present at work a few times a year. You will plan and give two short talks and get feedback on each. We do not promise to remove nerves."

items: Consumer law gives buyers rights, including on cancellation. This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.
Testimonials and reviews must be genuine. Fake reviews, and paid reviews that hide the payment, have been banned in consumer sales since 6 April 2025. Ask permission before you use anyone's words.
A low price attracts people who do not turn up.
If you show reviews on your own site, you are expected to take reasonable steps to keep fake ones out and to avoid showing only the good ones.

topics.title: Run a discovery conversation with a client

situation.text: A prospective client says, "We need a two-day leadership course. What would you charge?"

items: Ask what is happening that made them call.
Ask what they want to be different, and how they would know.
Ask what has been tried.
Ask who else has a view, and whether you can speak to them.
Listen more than you talk.
Play back what you heard and agree the next step.

why.text: A discovery conversation tests the request before you price it. It is the needs analysis done with the client in the room.
Ask about the situation and what it is costing them before you say anything about your product.

The CIPD's Learning at work 2023 survey found that 57% of learning practitioners said they identify the performance issue before recommending a solution, up from 32% in 2021. The CIPD Profession Map asks people professionals to question a problem to find its underlying causes and to listen carefully to a range of views.

try.text: Write eight questions for a first client conversation. None may mention your course.

try.title: The same call, two ways
try.text: Illustration. Before: "Two days for twelve people would be this much." After: "I can give you a range today. First, what has happened that made leadership the priority now, and what would you want to see change by spring?"

items: Clients may want a price before a conversation. Give a range and ask for thirty minutes.
Do not diagnose in the first five minutes.
Free consulting has a limit. Know yours.

topics.title: Scope and price the work so it can succeed

situation.text: You quote a day rate for delivery. Design, travel, follow-up and three rounds of changes come out of your own time.

items: List everything the work includes: discovery, design, materials, delivery, follow-up, evaluation.
Estimate the time for each.
State what is not included, and what changes cost.
Price the whole piece of work.
Include what it needs to succeed: manager briefing, follow-up.
Put it in writing.

why.text: Scope is the agreement about what will and will not be done. Unclear scope is a common cause of work that loses money or disappoints.
A price that leaves out follow-up sells an event that is likely to fade. Pricing figures vary widely by market and are not given here.

One well-known view, from the consultant Alan Weiss, is to set the fee by the value of the result to the client and not by the time you spend. He argues against billing by the day. Track your hours anyway so you know what the work costs you.

try.text: Take a past project. List every hour you spent. Compare it with what you charged for.

try.title: One line becomes six
try.text: Illustration. Before: "One day of delivery at my day rate." After: a single price that lists discovery calls, design, materials, the delivery day, a manager briefing and a follow-up session, and says that extra rounds of changes are charged for.

items: Discounting teaches the client your price was soft.
Design usually takes longer than delivery, often much longer. Track your own hours.
Agree expenses and cancellation terms.
