topics.title: Write a proposal the client can say yes to

situation.text: Your proposal opens with three pages about your company.

items: Open with the client's situation in their words.
State the result they want.
Describe what you will do, in steps.
Say what you need from them.
Give the price, dates and terms.
Offer two or three options.
Keep it short.

why.text: A proposal confirms a conversation. It should show you understood the problem before it describes the solution.
Options let the client choose how much to buy, not whether to buy.

try.text: Rewrite the first page of a proposal so the client's problem appears before your name.

try.title: The first paragraph
try.text: Illustration. Before: "Founded in 2015, we are a leading provider of leadership training." After: "You told us new team leaders are promoted for technical skill and then avoid hard conversations. You want them holding those conversations within three months."

items: Do not promise outcomes you cannot influence.
A proposal sent without a conversation is a weak bet. Talk first.
A client may rely on what your proposal says. Write only what you can deliver, and have your terms checked by someone qualified.

topics.title: Agree what success looks like before you start

situation.text: Three months in, the client says, "This is not what we expected."

items: Before you start, write down what success looks like and how it will be judged.
Say what training can and cannot change.
Name what the client must do.
Agree check-in points.
Raise problems early.
Record changes to the brief.

why.text: Disappointment often comes from expectations that were never stated. Writing them down exposes differences while they are cheap to fix.
Being clear about limits is part of the service. A client who expected a course to fix a management problem will blame the course.
Do not assume the client already has a way to judge success. In the CIPD's Learning at work 2023 survey, almost half of respondents lacked a systematic approach to evaluating learning.

items.title: Write it down
items.text: What success is, and how judged.

try.text: For one project, write three lines: what success is, what you cannot promise, what the client must do.

try.title: Three lines, agreed in week one
try.text: Illustration. Success: team leaders hold a monthly one-to-one with each person, checked by a short staff survey. We cannot promise: lower staff turnover. You will: give managers one hour to brief their people before the course.

items: Different people in the client hold different expectations.
Silence is not agreement.
Changes to the brief need a change to the price or the dates.

topics.title: Market your training without overclaiming

situation.text: A competitor's website promises "guaranteed transformation" and "brain-based learning that boosts retention by 80%".

items: Describe what people will do and be able to do.
Quote only results you can evidence.
Name the source of any figure.
Avoid brain language you cannot support.
Use real cases, with consent.
Say who it is not for.

why.text: Honest marketing is a commercial advantage with informed buyers and an ethical duty with all of them. The tests are the ones you apply to any learning claim.

In the UK, the CAP Code says marketing must not materially mislead. You must hold documentary evidence for any objective claim before you publish it, and you must not overstate what a product can do. This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.
A happy customer's words are not evidence that a course works. ASA advice says testimonials alone are unlikely to be enough to support a factual claim.

try.text: Audit your own website for claims. For each, write the evidence or remove it.

try.title: One claim, rewritten
try.text: Illustration. Before: "Our brain-based method boosts retention by 80%." After: "The course uses spaced practice and regular quizzing. Both are well supported by research on memory. We do not quote a retention figure because we have not measured one."

items: A statistic repeated across the industry may have no source.
Testimonials must be genuine. Keep proof that each one is real, keep the person's contact details, and ask their permission. A factual claim inside a testimonial still needs evidence.
"Evidence-based" is itself a claim.
Fake reviews, and paid reviews that hide the payment, have been banned in sales to consumers since 6 April 2025. Take care with the word "guarantee" too. The CAP Code has rules on it.

topics.title: Know the UK bodies and rules you work under
topics.theory: UK context: CIPD, LPI, Skills England, accessibility and data law

situation.text: A client asks whether you are "accredited" and whether the course meets "the regulations".

items: Know the professional bodies: CIPD for people professionals, the Learning and Performance Institute for learning practitioners.
Know who oversees skills policy in England.
Know the laws that touch your work: equality, data protection, health and safety, consumer rights.
Check each on its official site before you rely on it.
Say what you are and are not accredited for.

why.text: Training in the UK is mostly unregulated. Anyone can call themselves a trainer. Professional bodies offer membership, qualifications, accreditation and published standards. The CIPD has its Profession Map, which includes learning and development as a specialist area. The Learning and Performance Institute has its Capability Map. Some fields have regulators of their own.

The laws that matter most are general ones. Data protection law is the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, both amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The ICO says all of that Act's data protection changes were in force by 19 June 2026. One of them applies to every organisation that handles personal data: give people a clear way to complain and acknowledge a complaint within 30 days. Details change, so check the official page.

Skills England oversees apprenticeship standards in England. It became an executive agency on 2 June 2025 and took on the work of the Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education. It is now sponsored by the Department for Work and Pensions. The growth and skills levy builds on the apprenticeship levy. Since 1 August 2026 levy funds can pay for apprenticeships, foundation apprenticeships and short apprenticeship units in a set list of subjects. They do not pay for training in general.

Public sector clients must make their websites, apps, intranets and documents meet WCAG 2.2 level AA under the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018. They stay responsible when they buy from a supplier, so expect the requirement in your contract. The government's guidance also says every UK service provider has a duty under the Equality Act 2010 to consider reasonable adjustments for disabled people.

try.text: List the bodies and laws that apply to your next project. Find the official page for each.

try.title: Answering the accreditation question
try.text: Illustration. Before: "Yes, we are fully accredited." After: "Training is not a licensed profession here. I hold a CIPD Level 5 diploma and I am a member of a professional body. The course itself is not accredited by anyone. Here is how we handle data and accessibility."

items: This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.
Regulated sectors such as health, finance and aviation have their own training rules.
Do not claim an accreditation you do not hold.

From 1 August 2026 funds can be spent on apprenticeships, foundation apprenticeships and apprenticeship units. The same page says funding was withdrawn in September 2026 from 16 apprenticeship standards, three of them in leadership and management.

topics.title: Put the terms in writing
topics.theory: Contracts: who owns the materials, cancellation and liability

situation.text: You agree a programme by email. The client then cancels two days before, and shares your slides across the company.

items: Use a written agreement for every job.
Say who owns the materials and what the client may do with them.
Set cancellation and postponement terms.
Set payment terms.
State the limits of your liability and hold suitable insurance.
Cover confidentiality and data.

why.text: A written agreement protects both sides by settling the awkward questions before they arise. The ones that cause most trouble are ownership of materials, cancellation and payment.

By default, the person who creates a work is the first owner of the copyright. If you are a freelancer, the materials you make for a client stay yours unless you agree otherwise in writing. Staff are different. An employer owns what an employee makes as part of the job. A transfer of copyright needs a written, signed contract. Without one, the client may have only a limited right to use the work for the purpose it was made for. Get the agreement checked.

try.text: List the six points above. For your last job, mark which were written down.

try.title: One clause that prevents an argument
try.text: Illustration. Before: nothing in writing about the slides. After: "The trainer keeps copyright in all course materials. The client may copy them for its own staff. It may not pass them to other organisations or change them without written consent."

items: This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.
A client's standard terms may claim ownership of everything you make.
Insurers set conditions. Read them.
If you want the client to use your materials but not own them, give a licence that says who may use them, for what and for how long.

topics.title: Plan your own qualifications

situation.text: You have years of practice and no piece of paper. A tender asks for "a recognised training qualification".

items: List what clients in your market ask for.
Look at the routes: professional body qualifications, teaching awards, facilitation and coaching credentials.
Check the level, cost and time of each on the provider's own site.
Choose for what you will learn as well as the letters.
Keep a record of your development each year.

why.text: A qualification signals a baseline to buyers who cannot judge your work. It does not prove you can run a room.

CIPD offers a Level 3 Foundation Certificate in People Practice, a Level 5 Associate Diploma in Organisational Learning and Development and a Level 7 Advanced Diploma in Strategic Learning and Development. The Learning and Performance Institute offers membership grades, a free skills self-assessment and its own certificates in online facilitation and online learning design. There are also teaching awards for the further education sector, which were not checked for this page. Titles and levels change, so check the provider's site.

The CIPD Level 3 certificate covers people practice as a whole, with learning and development as one part of one unit. The Level 5 and Level 7 diplomas are the specialist learning and development routes. CIPD says the Level 7 diploma typically takes 16 to 24 months.

try.text: Write down three tenders or clients you want. Note what each asks for.

try.title: Reading a tender line
try.text: Illustration. A tender asks for "a recognised training qualification". You ask the buyer what they accept. They name a Level 5 diploma or equivalent experience with references. You now know whether to study, or to gather evidence of work you have already done.

items: Some credentials are sold on prestige and little else.
Experience and evidence of results count with many buyers.
Budget for renewal fees.

parts.title: Set the strategy
parts.summary: Running the strategy workshop and tying training to what the organisation needs.

topics.title: Run a training strategy workshop

situation.text: A client asks you to run a workshop to "set the training strategy" for next year.

items: Before the day, gather the organisation's goals, current training and any data.
Open with what the organisation is trying to do.
Map the gaps between that and what people can do now.
Sort the gaps: training, or something else.
Prioritise with the group.
Agree owners, dates and how success will be judged.
Send a one-page summary within two days.

why.text: A strategy workshop is a facilitated decision, not a presentation. Its output is a short list of priorities that the people in the room own.
The order matters: goals, then gaps, then causes, then priorities. Starting from a list of courses produces a catalogue.

try.text: Draft a half-day agenda for a strategy workshop. Give each block a question and an output.

try.title: One block of the agenda
try.text: Illustration. Block three, 40 minutes. Question: which of these gaps would training fix, and which need something else. Output: two lists on the wall, with one named owner beside each gap.

items: Without the decision-maker in the room, nothing is decided.
Groups list everything. Force a ranking.
A strategy with no budget is a wish.

topics.title: Tie training to what the organisation is trying to do

situation.text: The training plan is a list of popular courses. Nobody can say which business goal each one serves.

items: Get the organisation's goals for the year.
For each goal, ask what people must do differently.
Ask what stops them now.
Plan learning only where skill is the obstacle.
Link each programme to a goal and a measure.
Drop what links to nothing.

why.text: Training earns its budget by helping the organisation do what it is trying to do. The link runs from goal, to behaviour, to the skill behind it.
One practitioner's method starts from a measurable goal and works back to the actions people must take, before any content is chosen.

The link is often weak in practice. In the CIPD's Learning at work 2023 survey, learning practitioners were less likely than in 2021 to agree that their learning strategy supports business priorities. The CIPD Profession Map treats understanding the organisation's strategy and priorities as core knowledge for people professionals.

items.title: Only where skill is the obstacle

try.text: Take a training plan. Write the business goal next to each item, or mark it as an orphan.

try.title: One row of the plan
try.text: Illustration. Before: "Presentation skills, two days, open to all." After: "Goal: win more tenders. Behaviour: bid teams rehearse and answer the buyer's questions directly. Obstacle: no practice, no feedback. Programme: two rehearsal clinics per bid. Measure: tender feedback."

items: Goals change mid-year. Review.
Some training is required by law whatever the goals.
Leaders may not have clear goals. Help them state one.

topics.title: Map roles and skills before you plan courses

situation.text: A client wants a curriculum. Nobody can tell you who does what, or what each role needs to be able to do.

items: Draw how the work flows and who does each part.
List the roles.
For each role, list the tasks and the skills behind them.
Mark where skills are missing or held by one person.
Decide what to build, buy, borrow or redesign.
Then plan learning.

why.text: Training fills gaps in skill. Gaps are visible only against a picture of the roles and the work. Sometimes the answer is to change the role, not to train the person.
This is organisation design at its simplest. Larger redesigns are specialist work.

The CIPD Profession Map describes both halves of this. Organisation design covers who does what and how the work is done. Learning and development includes capability analysis, which means defining the capability needs of people, teams and the organisation.

try.text: For one team, map the work, the roles and the skills. Mark one gap and one single point of failure.

try.title: What the map showed
try.text: Illustration. A finance team of six. The map shows only one person can run the month-end close. The answer is not a course for everyone. It is a written procedure, a second person trained on the job, and one task moved to another role.

items: Job descriptions are often out of date. Ask people what they do.
Mapping can alarm people. Explain why.
Know when to bring in a specialist.

topics.title: Decide what not to train
topics.theory: Prioritising, and when training is the wrong answer

situation.text: The wish list has forty courses and the budget covers eight.

items: Score each request: link to a goal, size of the gap, whether skill is the cause.
Remove requests where training is not the answer, and say what is.
Rank the rest with the sponsor.
Fund the top few properly.
Tell people what was not chosen and why.

why.text: Saying no is part of strategy. Eight programmes done well, with follow-up, do more than forty events.
Requests where skill is not the cause should go back with a different recommendation.

The test of whether skill is the cause comes from performance analysis. Mager and Pipe's method starts by finding why people are not doing what they should, before any fix is chosen. Training is one possible fix among several.

try.text: Take ten training requests. Score each on the three tests. Rank them.

try.title: A request sent back
try.text: Illustration: a manager asks for a time-management course. The request links to a goal and the gap is real, but the cause is two understaffed shifts. You return it with a staffing recommendation and fund the next request on the list.

items: The loudest requester is not the highest priority.
Compliance training may be fixed. Protect the rest.
A no without an alternative is a brush-off.

The original publisher's page could not be found, so the page read is a bookseller record with the book's synopsis. The synopsis supports finding the cause of a performance problem before choosing a fix. The edition number was not stated on the page.

It does not name the author in its text and does not name the behaviour engineering model, so the page makes no claim about that model.

topics.title: Plan the change, not only the course

situation.text: A new system goes live on Monday. Training is scheduled. Nobody has explained why the change is happening.

items: Find out what is changing, for whom, and what they lose.
Make sure leaders have explained why.
Involve the people affected in how it is done.
Train close to when people need it.
Support the first weeks.
Listen for resistance and treat it as information.

why.text: Training is one part of a change. People also need to know why, to see leaders act on it, and to have the means to work the new way.

Kotter's eight steps and Prosci's ADKAR (awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement) are practitioner models. Use them as checklists, not as proven laws. The commonly quoted figure that 70 per cent of change efforts fail has no solid source. A 2011 review of five works that state it found no valid evidence behind it.

why.title: Do 70 per cent of change initiatives really fail?
why.found: Hughes reviewed five published works that state a 70 per cent failure rate for organisational change. He found no valid and reliable empirical evidence behind the figure.
why.means: Leave the 70 per cent figure out of proposals and slides, and question it when a client quotes it.

try.text: For one change, list what people gain, what they lose and what they need besides training.

try.title: Before and after
try.text: Illustration. Before: system training runs three weeks ahead of go-live, with no word from leaders. After: the director explains the reason, two users help shape the roll-out, training runs in go-live week, and floor support covers the first fortnight.

items: Training too early is forgotten by go-live.
Do not quote the 70 per cent figure.
You cannot train people into a change they were not told about.

topics.title: Design a custom course for a client, end to end

situation.text: A client signs off a bespoke course. You have six weeks.

items: Discover: the need, the people, the constraints.
Agree objectives and how success is judged.
Sketch the outline and test it with the client and two learners.
Build a rough version of one section.
Build the rest.
Pilot, and change it.
Deliver, follow up and review.

why.text: A custom course follows the same path as any design, with the client involved at each decision. Showing rough work early is cheaper than a polished surprise.
The stages draw on the earlier topics: needs, objectives, sequencing, materials, delivery, transfer and evaluation.
Working in short rounds with the client is the idea behind the Successive Approximation Model, an iterative alternative to a strict stage-by-stage design process.

try.text: Lay out a six-week plan for a custom one-day course. Mark each point where the client decides something.

try.title: Rough first
try.text: Illustration. Before: five weeks of building, then the client sees a finished deck and asks for a different focus. After: a one-page outline in week one, one rough section in week two, and each client decision dated in the plan.

items: Sign-off by committee is slow. Name one decision-maker.
Client examples make it relevant. Ask for them early.
Leave time to change it after the pilot.

topics.title: Design a custom retreat or offsite for a client

situation.text: A leadership team wants two days away "to bond and think about the future".

items: Agree the one or two outcomes the sponsor wants.
Find out who is coming and what is unsaid between them.
Choose a venue for the work, not the brochure.
Design the arc: arrive, open up, do the hard work, decide, close.
Protect sleep and free time.
Write the duty-of-care plan.
Design the first week back.

why.text: An offsite takes people out of routine, which makes some conversations possible. It also costs a great deal of senior time, so the purpose has to justify it.
The risks are the ones covered in the retreat topics: intensity without follow-up, pressure to disclose, and long days.

try.text: Sketch a two-day offsite: outcomes, the arc of each day, and what happens in the first week back.

try.title: From bonding to an outcome

items: "Bonding" is not an outcome. Ask what would be different.
Activities that exclude some people damage the group.
Check insurance, access and dietary needs.

parts.title: Run the programme

topics.title: Plan the programme: scope, roles, risks and dates

situation.text: The programme has twelve cohorts, four trainers and three venues. It lives in your head.

items: Write the scope: what is in and out.
List the pieces of work and who owns each.
Put them in order with dates.
List the risks and what you would do about each.
Agree how and when you report.
Keep one plan that everyone can see.

why.text: A programme is a set of related projects and other work, managed together towards a shared aim. Missed handoffs and unclear ownership are common ways for it to go wrong.
The basics are the same in every method: scope, owners, dates, risks and a single shared plan.

try.text: For one programme, write the scope in five lines and name an owner for each piece of work.

try.title: Out of your head
try.text: Illustration. Before: twelve cohorts, four trainers and three venues held in memory and email. After: a one-page scope, a list of work with one owner each, dates with dependencies marked, and five risks with a response, all in one shared plan.

items: A plan nobody updates is fiction.
Dependencies are a common cause of delay. Mark them.
Too much method for a small job wastes time.
Once the plan is agreed, decide who can approve a change to scope or dates. Record each change.

topics.title: Plan the logistics and assess the risks
topics.theory: Event logistics, venue, insurance and risk assessment

situation.text: The venue is booked. Nobody has asked about access, the fire procedure or what happens if a trainer is ill.

items: Visit or get a full description of the venue.
Check access, travel, food, equipment and connectivity.
Write a risk assessment: what could cause harm, to whom, how likely and how serious, and what you will do.
Check insurance for the event and the activities.
Name who is in charge on the day.
Have a back-up for the trainer and the technology.

why.text: Logistics decide whether people can attend and attend to the content. A risk assessment means identifying what could cause harm, judging how likely and how serious it is, and deciding what you will do about it. Employers with five or more employees must record the significant findings. Write yours down whatever your size, so that others can follow it.
Employers and organisers have legal duties for health and safety. What applies depends on the event. This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.

Employers' liability insurance is required by law for most employers, with cover of at least £5 million from an authorised insurer. Venues and clients often set their own insurance conditions as well. Read the contract and ask your insurer what the activities need. If you are self-employed with no staff, health and safety law still applies where your work could put other people at risk.

try.text: For your next event, write five risks, each with a likelihood and a response.

try.title: One risk, written down
try.text: Illustration: 'Trainer ill on the day. Unlikely, serious. Response: a second trainer holds the slides and plan, and the client has both mobile numbers.' Four more lines like this make a usable assessment for a classroom day.

items: Outdoor and physical activities need their own assessment and a qualified provider.
Ask about dietary and access needs early.
Check cancellation terms with the venue.
Review the assessment when something changes, such as the venue, the group or the activity.

topics.title: Brief and check the people you bring in

situation.text: You win more work than you can deliver and bring in an associate you met once.

items: Watch them work, or see evidence, before you put them in front of a client.
Brief them on the client, the aims and the reasons behind the design.
Agree what may be adapted and what may not.
Put terms in writing: fees, materials, confidentiality, contact with the client.
Get feedback after each delivery.

why.text: An associate delivers under your name. The client judges you by them.
The same holds for venues, caterers and activity providers. Briefing and checking take time and cost less than a poor day.

try.text: Write a one-page brief for an associate on one session: aims, audience, what is fixed, what is flexible.

try.title: A brief that explains why
try.text: Illustration. Before: the associate gets the slides the night before. After: a one-page brief gives the client's aim, the reason for each activity, what is fixed and what can flex. You observe the first delivery and swap notes afterwards.

items: This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.

Employment status decides how an associate is taxed. If they work through their own limited company, the off-payroll working rules (IR35) may apply. Outside the public sector, a small client leaves the status decision to the associate's company. Larger clients decide it themselves. HMRC's Check Employment Status for Tax tool gives its view.
Activity providers need their own insurance and qualifications.

Work with children or with adults in care settings may call for a DBS check. Anyone can be asked for a basic check. Standard and enhanced checks are only for roles the law makes eligible. Since January 2026 a self-employed person in an eligible role can apply for an enhanced check through an umbrella body.

topics.title: Run a programme in Google Workspace

situation.text: You run programmes with files across email, a laptop and three people's drives.

items: Create one shared folder per programme, with the same structure each time.
Keep the plan and tracker in a spreadsheet.
Write briefs and session plans in documents, with comments for review.
Use forms for sign-up, needs and feedback.
Put sessions in a shared calendar with joining details.
Set sharing permissions deliberately.

why.text: Google Workspace gives you documents, spreadsheets, forms, a calendar, storage and video calls that work together. Its strength is several people editing the same file.
The method is the same as any programme: one plan, named owners, one place for files. That method carries over if the tool changes.

In Drive you share a file or folder with named people as Viewer, Commenter or Editor, and set general access to Restricted or to anyone with the link. On a work or school account, a shared drive holds files that belong to the team and stay when someone leaves. Forms can send responses to a linked spreadsheet. Comments in Docs can be assigned to a person. A Calendar event can carry a Google Meet link.

items.text: Docs for the words, Forms for the input.

try.text: Build a template folder for a programme: plan, tracker, brief, session plans, forms, materials.

try.text: Illustration. Before: plans in email, slides on a laptop, feedback in someone's personal drive. After: one programme folder with the same six subfolders every time, and the feedback responses kept in a separate folder that only the two people who need them can open.

items: Some clients cannot open outside files. Ask.
Feedback forms hold personal data. A file takes on the access of the folder it sits in, so keep responses in a folder with limited access.
A copy made for each cohort drifts from the master.

topics.title: Run a programme in Notion

situation.text: You want one place for the plan, the sessions, the people and the notes, and a spreadsheet is straining.

items: Make a database of sessions: date, cohort, trainer, venue, status.
Make a database of tasks, linked to sessions.
Add views: a calendar for dates, a board for status, a table for detail.
Keep a page per programme that pulls these together.
Save a database template for a standard session, so each new one starts the same way.
Share the programme page with the client as a guest, with Can view access.

why.text: Notion combines pages with databases that can be linked and shown in different views. That suits a programme, where the same sessions need to be seen by date, by owner and by status.
It takes more set-up than a spreadsheet and some clients will not use it. A guest needs their own Notion account to open a page you share with them.

A relation property links items in one database to items in another, which is how tasks attach to sessions. Notion offers table, board, calendar, timeline, list, gallery and chart layouts, and each view keeps its own filters and sorts. The calendar layout needs a date property.

items.title: A template
items.text: Start each session the same way.

try.text: Build a sessions database with five properties and three views.

try.title: One list, three ways to see it
try.text: Illustration: twelve sessions are entered once. You look at them by date when you book rooms, by status in the weekly check, and as a full table when you prepare the client report.

items: An elaborate workspace becomes a hobby. Keep it plain.
Check where data is stored against your client's rules.
Have a way to export. Notion exports pages and databases as PDF, HTML, or Markdown and CSV.
The features named here were checked against the product help pages on 17 November 2026. Tools change, and each workspace has a limit on guests, so check before you plan around one.

quiz.q: What two databases does a programme need?
quiz.a: Sessions and tasks, linked.

quiz.a: The same sessions can be seen by date, owner or status.

quiz.q: What is the cost compared with a spreadsheet?

openPoints: Where Notion stores data: not checked. The watch item telling the reader to check this against the client's rules is kept as it makes no factual claim.
'Keep a page per programme that pulls these together': the feature that shows an existing database on another page was not checked on a help page. The step is left in general words.
Reusing a whole programme set-up, for example by duplicating a page: not checked.
Guest limits by plan: the help page says a limit exists but gives no number.
checkFindings: Build note followed: features researched, a checked-on date added to the watch part, and the method kept ahead of the tool.
Databases with properties, and calendar, board and table views: confirmed. Notion's page lists seven layouts in all. The same database can be shown in several views, each with its own settings.
Linking tasks to sessions: confirmed as the relation property. Rollups exist and summarise related pages. Rollups are not named on the page.

Correction: 'Turn the set-up into a template'. Notion's database templates work only inside the database where they are made. The step now describes a template for a standard session. Reusing a whole programme set-up was not confirmed on a help page.

Correction: 'Share a read-only view with the client'. Notion shares pages, and the levels are Full access, Can edit, Can comment and Can view (plus two database-only levels). Outside people are guests and need a Notion account. A public web link is the alternative for viewing without an account. Workspaces have a guest limit, with the number not stated on the page read.
Export: PDF, HTML, and Markdown and CSV confirmed, for a page, a database or the whole workspace. PDF export with subpages needs a Business or Enterprise plan. Guests need Full access to export.
The stale sentence saying the features had not been checked was removed.

topics.title: Collect only the learner data you need
topics.theory: Learner data and privacy under UK law

situation.text: The sign-up form asks for date of birth, home address and "any medical conditions".

items: List what you need to run the programme, and collect only that.
Tell people what you collect, why, and how long you keep it.
Take extra care with health and similar information.
Limit who can see it.
Delete or anonymise it when you no longer need it.
Agree with the client who is responsible for what.

why.text: UK data protection law sets principles that include collecting only what is needed, using it for a stated purpose and keeping it no longer than necessary. You also need a lawful basis before you collect anything, and your privacy information must state it. Some kinds of information, called special category data, get extra protection. Health data is one of them.
Feedback, assessment results and attendance are personal data. This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.

The law is the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amended both and did not replace them. Among its changes, you must give people a way to complain to you about how you use their data and acknowledge a complaint within 30 days. The law sets no fixed retention periods. You decide how long you need the data and must be able to justify it.

items.title: Delete
items.text: When you no longer need it.

try.text: Take one of your forms. For each field, write why you need it, or remove it.

try.title: A sign-up form, trimmed
try.text: Illustration. Before: name, date of birth, home address, 'any medical conditions'. After: name, work email, and 'Is there anything we can do to help you take part?' A short note says why each is asked and when it will be deleted.

items: Access needs can be asked without asking for a diagnosis.
Sharing individual results with managers needs a lawful basis. Tell people before they take part.
A breach that is likely to put people at risk must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours of your becoming aware of it. Keep a record of every breach.
A tool or supplier outside the UK that can reach learner data may count as an international transfer, which has its own rules. Ask where the data is held.

quiz.q: How much learner data should you collect?
quiz.a: Only what you need to run the programme.

quiz.q: What must you tell people?
quiz.a: What you collect, why, and how long you keep it.

quiz.q: Are feedback and assessment results personal data?
quiz.a: Yes.

topics.tierReason: Legal and regulatory topic. The practice follows ICO guidance on UK data protection law.
openPoints: The ICO pages on the principles, data minimisation and storage limitation carry a notice that they are under review because of the 2025 Act and may change. Recheck them.
'Agree with the client who is responsible for what' refers to controller and processor roles. The ICO page on controllers and processors was not opened, so the page does not use those terms.

Whether asking about access needs without a diagnosis avoids collecting health data was not checked. An answer about adjustments can still reveal health information, so treat those answers with the same care.

The ICO's brief guide to international transfers did not mention the 2025 Act when read. The statement that the Act reworded the test comes from the ICO's page on what the Act means for organisations.
checkFindings: The buildNote asks for a qualified source and a clear not-legal-advice note. Eight ICO pages now support the topic, and the existing not-legal-advice note is kept unchanged.

Lawful basis was missing from the topic. The ICO now lists seven lawful bases, including recognised legitimate interests, which the 2025 Act added. The page now says a lawful basis is needed before collecting and must be stated in privacy information. It does not list the bases.
The breach item was vague. It now gives the ICO's rule: report notifiable breaches within 72 hours and record all breaches.
'Delete' is widened to 'delete or anonymise', as the ICO allows either. The 'remember' card with the title 'Delete' is left as it is.

Added that the 2025 Act amends and does not replace the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, and its new duty to handle data protection complaints (acknowledge within 30 days). The ICO's update of 19 June 2026 says all the Act's data protection provisions are in force.

Added a watch item on international transfers. The ICO says giving an organisation outside the UK access to personal data counts as a transfer, even when small or infrequent. It also says the 2025 Act reworded the transfer test without materially changing what you can do.
The ICO special category page (updated October 2026 for the 2025 Act) confirms health data is special category and needs an Article 9 condition as well as a lawful basis.
Data minimisation and storage limitation match the draft. The ICO adds that the law sets no specific time limits, which is now on the page.

topics.title: Gather proof with consent
topics.theory: Case studies and testimonials, gathered honestly

situation.text: You want a case study for your website. The programme went well and the client is pleased.

items: Ask permission in writing, from the organisation and from anyone named or quoted.
Use their words and do not improve them.
Report what happened, including the limits.
Claim contribution, not sole cause.
Let them see it before it is published.
Remove it if they ask.

why.text: A case study is evidence only if it is true and typical of what you say it shows. A hand-picked success presented as the norm misleads.
Consent protects the people involved and your relationship with the client.

UK advertising rules say the same. Under the CAP Code you must hold evidence that a testimonial is genuine, contact details for whoever gave it, and their permission to use it. A testimonial must not be edited or taken out of context in a way that misleads.

try.text: Draft a consent request for a case study. Say what you will publish, where, and how to withdraw.

try.title: A quote from a feedback form
try.text: Illustration. Before: a line from an anonymous feedback form goes on the homepage. After: you email the person, show the exact quote and where it will appear, get a yes in writing, and file that email.

items: This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.
Ask permission before you use photographs of people in your marketing.
A quote given in a feedback form was not given for marketing.

Fake consumer reviews, and reviews that hide a reward, have been banned under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 since April 2025. Showing only the positive reviews can also mislead. If you reward someone for a review, say so.

quiz.q: What do you need before publishing a case study?
quiz.a: Written permission from the organisation and anyone named or quoted.

quiz.q: What should you claim?
quiz.a: Contribution, not sole cause.

quiz.q: What makes a case study evidence?
quiz.a: It is true, and typical of what you say it shows.

topics.tierReason: Legal and business practice topic. The consent and honesty steps follow the CAP Code and consumer law guidance, not experimental tests.
openPoints: Brinkerhoff, The Success Case Method (Berrett-Koehler): not found or opened. The shared web search allowance for this session ran out part way through, and pages can only be opened here after a search has returned them. Note that the method studies the most and least successful cases on purpose, so it sits a little awkwardly beside the topic's 'typical' test. Confirm before listing it.

The 2024 Act's review rules are framed around consumers. How far they reach a trainer who sells only to organisations was not settled by the pages read. The CAP Code rules on testimonials apply to marketing in general.
Data protection rules on using named quotes and photographs in marketing (ICO) were not checked for this topic. The ASA advice says data protection duties apply when seeking permission.
checkFindings: ASA and CAP advice (page dated 21 September 2026) confirms the topic's core steps. Rule 3.47 requires evidence that a testimonial is genuine and contact details for the giver. Rule 3.50 requires permission. Rule 3.48 says it must relate to the product, and rule 3.49 says claims in it must not mislead. Added to 'why'.
'Use their words and do not improve them' matches the ASA advice that a testimonial must reflect what the person said and must not be edited misleadingly.

The fake-review ban is in paragraph 13 of Schedule 20 to the 2024 Act, in force from 6 April 2025. It covers fake consumer reviews, concealed incentivised reviews, and publishing reviews in a misleading way, such as showing only the positive ones. The CMA guidance says it reaches reviews a trader publishes on its own site. Added as a watch item.
CAP Code rules 3.45 and 3.46 now mirror this: say when a review was incentivised, and do not publish reviews in a misleading way.
'Photographs of people need consent' was stated as a rule with no source. Reworded as practice.
The not-legal-advice note is kept unchanged.

topics.title: Close out and hand over
topics.theory: Closing a programme and keeping the lessons

situation.text: The last session ends. Everyone moves on, and the same mistakes appear in the next programme.

items: Hold a review with the client and the team.
Ask what worked, what did not, and what to change.
Report results against what was agreed.
Hand over materials, data and open actions, with owners.
File the final versions.
Agree any follow-up and who does it.
Thank people.

why.text: Closing well makes sure the organisation keeps what it paid for and that you learn from the work. Without a review, experience is not turned into improvement.
A structured review after a project is a form of debrief.

why.title: Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 46 samples compared people and teams who held debriefs with controls who did not. Debriefs improved later performance by roughly 20 to 25 per cent (d = 0.67), with similar results for teams and individuals.
why.means: Hold a structured review that looks at what happened and what to change, and keep it about learning, not blame.

try.text: Write a one-page close-out for a finished programme: results, lessons, handover.

try.title: A one-page close-out
try.text: Illustration. Results against the three agreed measures. Three lessons, each with an owner. Handover: final materials filed, attendance data passed to the client, learner feedback deleted on a stated date. One follow-up session, dated and owned.

items: A review that looks for blame teaches nothing.
Delete learner data you no longer need.
Follow-up promised at close-out needs a date.
Do not save every lesson for the end. Note lessons as the programme runs and give each one an owner.

deeper.text: Every link was opened on 17 November 2026 and supports what this page says. Papers were read in summary, not in full. Books were checked from the publisher's description.

topics.bodyStatus: 3 sources checked on 17 November 2026. Some points still to check.

quiz.q: What three questions does the review ask?
quiz.a: What worked, what did not, and what to change.

quiz.q: What do you hand over?
quiz.a: Materials, data and open actions, with owners.

quiz.q: Why review at all?
quiz.a: So experience is turned into improvement.

topics.tierReason: Close-out and handover are project management practice. The review step has indirect support from a meta-analysis of debriefs, which did not study programme close-outs.
openPoints: The PubMed and journal pages for Tannenbaum and Cerasoli would not load from this session. The abstract was read on the Epistemonikos index record and in a copy of the article hosted by the Center for Evidence-Based Management, and both agree. The link given is the PubMed record returned by search. Open it once to confirm before publishing.
Association for Project Management, Body of Knowledge: not opened. The Teal Book stands in for closure and lessons learned.
checkFindings: Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013) confirmed: 46 samples, debrief compared with no-debrief controls, d = 0.67, which the authors put at about 20 to 25 per cent. The studies were of after-action reviews and debriefs after tasks, often in simulations. They were not of programme close-outs, so the topic is rated D and the page should not claim the figure for close-out reviews.

The Teal Book closure guidance matches the 'do' steps: confirm what was delivered, hand ongoing risks, issues and actions to a named authority that accepts them, record lessons, and archive records in line with the retention policy.

The Teal Book says lessons should be captured throughout the work, not only at the end, and that people must be able to raise them without fear of blame. The first point was missing and is added as a watch item. The second supports the existing blame warning.
No text needed correcting.
